nodes.name: Three geographically separated academies
nodes.note: Alexandria (dry, preserves papyrus), a western site, an eastern site. The Third Century Crisis will destroy at least one. Redundancy is the only defence and it is not optional. CALENDAR FLOOR is set by diffusion, not by construction: the economy needs roughly a generation to train the trades, form the capital and build the suppliers. Money cannot buy this down. THE STATE WILL ACTIVELY RESIST THIS. A large private association operating across several provinces is precisely what Roman government fears: a faction. Trajan refuses Pliny even a licensed fire brigade at Nicomedia for this reason (Ep. 10.34). You need senatorial or imperial cover before you attempt it, and you should site the three houses under three different patrons so that it does not look like one organisation.

nodes.name: Aerial bombing
nodes.note: Drop bombs from an aircraft onto targets below. Early bombs were heavy artillery shells with impact fuses. Later, purpose-designed bombs with light cases and heavy charges. Extremely dangerous for the pilot (instability, wind drift, primitive aiming). Devastatingly effective against stationary targets. The State will demand this.

nodes.name: Aerial photography
nodes.note: Mount a camera on an aircraft and photograph the ground below. Vertical photographs from height show cities, fields, fortifications with complete clarity and no perspective distortion. Absolutely invaluable for military reconnaissance and mapping. The camera must be light and the aircraft must be stable.

nodes.name: Aerial reconnaissance
nodes.note: An aircraft with a trained observer flies over enemy territory, notes positions of troops and defenses, and reports back. The observer is fast, covering in hours what a scout takes weeks to do. The State will fund this immediately. Requires pilot and observer to work in concert and to return safely.

nodes.name: Aerodrome (landing field)
nodes.note: An open field of level ground, grass or gravel, at least 500 meters long and 100 meters wide. Aircraft need room to take off into wind and to land without hitting obstacles. A brick or gravel surface prevents mud. Early aerodromes were called flying grounds. They must be maintained and guarded.

nodes.name: Cambered aerofoil section
nodes.note: Cayley's central discovery: a curved (cambered) plate lifts far better than a flat plate at the same angle of attack. The reason is non-obvious and requires experiment: curved surfaces create lower pressure on the back side. A wing with a cambered section can generate substantial lift at shallow angles. This is not merely a geometry trick; it is the foundation of mechanical flight. [AUDIT: capability prerequisite(s) cap_tol_100um were inferred by rome/sim/treetool.py repair, not stated by the author. Treat them as a floor, not a specification.] [AUDIT: State interest and suspicion were unset and have been defaulted from the category.]

nodes.name: Aileron for roll control
nodes.note: Small hinged surfaces at the wing trailing edge, operated by pilot cables. When one goes up, the other goes down, creating differential lift without twisting the main wing. Simpler than warping and less stressful on structure. The aileron is a later refinement, but does the same job. [AUDIT: State interest and suspicion were unset and have been defaulted from the category.]

nodes.name: Airspeed indicator
nodes.note: A pitot tube measures dynamic pressure, which is velocity squared. Display it on a dial. A pilot cannot fly safely by feel; speed is invisible. This is the most important instrument. Early versions used a simple gauge; later ones an anemometer-style rotor. Without it, powered flight is nearly impossible. [AUDIT: capability prerequisite(s) cap_tol_100um were inferred by rome/sim/treetool.py repair, not stated by the author. Treat them as a floor, not a specification.]

nodes.name: Altimeter (aneroid barometer)
nodes.note: An aneroid capsule responds to atmospheric pressure. As altitude increases, pressure drops, the capsule expands slightly, and a mechanical linkage moves a dial. Needs to be calibrated carefully and compensated for temperature. Essential for instrument flying; a pilot cannot judge altitude reliably by eye.

nodes.name: Artificial horizon (gyroscopic)
nodes.note: A rapidly spinning gyroscope maintains its orientation regardless of aircraft motion. Mount a ball or card inside the gyroscope's frame so the pilot sees whether wings are level and nose is up or down. Requires extreme precision in bearing design and high spin speeds. Essential for flying through clouds or darkness.

nodes.name: Autogyro (powered rotor-wing)
nodes.note: A propeller on the nose for forward thrust, and a rotor overhead spinning freely (autogiro: self-turning). As the aircraft moves forward, air flowing through the rotor keeps it spinning, generating lift. Simpler than a helicopter because the rotor needs no engine drive, only control linkages. Can take off and land in short distances. Invented much later than the helicopter.

nodes.name: Ballast and descent control
nodes.note: A balloon achieves altitude by dropping sand ballast and descends by venting gas. These are its only two controls. Altitude is controlled by these two levers exclusively. A ballast bag with a line to the basket lets the aeronaut modulate buoyancy by hand.

nodes.name: Balloon valve
nodes.note: A rope-pulled valve at the balloon's crown vents gas, allowing descent. Without it, a free balloon cannot descend safely. The valve must be airtight when closed but operate smoothly when pulled. A cone of leather over an iron frame, sealing under the weight of gas, is the only control a balloon has besides dropping ballast.

nodes.name: Biplane structure
nodes.note: Two main lifting surfaces separated vertically, braced together with struts and wire cables. This is strong, stiff, and light. All early aircraft were biplanes because they could be built from wood and wire. Drag is slightly higher than a monoplane, but the structural advantage is decisive when materials are weak. [AUDIT: State interest and suspicion were unset and have been defaulted from the category.]

nodes.name: Separation of forces: lift, drag, thrust, control
nodes.note: Cayley's single most important insight: lift and drag are separate. To fly, you need lift enough to equal weight, drag small enough that power can overcome it, thrust strong enough to overcome drag and accelerate, and control to direct the craft. These four are independent problems. Before Cayley, people treated flying as one vague problem. After him, it became engineering. [AUDIT: State interest and suspicion were unset and have been defaulted from the category.]

nodes.name: Coal gas for ballooning
nodes.note: Destructive distillation of coal produces a mixture rich in hydrogen and methane: coal gas. Vastly cheaper than chemical hydrogen. A coal-gas plant can fill balloons continuously. Requires establishing a permanent retort house and managing by-products. The lift is slightly less than pure hydrogen but the cost difference is transformative. [AUDIT: capability prerequisite(s) cap_heat_1300 were inferred by rome/sim/treetool.py repair, not stated by the author. Treat them as a floor, not a specification.]

nodes.name: Compass for navigation
nodes.note: A magnetized iron needle on a silk thread points north. Rome has this. A compass in an aircraft allows navigation when landmarks are obscured. Mount it in a card marked with degrees.

nodes.name: Mounted engine under balloon
nodes.note: Suspend a small petrol engine and propeller in a wooden framework below an elongated envelope. The propeller drives air backward, creating thrust. The envelope provides lift. Requires a very light engine relative to power output and extreme care in weight balance. This is a dirigible, controllable by the pilot.

nodes.name: Elevator for pitch control
nodes.note: A hinged horizontal surface at the tail. When deflected up, the tail rises, and the nose drops. Down elevator raises the nose. This control pitch. It is the most critical: pitch controls altitude, and loss of pitch control is fatal in seconds.

nodes.name: Elongated balloon envelope
nodes.note: Instead of a sphere, make the envelope elongated, pointed at both ends. This shape reduces drag hugely when the balloon drifts. The envelope must still be sealed and symmetrical. This is the form needed for a dirigible: long, narrow, and pointed. [AUDIT: capability prerequisite(s) cap_tol_100um were inferred by rome/sim/treetool.py repair, not stated by the author. Treat them as a floor, not a specification.]

nodes.name: Flying boat
nodes.note: An aircraft whose fuselage is a boat hull. No need for an aerodrome; water launches are smooth and the hull provides flotation. Useful for long-range reconnaissance and transport. Requires excellent hydrodynamic design to minimize drag on the step and excellent corrosion control.

nodes.name: Simple glider
nodes.note: Build a wooden frame, cover with linen, add cambered wings and a tail. Tow it behind a horse or launch it downhill. It will glide and may kill the pilot if control is lost. But gliding flight teaches you what lift feels like, what turns require, and most importantly, what happens when you lose control. This is the cheap school, conducted at non-fatal altitudes.

nodes.name: Goldbeater's skin envelope
nodes.note: Goldbeater's skin, the cleaned intestine of oxen, is the best gas-tight material known. Thin, tough, airtight when sealed with alum and honey. Costs vastly more than linen but holds hydrogen. No rubber exists. This is the single choice for long-endurance gas bags.

nodes.name: Helicopter rotor system
nodes.note: Two or more large aerofoil blades rotating at high speed about a vertical axis. The blades generate lift and must be able to change pitch to control thrust direction. This is mechanically complex and unstable without careful design. A helicopter can hover and land vertically, but is harder to fly than an airplane.

nodes.name: hot_air_balloon
nodes.note: Reference technology already in vocabulary. Hot air balloon relies on density difference: warm air inside the envelope is lighter than ambient air. Foundation for all free balloons.

nodes.name: Hydrogen safety limits
nodes.note: Hydrogen is extraordinarily buoyant but ignites violently with air. A spark, a flame, static electricity, or friction will ignite any mixture between 4 percent and 75 percent hydrogen in air. This is not anecdotal: it is absolute chemistry. You cannot escape it by procedure; you mitigate by isolation (no open flames, grounding, no sparking equipment) and by accept that the risk is real and permanent. Helium does not exist. Coal gas is safer by dilution. [AUDIT: State interest and suspicion were unset and have been defaulted from the category.]

nodes.name: Hydrogen from iron and acid
nodes.note: Dilute sulfuric acid (from distillation) reacts with iron to produce hydrogen gas. Must be generated in sealed vessels with a tube fed to the envelope. Dangerous: hydrogen ignites explosively in air. Filling a balloon takes hours. This is the reliable source until coal gas is available. Rate is limited by acid strength and temperature control. [AUDIT: capability prerequisite(s) cap_tol_100um were inferred by rome/sim/treetool.py repair, not stated by the author. Treat them as a floor, not a specification.]

nodes.name: Jet engine (centrifugal compressor)
nodes.note: A centrifugal compressor spins at thousands of rpm, sucking air in at the center and throwing it outward into a combustion chamber. The challenge is not compression but surviving high temperature. Combustion temperatures are 1000C+, and metal strength drops catastrophically above 600C. Nickel alloys are essential. Even then, turbine blades fail unless cooled internally.

nodes.name: Jet engine principle
nodes.note: Newton's third law: jet out the back, thrust forward. A compressor forces air in, fuel burns in a combustion chamber, hot gas expands and exits at high velocity. No piston engine, no propeller. Much simpler mechanically than reciprocating engines but requires materials that survive continuous high temperature under pressure. [AUDIT: capability prerequisite(s) cap_tol_10um were inferred by rome/sim/treetool.py repair, not stated by the author. Treat them as a floor, not a specification.]

nodes.name: Kite
nodes.note: A framed silk or linen panel tied to cordage is humanity's first controlled aerofoil. Rome has all materials. The curved bow of a framed kite's sides produces lift from asymmetric air flow; this was never trivial to understand. Kites serve tethered observation, signalling and scientific experiment.

nodes.name: Light petrol engine
nodes.note: An aircraft engine must deliver high power per kilogram. This requires aluminium alloys for the crankcase, fine tolerances for bearings and pistons, and very high speeds (1000 rpm+). A typical aero engine in 1910 delivered 10-30 horsepower at 200 kg. This is a metallurgy and precision problem first, a thermodynamics problem second. [AUDIT: State interest and suspicion were unset and have been defaulted from the category.]

nodes.name: Monoplane cantilever wing
nodes.note: One wing, supported only at the fuselage, with no external bracing. This requires a wing strong enough to cantilever its own load in bending. Needs steel or aluminium spars and good materials science to avoid failure. Much less drag than biplane, but much more demanding structurally. Not practical until materials improve. [AUDIT: State interest and suspicion were unset and have been defaulted from the category.]

nodes.name: Tethered observation balloon
nodes.note: A single large envelope of stitched linen or silk, sealed with beeswax, displaces enough warm air to lift a man. Must be tethered to cordage or risk becoming uncontrolled. The State values this for reconnaissance, signalling and military observation. A man in the sky appears miraculous; mitigation is training and controlled small-scale trials, not secrecy.

nodes.name: Parachute
nodes.note: A cone of stiff linen attached to a harness. When opened in free fall, it spreads and catches air, slowing descent to survivable speeds. Requires both invention and extraordinary nerve to test. A man who falls from the sky with a cloth and lives appears either blessed or damned. The key insight is that air resistance, not upward force, saves you. [AUDIT: capability prerequisite(s) cap_tol_100um were inferred by rome/sim/treetool.py repair, not stated by the author. Treat them as a floor, not a specification.]

nodes.name: Pitot tube
nodes.note: A simple tube with an opening into the airstream and a side port. Dynamic pressure at the front is higher than static pressure at the side. The difference is proportional to velocity squared. This is purely fluid statics, not magic.

nodes.name: Power-to-weight ratio and flight
nodes.note: A powered airplane needs enough power to overcome drag at the speed where wings produce lift sufficient for the weight. This requires roughly 5 to 10 kg of aircraft per horsepower. Achieving this needs an engine weighing very little per horsepower and an airframe weighing little. Both are metallurgy and precision problems, not power problems. Weak engines cannot overcome this limit regardless of design. [AUDIT: State interest and suspicion were unset and have been defaulted from the category.]

nodes.name: Powered aeroplane
nodes.note: An aircraft with engine and propeller that achieves sustained powered flight. Requires cambered wings tested in a wind tunnel, three-axis control, a light high-revving engine, and a structure so light it feels built from nothing. Testing kills the pilot. Only possible if all prerequisites are honest. The Wright brothers succeeded because they honored this checklist.

nodes.name: Propeller as rotating aerofoil
nodes.note: A propeller is not a screw pushing against air like a screw in water. It is a rotating wing. Each blade is an aerofoil twisted to increasing angle as you go outward. It generates lift in a rotating plane, and that lift acts as thrust. Design requires aerofoil theory and matching pitch to engine speed. Inefficiency at the tips limits diameter. [AUDIT: State interest and suspicion were unset and have been defaulted from the category.]

nodes.name: Radial engine
nodes.note: Cylinders arranged radially around a central crankshaft. Air cooling is excellent, and the engine is compact. Most effective for aircraft because the short length and small diameter reduce drag. Requires precise balancing and very strong crankshafts to handle the unbalanced forces. [AUDIT: State interest and suspicion were unset and have been defaulted from the category.]

nodes.name: Rigid airship frame
nodes.note: Instead of one envelope, build a rigid skeleton of wooden rings and longerons, then cover with fabric and fill with gas. This allows huge structures and multiple gas cells for safety. Requires aluminium or steel girders to keep weight manageable. The Zeppelin approach: rigid frame, gasbags inside, and structural load is borne by the frame, not the envelope.

nodes.name: Rotary engine
nodes.note: The entire engine block rotates with the propeller while the crankshaft stays fixed. The piston heads are cooled by rotation. High power at low weight. Much more complex than radial but delivers slightly better power. Used extensively in WWI aircraft. Requires very careful design to handle gyroscopic forces. [AUDIT: State interest and suspicion were unset and have been defaulted from the category.]

nodes.name: Rudder for yaw control
nodes.note: A hinged vertical fin at the tail. When deflected, it yaws the aircraft left or right. Essential for turning when wing warping or ailerons are used. Without it, the aircraft will slip sideways during a turn.

nodes.name: Stressed-skin fuselage
nodes.note: Instead of a skeleton covered with skin, build the skin to carry bending loads. Aluminium sheet riveted to aluminium frames creates a strong, light, rigid structure. Requires precision sheet-metal work and tens of thousands of rivets. The monocoque: a form where the outer surface is the structure. This is how modern aircraft are built. [AUDIT: State interest and suspicion were unset and have been defaulted from the category.]

nodes.name: Three-axis control: roll, pitch, yaw
nodes.note: The pilot must control three independent axes: roll (banking), pitch (nose up or down), and yaw (turning). Roll is achieved by wing warping or ailerons, pitch by elevator, yaw by rudder. A glider without all three controls is uncontrollable. Testing this kills people. But the Wright brothers realized that CONTROL, not lift or power, was the missing piece.

nodes.name: Varnished silk envelope
nodes.note: Multiple coats of shellac varnish on silk create an airtight seam-sealed envelope. Much cheaper than goldbeater's skin, almost as airtight. Handles thermal stress better than intestine. This is the practical choice for large balloons when cost matters.

nodes.name: Wind tunnel for lift and drag measurement
nodes.note: A wooden box with a powerful fan at one end and a test section. Measurement is done with a water manometer: a bent tube of glass half-filled with water, showing pressure difference as height difference. You can test aerofoil shapes, measure lift and drag without dying. This is the tool that transforms flight from experiment to engineering. Build it first, use it to learn, then design based on data.

nodes.name: Wing warping
nodes.note: Twist the entire wing by pulling cables to alter the angle of attack at wing tips. This causes differential lift and forces the aircraft to roll. No moving surfaces are needed; the wing itself twists. This is elegant and strong, but requires great care in cable routing and tensioning. The Wright brothers used this. It works. [AUDIT: State interest and suspicion were unset and have been defaulted from the category.]

nodes.name: Symbolic algebra and equation notation
nodes.note: Diophantus is c. 250 AD and syncopated; you are jumping 1400 years to Viete and Descartes.

nodes.name: Gravimetric and volumetric analysis
nodes.note: Not optional and not glamorous. Without quantitative analysis every process in your programme is a folk recipe that degrades with each retelling. This node is what makes the corpus reproducible by people you never met. [AUDIT: capability prerequisite(s) cap_heat_1300 were inferred by rome/sim/treetool.py repair, not stated by the author. Treat them as a floor, not a specification.]

nodes.name: Electric arc furnace, carbides and ferroalloys
nodes.note: Temperatures no fuel-fired furnace reaches. Gives calcium carbide (hence acetylene), ferrosilicon, ferromanganese, tungsten and chromium steels, and high-purity graphite for the semiconductor programme. CALENDAR FLOOR is set by diffusion, not by construction: the economy needs roughly a generation to train the trades, form the capital and build the suppliers. Money cannot buy this down.

nodes.name: Arc lighting and incandescent lamps
nodes.note: Light without fire, in a city terrified of fire, is one of the great political gifts you can make. Rome's insulae burn constantly and the fear is real. Carbon filaments first; tungsten needs a metallurgy you will not have for a long time. [AUDIT: capability prerequisite(s) cap_vac_1e3 were inferred by rome/sim/treetool.py repair, not stated by the author. Treat them as a floor, not a specification.]

nodes.name: Decimal positional notation, zero, negative numbers, decimal fractions
nodes.note: Highest return on personal hours in the entire tree. Frame as recovered from Indian sources, which is even true. Sell it to bankers and the fiscus first; they will adopt it for self-interest and carry it for you.

nodes.name: Six months of doing nothing but listening
nodes.note: Learn real prices, real law, real dialect, who is who. Every failed bootstrap plan skips this. Acting confidently on wrong assumptions in month one is the most likely way to die in year one.

nodes.name: Atoms, elements, atomic weights, stoichiometry, the periodic table
nodes.note: You can write the periodic table from memory on day one. It is worth roughly 150 years of chemistry. It only becomes operational once you have the analytical balance, so write it early and prove it later.

nodes.name: Analytical balance reading to 1 milligram
nodes.note: Agate or hardened steel knife edges, a beam stiff enough not to sag, damping, a draught shield, and a master weight set. This is the instrument that converts alchemy into chemistry. Nothing downstream is reproducible without it. [AUDIT: capability prerequisite(s) cap_tol_100um were inferred by rome/sim/treetool.py repair, not stated by the author. Treat them as a floor, not a specification.]

nodes.name: Mercury barometer, and the first hard vacuum
nodes.note: The Torricellian space above the column is free vacuum and it will shock every philosopher in the Empire, because Aristotle says it cannot exist. Handle that argument carefully; it is a bigger cultural event than a technical one. [AUDIT: capability prerequisite(s) cap_vac_1torr were inferred by rome/sim/treetool.py repair, not stated by the author. Treat them as a floor, not a specification.]

nodes.name: Water-driven double-acting bellows
nodes.note: The single highest-leverage mechanical change available to Roman metallurgy. Continuous high-volume blast is what separates a bloomery from a blast furnace. [AUDIT: capability prerequisite(s) cap_tol_100um were inferred by rome/sim/treetool.py repair, not stated by the author. Treat them as a floor, not a specification.]

nodes.name: Bulk steel: converter and open hearth
nodes.note: Cheap steel in thousands of tonnes rather than kilogrammes. Note the phosphorus problem: acid linings cannot remove it and most European ores contain it, so you need the basic lining (Thomas and Gilchrist) with a dolomite hearth. Missing this cost Bessemer years, and knowing it in advance saves you them. CALENDAR FLOOR is set by diffusion, not by construction: the economy needs roughly a generation to train the trades, form the capital and build the suppliers. Money cannot buy this down.

nodes.name: Tall shaft blast furnace and cast iron
nodes.note: The biggest single technology gap between Rome and contemporary Han China, which has had cast iron for 500 years. Height, continuous blast and a limestone flux turn a bloomery into a foundry. High risk: the first two or three furnaces will chill, scaffold or burn through. This becomes the financial engine of the middle game. CALENDAR FLOOR is set by diffusion, not by construction: the economy needs roughly a generation to train the trades, form the capital and build the suppliers. Money cannot buy this down. [AUDIT: capability prerequisite(s) cap_heat_1300 were inferred by rome/sim/treetool.py repair, not stated by the author. Treat them as a floor, not a specification.]

nodes.name: Cylinder boring mill
nodes.note: Wilkinson's machine, and the actual reason there was no useful steam engine before 1775. The bar must be supported at both ends so it cannot follow the existing crooked hole. Without this there is no piston that seals, and without that there is no engine.

nodes.name: Differential and integral calculus
nodes.note: Archimedes' method of exhaustion is the nearest Roman-available foundation, and it is a good one. Present as completing Archimedes.

nodes.name: Camera obscura with lens
nodes.note: Immediate cultural value as a drawing and surveying aid, and it teaches optics to your students far faster than argument. Alhazen is 900 years away and the principle is already latent in Aristotle's pinhole observations.

nodes.name: Oxygen and hydrogen in quantity
nodes.note: Gate on the oxy-hydrogen flame, fused quartz, balloons, and the hydrogen reduction of germanium oxide.

nodes.name: Sustained 700 C (pottery kiln)
nodes.note: ROME ALREADY HAS THIS. Updraught pottery kiln, wood fired. Free starting capability. Glazes, bricks, lime, glass working.

nodes.name: Sustained 1100 C (hand-blown charcoal)
nodes.note: ROME ALREADY HAS THIS. Bloomery iron, bronze casting, glass melting. A man on a bellows tops out near here. Everything above this rung needs a machine.

nodes.name: Sustained 1300 C (water-blown continuous blast)
nodes.note: Liquid cast iron lives here. The jump from 1100 to 1300 is not more fuel, it is more AIR, continuously. This single rung is the difference between a bloomery civilisation and a foundry civilisation.

nodes.name: Sustained 1600 C (regenerative preheat)
nodes.note: Siemens regenerative preheat recycles flue heat into the incoming air. Crucible steel, open hearth, porcelain. You cannot get here by burning more charcoal; you must recycle the heat you are already throwing away.

nodes.name: 2000 C localised (oxy-hydrogen blowpipe)
nodes.note: A flame, not a furnace: small volume only. Fused quartz working, platinum melting, lime light.

nodes.name: 3000 C+ (electric arc / resistance)
nodes.note: No chemical flame reaches here. Calcium carbide, ferroalloys, tungsten, artificial graphite, synthetic corundum.

nodes.name: Absolute electrical units
nodes.note: A coil of known geometry and the Earth's field give absolute current with no calibrated instrument to start from. This is how the electrical metrology bootstrap escapes its own circularity.

nodes.name: Reproducible length standard
nodes.note: Master bars in bronze, in triplicate, in three cities. Without this nothing you write down survives you.

nodes.name: Interferometric length (wavelengths of light)
nodes.note: Length measured against a physical constant instead of a bar of metal.

nodes.name: Mass to 1 milligram
nodes.note: Agate knife edges. The instrument that turns alchemy into chemistry.

nodes.name: Temperature to a few degrees (liquid in glass)
nodes.note: Fixed points at melting ice and boiling water. Without a repeatable scale no thermal recipe can be transmitted to anyone not standing beside you.

nodes.name: High temperature (clay contraction and colour pyrometry)
nodes.note: Wedgwood-style contraction pyrometer plus a calibrated colour scale. You cannot control a furnace whose temperature you cannot read.

nodes.name: Time to the millisecond (chronograph, tuning fork)
nodes.note: Ballistics, engine indicating, telegraphy.

nodes.name: Time to the second (pendulum)
nodes.note: Navigation, physics, and later every electrical measurement.

nodes.name: Local electric power, kW scale
nodes.note: One dynamo on the millpond shaft you already built. Enough for arc lights, electroplating, a laboratory.

nodes.name: Grid electric power, MW scale
nodes.note: The precondition for every energy-intensive process: arc furnaces, electrolysis, aluminium, and the sustained laboratory power a purity programme eats.

nodes.name: Muscle and animal power
nodes.note: ROME HAS THIS. A man sustains roughly 75 W; an ox perhaps 400 W. Free, and the reason Roman industry is shaped the way it is.

nodes.name: Steam power, portable, hundreds of kW
nodes.note: Power where there is no river. Until you need that, water is cheaper and needs a far shorter prerequisite chain.

nodes.name: Water power, tens of kW on one shaft
nodes.note: ROME ALREADY HAS THIS and barely uses it for anything but grinding grain. Barbegal runs 16 overshot wheels. The technology gap is imagination, not engineering.

nodes.name: Purity 99% (careful classical refining)
nodes.note: Cupellation, fire refining, recrystallisation. Rome nearly reaches this for silver and gold already.

nodes.name: Purity 99.99% (electrorefining, fractional crystallisation)
nodes.note: You cannot claim a purity you cannot measure, so this rung is gated on quantitative analysis as much as on process.

nodes.name: Purity 99.9999% (fractional distillation of volatile compounds)
nodes.note: Purify the COMPOUND, not the element. Germanium tetrachloride boils at 86 C and fractionates like brandy; germanium metal does not.

nodes.name: Purity 1 part in 1e9 (zone refining)
nodes.note: No chemistry reaches here. A travelling molten zone sweeps impurities to one end because most are more soluble in liquid than in solid. This one trick is what makes semiconductors possible at all.

nodes.name: Tolerance 0.1 micron (interferometric)
nodes.note: Measured in wavelengths of light. Optical surfaces, diffraction gratings, semiconductor lithography much later.

nodes.name: Tolerance 0.1 mm (file, scraper, gauge)
nodes.note: Needs a reference plane to scrape against and a gauge to check with. Clock wheels, lock work, decent screw threads.

nodes.name: Tolerance 0.01 mm (slide rest, lead screw, micrometer)
nodes.note: Take the tool out of the operator's hand and accuracy stops depending on his wrist. Steam pistons, interchangeable parts, precision instruments.

nodes.name: Tolerance 1 mm (skilled hand craft)
nodes.note: ROME ALREADY HAS THIS, and is very good at it. Carpentry, masonry, bronze casting, the Antikythera gearwork. Free.

nodes.name: Tolerance 1 micron (lapping, grinding, optical flats)
nodes.note: Lapping with loose abrasive plus interference fringes to check. Gauge blocks, ball bearings, lens moulds, injector nozzles.

nodes.name: High vacuum, about 1e-3 torr (Sprengel mercury drop)
nodes.note: THE cheap shortcut. Falling mercury drops each trap a slug of gas and carry it out. No pistons, no seals, no tolerances. Incandescent lamps and discharge tubes live here.

nodes.name: Very high vacuum, 1e-6 torr (diffusion pump plus getters)
nodes.note: Needs a motor for the backing pump. Vacuum tubes, X-ray tubes, evaporated coatings.

nodes.name: Ultra high vacuum, 1e-9 torr (bakeable metal systems)
nodes.note: Metal gaskets, bakeout, ion pumps. Surface science and semiconductor processing.

nodes.name: Rough vacuum, about 1 torr (piston pump)
nodes.note: A leather-sealed piston pump. Barometry, the Magdeburg demonstration, condensers. Not enough for any electron device.

nodes.name: Systematic case hardening, quenching and tempering
nodes.note: Roman smiths do all of this already but inconsistently and without a temperature scale. Give them temper colours on polished steel as a repeatable index and the reject rate collapses. Cheap, immediate, militarily valuable, entirely unmagical. [AUDIT: capability prerequisite(s) cap_heat_1100 were inferred by rome/sim/treetool.py repair, not stated by the author. Treat them as a floor, not a specification.]

nodes.name: Blister steel by cementation
nodes.note: Bar iron packed in charcoal in a sealed chest, held at roughly 1000 C for days. Carbon diffuses in slowly, on the order of millimetres per day, so use thin bars. Consistent steel in quantity for the first time.

nodes.name: Coppiced charcoal at industrial scale
nodes.note: Charcoal supply, not ore, is the real ceiling on pre-coke iron output, and it deforests regions. Coppice rotation of 15-20 years on dedicated land is the answer. Budget the land or your furnace will starve. [AUDIT: capability prerequisite(s) cap_heat_1300 were inferred by rome/sim/treetool.py repair, not stated by the author. Treat them as a floor, not a specification.] [AUDIT: State interest and suspicion were unset and have been defaulted from the category.]

nodes.name: Activated carbon production and use
nodes.note: Charcoal is heated with steam at 900 C. Water reacts with carbon, gasifying the interior and creating a porous structure with enormous surface area, up to 3000 m2/g. Activated carbon adsorbs colour, odour and trace contaminants. It is used for water treatment and gas purification. [AUDIT: State interest and suspicion were unset and have been defaulted from the category.]

nodes.name: Alizarin synthesis: oxidation of anthraquinone
nodes.note: Anthraquinone is easily extracted from coal tar. Oxidation with air and catalysts yields alizarin. Before synthesis, alizarin dye came from madder root cultivation in fields, so synthetic alizarin crashed the price by 99%, destroying the madder industry. This is the first wholly synthetic industrial organic dye and set the pattern for the twentieth century.

nodes.name: Leblanc process waste: calcium carbide and the alkali waste problem
nodes.note: One tonne of soda ash from Leblanc produces three tonnes of toxic sulfide waste. Dumping it into rivers creates hydrogen sulfide gas and kills fisheries. Britain's Alkali Act of 1863 was the first environmental regulation in history, requiring soda makers to absorb 95% of the acid mist. This made Leblanc uneconomical where Solvay could operate.

nodes.name: Ammonia recovery and regeneration in soda plants
nodes.note: The Solvay cycle is only better than Leblanc if you actually recover the ammonia. This requires distilling the mother liquor under controlled heat and condensing the vapour in a coil condenser. Without ammonia recycling, Solvay is just another expensive acid-soda process.

nodes.name: Aniline from benzene via nitrobenzene
nodes.note: Oleum nitrates benzene to nitrobenzene in minutes. Reduction with iron powder in dilute acid yields aniline. Aniline is a colourless liquid, bp 184 C, that polymerises in air to a black tar unless kept dry. It is the keystone of synthetic dyes and must be kept under nitrogen or mineral oil.

nodes.name: Anthracene extraction and oxidation
nodes.note: Anthracene is the highest boiling component of coal tar. It crystallises readily and is extremely pure after recrystallisation. Oxidation of anthracene yields anthraquinone, which is further oxidised to alizarin. Anthracene is also photosensitive and used in photochemistry. [AUDIT: State interest and suspicion were unset and have been defaulted from the category.]

nodes.name: Aspirin synthesis from salicylic acid
nodes.note: Salicylic acid tastes bitter and upsets the stomach. Acetylation to aspirin does not reduce the anti-inflammatory effect but eliminates most gastrointestinal irritation. Aspirin revolutionises medicine; mass manufacture becomes possible after the synthesis chain is optimised.

nodes.name: Azo dyes: diazotisation and azo coupling
nodes.note: Aniline plus nitrous acid yields ArN2+ diazonium salt. This is weakly stable in acid at 0 C and couples to nucleophilic aromatics yielding azo dyes with colours from bright red to deep black. Azo dyes are wash-fast because the ArN=NAr group is chemically stable. Millions of tonnes are made industrially each year.

nodes.name: Bakelite: phenol-formaldehyde plastic
nodes.note: Phenol and formaldehyde condense at 150-180 C in the presence of acid catalyst. The resin is thermoset: once cured, it cannot be remelted. Bakelite is hard, brittle, and heat-resistant. It is used for electrical insulation, radio bodies, and industrial equipment. It was the first fully synthetic plastic and dominated the 1920s.

nodes.name: Benzene extraction from coal tar
nodes.note: Benzene boils at 80 C, well separated from toluene at 111 C. A fractionating column with 20-30 trays yields benzene at 99% purity. Benzene vapour is intensely toxic; chronic exposure causes aplastic anaemia. Early workers in benzene manufacturing died of leukaemia within a few years of exposure.

nodes.name: Black powder: gunpowder production
nodes.note: Rome already has gunpowder. This node exists to prevent anachronism: Rome does NOT have potassium nitrate or saltpetre. The nitrum of Roman texts is sodium carbonate natron, entirely different.

nodes.name: Blasting cap and fulminate detonator
nodes.note: A blasting cap is useless without an initiator: a tiny shock-sensitive charge inside. Mercury fulminate explodes from spark, friction or impact. The detonator shock wave initiates the main explosive charge. Without the detonator, TNT and dynamite are inert. The detonator is what makes high explosives strategically useful.

nodes.name: Bleaching powder: mixed calcium hypochlorite
nodes.note: Chlorine dissolves directly into lime slurry. The product is a mixture of Ca(OCl)2, CaCl2, and excess lime that is chemically stable and safe to handle dry. It became the standard bleach for cloth and later drinking water because chlorine gas is too corrosive and dangerous to transport.

nodes.name: Casein plastics from milk protein
nodes.note: Milk is acidified to precipitate casein protein. The wet casein is dried and mixed with formaldehyde, then heated and moulded. The product is hard, waterproof, and can be dyed. Casein plastic was used for buttons, fountain pens, and jewellery until phenolic plastics displaced it.

nodes.name: Catalysis and catalyst theory
nodes.note: The kernel: some substances accelerate reaction without participating in it. This explains why platinum speeds many reactions and why heated iron catalyses ammonia decomposition. You cannot build a contact process or ammonia synthesis without understanding this.

nodes.name: Caustic soda: concentration and purification
nodes.note: Caustic soda boils above 100 C, so direct heating to dryness would decompose it. Vacuum evaporation keeps temperature below 100 C while removing water. The product is chemically pure but must be handled in glass or lead; iron is attacked immediately and dissolved. [AUDIT: capability prerequisite(s) cap_vac_1torr were inferred by rome/sim/treetool.py repair, not stated by the author. Treat them as a floor, not a specification.]

nodes.name: Celluloid: nitrocellulose plastics
nodes.note: Nitrocellulose becomes plastic when mixed with camphor. Sheet is then made by rolling between heated cylinders. Celluloid revolutionises photography by replacing glass plates, enables flexible film stock, and is used for combs, buttons, piano keys. The material is flammable and degrades over time to become increasingly brittle. [AUDIT: capability prerequisite(s) cap_heat_1600 were inferred by rome/sim/treetool.py repair, not stated by the author. Treat them as a floor, not a specification.]

nodes.name: Industrial centrifuge for separation
nodes.note: A scroll inside a spinning cylinder conveys sediment toward the outlet while supernatant overflows a weir. Centrifugal force is 1000 times gravity, so settling that would take hours happens in minutes. Bearing wear from the immense centrifugal force is the main maintenance burden.

nodes.name: Chlor-alkali process: asbestos diaphragm cell
nodes.note: Asbestos diaphragm avoids mercury entirely. Chlorine is produced at the anode, hydrogen at the cathode. The diaphragm prevents mixing while allowing ions to pass. Caustic product is dilute (5-10%) so requires concentration by evaporation. Eventually diaphragm cells replace mercury because the health cost of mercury is unsustainable, but asbestos dust also kills workers decades later.

nodes.name: Chlor-alkali process: mercury cathode cell
nodes.note: Mercury wets the cathode, preventing hydrogen evolution and protecting sodium metal that would otherwise form. Sodium amalgamates into the mercury, is drawn off and reacted with water to yield NaOH. This yields caustic soda of exceptional purity, but mercury is volatile and extremely toxic. Worker exposure to mercury vapour causes tremor, gingivitis and permanent neurological damage. The process dominates industry for fifty years but is eventually abandoned because of environmental and health costs.

nodes.name: Chromatography: column and paper methods
nodes.note: A solution of mixed compounds is percolated through a column of silica gel or charcoal. Compounds with different affinities for the stationary phase elute separately. Paper chromatography using capillary action works in smaller scales and requires only filter paper and solvent.

nodes.name: Coal tar fractionation and distillation
nodes.note: Coal tar boiling below 300 C contains benzene, toluene, phenol. Above 300 C come naphthalene and anthracene. Fractional distillation with bubble-cap trays gives cuts of surprising purity if reflux is high. The vapour pressure differences are only a factor of two, so reflux ratio must exceed 10:1 to separate them properly.

nodes.name: Contact process for sulfuric acid using platinum catalyst
nodes.note: Platinum refuses to poison and remains active indefinitely. The trick: SO2 feed purity above 99.5% or the catalyst silts up. Temperature control to 400-450 C is critical - too hot and equilibrium shifts wrong, too cool and kinetics stall. This yields acid with 98% sulfur recovery, halving the cost versus lead chamber.

nodes.name: Vanadium pentoxide catalyst for contact sulfuric acid
nodes.note: Vanadium catalyst poisons slowly from trace impurities in SO2 feed, requiring periodic regeneration, but costs one-twentieth of platinum. The silica support geometry matters: small pellets expose more surface but choke flow; large pellets flow freely but starve for area. Industrial practice settles on 3-5mm rings.

nodes.name: Continuous versus batch processing decision
nodes.note: Continuous reactors have lower capital cost per tonne when scale is large and products are stable. Batch processes suit pharmaceutical work where recipes change frequently and product shelf-life is measured in months. Continuous operation demands process control; any upset propagates downstream. [AUDIT: State interest and suspicion were unset and have been defaulted from the category.]

nodes.name: Glass-lined steel vessels
nodes.note: Glass fuses to steel at 1400 C. The thermal expansion mismatch between glass and steel causes peeling if temperature gradients are steep. Industrial practice uses special borosilicate glasses and slow heating and cooling. Glass-lined vessels combine steel strength with glass's chemical resistance.

nodes.name: Corrosion-resistant plant: lead and lead-lined vessels
nodes.note: Sulfuric acid dissolves iron instantly but is nearly inert to lead. The acid tank is lined with lead sheet, joined by soft-solder, and sealed with a lead gasket. Lead is soft, so it is cast thick to resist rupture from external mechanical stress. This was the standard until stainless steel displaced it in the 1950s.

nodes.name: Stainless steel vessels for corrosive service
nodes.note: Chromium above 13% in steel passivates the surface, preventing corrosion. Nickel is added for chloride resistance. 304 stainless is austenitic and weldable. Costs three times as much as carbon steel but outlasts it by an order of magnitude in corrosive service. Stainless steel eventually became the material of choice for all chemical plant.

nodes.name: Corrosion-resistant vessels: acid-resistant stoneware
nodes.note: High-fired stoneware has sufficient mechanical strength for small vessels and is inert to all acids. The glaze must be ash-based or lead-based and fully matured. Stoneware is cheaper than lead but brittle, so it is used for containers and small reaction vessels up to ten litres. Industrial-scale acid storage still required lead-lined iron.

nodes.name: Crystallisation and crystal separation
nodes.note: Cooling a saturated solution nucleates crystals that grow if undisturbed. Temperature control to within 1 C is essential. Impurities prefer to stay dissolved, so crystals are purer than the starting solution. This is the principal method of refining all salts. [AUDIT: State interest and suspicion were unset and have been defaulted from the category.]

nodes.name: Cyanamide process: nitrogen fixation by carbide
nodes.note: Calcium carbide is made by arc furnace: limestone and coke to 3000 C in one step. The carbide then reacts with nitrogen gas at 1000 C to yield calcium cyanamide, which hydrolyses to ammonia. This route predates Haber-Bosch and requires less pressure, but yields fewer tonnes per unit energy. Arc furnace demands kilowatts of electric power.

nodes.name: Deacon process: oxidation of hydrogen chloride to chlorine
nodes.note: Converts otherwise-waste HCl from nitrification into chlorine gas. The copper chloride catalyst cycles between Cu(II) oxide and Cu(I) chloride. Temperature above 1600 C is critical; below that, conversion drops sharply. Heat recovery from the exothermic reaction is essential to the economics.

nodes.name: Synthetic detergent from petroleum sulfonic acid
nodes.note: Synthetic detergents are made by sulfonation of alkenes from cracking petroleum fractions. The sulfonic acid is neutralised with soda ash. Detergent molecules have a long nonpolar hydrocarbon tail that dissolves in grease and a polar sulfonate head that dissolves in water. Synthetic detergents work better in cold water than soap and do not leave scum.

nodes.name: Dynamite: nitroglycerin in diatomaceous earth
nodes.note: Nitroglycerin soaks into diatomaceous earth, rendering it safe from accidental detonation during handling but equally detonatable by blasting cap. This makes large-scale mining and construction possible. The name dynamite became synonymous with Nobel's wealth and the peace prize. [AUDIT: capability prerequisite(s) cap_heat_1300 were inferred by rome/sim/treetool.py repair, not stated by the author. Treat them as a floor, not a specification.]

nodes.name: Electric arc nitrogen fixation: nitrogen oxides from air
nodes.note: The arc-furnace method is energy-intensive but simple. At 3000 C, nitrogen and oxygen in air briefly combine to NO, which is then absorbed in water and oxidised to HNO3. This was the first synthetic method and remains a fallback when electricity is cheap. It yields only 2-3% conversion per pass, so most gas is unreacted.

nodes.name: Electroplating: deposition of nickel, chromium and precious metals
nodes.note: The object to be coated is the cathode. Current density must be controlled; too high and the deposit is burnt and powdery, too low and adhesion suffers. Electroplating of chromium requires three stages: copper strike, nickel, then thin chromium for corrosion resistance. [AUDIT: capability prerequisite(s) cap_power_water were inferred by rome/sim/treetool.py repair, not stated by the author. Treat them as a floor, not a specification.]

nodes.name: Surface evaporator for concentration
nodes.note: Copper or iron tubes are immersed in the liquid to be concentrated and steam is passed through them. Boiling point elevation means the solution boils above 100 C at higher concentration; temperature control is critical to avoid bumping and foaming. [AUDIT: State interest and suspicion were unset and have been defaulted from the category.]

nodes.name: Filter press: plate-and-frame filtration
nodes.note: Slurry is pumped into the space between cloth-lined plates, then pressure forces liquid through cloth while solids accumulate. When blocked, plates are separated and solids are knocked out. This is tedious but effective at achieving 1-2 micron clarity. Continuous filter designs exist but are slower. [AUDIT: State interest and suspicion were unset and have been defaulted from the category.]

nodes.name: Formaldehyde oxidation of methanol
nodes.note: Methanol vapour is oxidised over silver gauze at 600 C. Formaldehyde is produced as an equilibrium mixture with methanol and water; the product is stabilised by dissolving in water as formalin. Formaldehyde is a cross-linking reagent for proteins and cellulose, essential for resins.

nodes.name: Fractionating column with bubble caps
nodes.note: Bubble caps are short tubes with caps, welded into copper trays so vapour must bubble through liquid, creating intimate contact. At each tray, liquid and vapour come to partial equilibrium. Boiling point differences of just 10 C become separable if you run fifty trays with high reflux. This is the workhorse of the petrochemical industry.

nodes.name: Mercury fulminate preparation
nodes.note: Mercury is dissolved in dilute nitric acid and ethanol added. After a few hours, white crystals of mercury fulminate form. These are highly shock-sensitive and explode from any mechanical disturbance. Synthesis must be done in tiny batches and handled with extreme caution. Lead fulminate is safer but less reliable. [AUDIT: capability prerequisite(s) cap_heat_1300 were inferred by rome/sim/treetool.py repair, not stated by the author. Treat them as a floor, not a specification.]

nodes.name: Gelignite: nitroglycerin in colloidal cellulose
nodes.note: When nitroglycerin is mixed with nitrocellulose dissolved in acetone or diethyl phthalate, the cellulose swells and gelatinises, creating a putty. Gelignite is more powerful than dynamite and handles more safely. It is the standard explosive for controlled demolition. [AUDIT: capability prerequisite(s) cap_heat_1300 were inferred by rome/sim/treetool.py repair, not stated by the author. Treat them as a floor, not a specification.]

nodes.name: Glycerol production and purification
nodes.note: Soap manufacture produces a glycerol-rich lye as byproduct. The lye is acidified and glycerol is extracted with ethanol, then distilled under vacuum. Glycerol is a primary feedstock for nitroglycerin and explosives, and also a humectant in textiles and pharmaceuticals. [AUDIT: capability prerequisite(s) cap_vac_1torr were inferred by rome/sim/treetool.py repair, not stated by the author. Treat them as a floor, not a specification.]

nodes.name: Guncotton: nitration of cellulose
nodes.note: Linen is nitrated with mixed acid at 0 C. Temperature control is absolutely critical; deviation to 5 C causes runaway and explosion. Guncotton is more powerful than black powder and is initially unstable, spontaneously heating if stored damp. Modern stabilisation uses diphenylamine to suppress decomposition. [AUDIT: capability prerequisite(s) cap_heat_1300 were inferred by rome/sim/treetool.py repair, not stated by the author. Treat them as a floor, not a specification.]

nodes.name: Haber-Bosch synthesis of ammonia
nodes.note: At atmospheric pressure, ammonia synthesis requires 1000 C to reach useful conversion. At 200 atmospheres, equilibrium shifts right so that 400-500 C gives industrial conversion. The iron catalyst works because iron nitride acts as an intermediate, regenerating quickly. Regenerative heat exchange between inlet and outlet gases is mandatory to keep the furnace economical. One plant feeds the entire world's fertiliser supply.

nodes.name: Indigo synthesis from N-phenylglycine
nodes.note: Synthetic indigo is prepared by alkali fusion of a glycine-aniline intermediate at exactly 180 C. Unlike alizarin, indigo is sparingly soluble in water so it is used by converting to the reduced leuco base. When synthetic indigo was commercialised in 1897, indigo-dyeing agriculture in India and West Indies collapsed. Millions of farmers lost their livelihood. This is the first and most politically consequential chemical synthesis.

nodes.name: Industrial hygiene and occupational chemical poisoning
nodes.note: Phosphorus necrosis (phossy jaw) comes from white phosphorus dust eroding jaw bone. Mercury causes tremor and neurological damage. Lead accumulates in bone and poisons the nervous system. Benzene vapour causes aplastic anaemia. Chlorine gas causes pulmonary oedema. No safe level exists; only elimination of exposure through ventilation and process redesign stops the poisoning. [AUDIT: capability prerequisite(s) cap_heat_1300 were inferred by rome/sim/treetool.py repair, not stated by the author. Treat them as a floor, not a specification.]

nodes.name: Ion exchange resins for water softening and purification
nodes.note: Phenolic or acrylic polymer beads are cross-linked with divinylbenzene and charged with either H+ cations or OH- anions. Water percolated through the column exchanges Ca2+ for H+, softening and acidifying simultaneously. The resin is regenerated with acid or base. Ion exchange is essential for producing ultrapure process water and boiler feedwater. [AUDIT: capability prerequisite(s) cap_pure_4N were inferred by rome/sim/treetool.py repair, not stated by the author. Treat them as a floor, not a specification.]

nodes.name: Friction matches: red phosphorus safety match
nodes.note: Match heads are formed by dipping wooden sticks into a paste of red phosphorus, antimony sulfide, potassium dichromate, glue and ground glass. The glass provides friction. Friction heats the phosphorus enough to ignite the sulfide and then the wood. Early white phosphorus matches were poisonous and workers developed phossy jaw; red phosphorus matches solved this. [AUDIT: capability prerequisite(s) cap_heat_1300 were inferred by rome/sim/treetool.py repair, not stated by the author. Treat them as a floor, not a specification.] [AUDIT: State interest and suspicion were unset and have been defaulted from the category.]

nodes.name: Naphthalene extraction and purification
nodes.note: Naphthalene boils at 218 C and crystallises easily. Multiple crystallisation cycles yield pure white needles. Naphthalene is used as a mothball, as a precursor to phthalic anhydride for plasticisers, and in dye synthesis. Its toxicity is low but volatility is significant in enclosed spaces. [AUDIT: State interest and suspicion were unset and have been defaulted from the category.]

nodes.name: Nitroglycerin synthesis and stabilisation
nodes.note: Nitroglycerin is prepared by adding glycerol dropwise to a mixture of nitric and sulfuric acid at 10 C or below. It is a contact explosive - shock or friction detonates it with no need for a fuse. It is also unstable on storage and can spontaneously explode. Absorption onto diatomaceous earth (dynamite) is the only practical way to handle it safely.

nodes.name: Nylon 6,6 synthesis and polymerisation
nodes.note: Adipic acid is made by oxidising cyclohexane with HNO3. Hexamethylenediamine comes from adiponitrile and ammonia. These are condensed at 250 C under controlled pressure, forming long polyamide chains. Nylon has a melting point of 265 C and can be drawn to strong fibres. Nylon is the first fully synthetic fibre and is used for everything from stockings to parachutes.

nodes.name: Oleum (fuming sulfuric acid) production
nodes.note: Oleum contains free SO3 dissolved in H2SO4. It is phenomenally corrosive and must be stored in glass-lined steel or lead, never iron. Used for nitration of aromatics where ordinary sulfuric acid is too dilute. The hazard is water contact - violently exothermic absorption of moisture releases heat that can vaporize the whole batch.

nodes.name: Ostwald process: oxidation of ammonia to nitric acid
nodes.note: Platinum gauze at 800-900 C oxidises ammonia to nitrogen oxides in seconds. The nitrogen oxides are then absorbed in water to yield nitric acid. This is cheaper than the saltpetre-based or lead chamber methods and yields pure dilute acid. Platinum is essential; iron corrodes instantly under these conditions.

nodes.name: Phenol extraction from coal tar and synthesis
nodes.note: Coal tar contains phenol in the middle boiling fraction. Early sources used distillation. Later, benzene is sulfonated and the sulfonate is fused with molten alkali at 300 C to yield phenol. Phenol is corrosive to skin, denatures proteins and was the first antiseptic used by Lister.

nodes.name: White phosphorus extraction from bone ash
nodes.note: Bone ash is calcined phosphate. Heating with carbon in a closed retort at 1300 C reduces it to phosphorus vapour. The vapour is condensed under water to white phosphorus. This method dates to 1669 and predates the identification of phosphorus as an element by 100 years.

nodes.name: Silver halide photographic chemistry
nodes.note: Silver halide crystals are formed by mixing silver nitrate and sodium halide. Gelatin is added as a binder. Development is performed with reducing agents like hydroquinone or metol in alkaline conditions. Each step requires strict control of temperature, pH and oxidising impurities. Photographic film is the foundation of cinema and still photography.

nodes.name: Picric acid: trinitrophenol synthesis
nodes.note: Phenol is nitrated to yield a yellow acid that is surprisingly stable. Picric acid is used as a dye and in photoflash powder. Its use as a military explosive faded when TNT became available because TNT is more powerful and much less hygroscopic.

nodes.name: Polyethylene synthesis under high pressure
nodes.note: Ethylene is exposed to 1000 atmospheres and 150 C in the presence of an organic peroxide free-radical initiator. Polymer chains grow and link randomly. The product is low-density branched polyethylene. A later low-pressure process using a Ziegler catalyst yields linear high-density polyethylene, which is stronger and more useful.

nodes.name: Potash mining and refining
nodes.note: Potash salts like sylvinite are mined like any mineral ore. The mined rock is then dissolved in water, filtered to remove insoluble matter, and crystallised. Potassium is essential to agriculture: wheat and potatoes are heavy exporters of K2O, depleting soils rapidly without replenishment. [AUDIT: capability prerequisite(s) cap_tol_100um were inferred by rome/sim/treetool.py repair, not stated by the author. Treat them as a floor, not a specification.]

nodes.name: Bourdon tube pressure gauge and safety relief valve
nodes.note: The Bourdon tube uncurls proportionally to pressure, moving a needle on a dial. The relief valve must crack at exactly the safe pressure or the autoclave becomes a bomb. Precision here saves lives.

nodes.name: High-pressure autoclave and steam digester
nodes.note: High pressure demands absolute rigidity and control. The drum must withstand internal stress while keeping temperature uniform. Failures are catastrophic. The riveted seams are the critical weak point; you need sub-millimetre alignment and reliable riveting technique.

nodes.name: Polyvinyl chloride (PVC) synthesis
nodes.note: Vinyl chloride is made by acetylene plus HCl or ethylene dichloride cracking. Polymerisation in aqueous emulsion yields PVC plastic. Plasticisers are added to make flexible sheet; unplasticised PVC is rigid and chemical-resistant. PVC is the most widely used plastic on Earth. Thermal decomposition releases hydrogen chloride, making fires extremely dangerous.

nodes.name: Ammonia as refrigerant in compression cycles
nodes.note: Ammonia has a high latent heat and boils at -33 C. Liquid ammonia evaporates in the cold box and is compressed back to liquid, rejecting heat in the condenser. Ammonia is toxic and requires sealed copper tubing, but it is non-reactive with copper and iron. Industrial food freezing and ice manufacturing rely on ammonia refrigeration.

nodes.name: Saccharin synthesis
nodes.note: Toluene is sulfonated with oleum, giving toluenesulfonic acid. Oxidation with permanganate to toluic acid, then reaction with ammonia and loss of water yields saccharin. Saccharin is 500 times sweeter than sugar by mass and costs one-tenth as much at scale. Food preservation becomes possible without cane sugar.

nodes.name: Salicylic acid: hydroxylation of benzenesulfonic acid
nodes.note: Benzene is sulfonated to benzenesulfonic acid. Molten alkali at 300 C causes Ar-SO3H to be replaced by Ar-OH, yielding phenol. Phenol is then converted to salicylic acid. Salicylic acid is acetylated to yield aspirin, the world's most widely used pharmaceutical.

nodes.name: Smokeless powder: nitrocellulose ballistic propellant
nodes.note: Nitrocellulose particles are stabilised with diphenylamine or similar hindered amine to suppress autocatalytic decomposition. Grain size and shape control burn rate. Smokeless powder has three times the energy density of black powder, enabling lighter rifles, higher velocities, and longer effective ranges.

nodes.name: Hard soap from oil and caustic soda
nodes.note: Rome does not have soap as a cleanser. This is already in the vocabulary; do not redefine it. It is included here to prevent anachronism. [AUDIT: capability prerequisite(s) cap_tol_100um were inferred by rome/sim/treetool.py repair, not stated by the author. Treat them as a floor, not a specification.] [AUDIT: State interest and suspicion were unset and have been defaulted from the category.]

nodes.name: Solvay process: ammonia-soda manufacturing
nodes.note: The genius: ammonia is expensive so you recycle it. Limestone calcines to CO2 which carbonates the ammonia-brine. NaHCO3 precipitates, is filtered, then thermally decomposed to soda ash. The ammonia is recovered by treating the residue with lime and distilling. Leblanc loses all this to slag mountains. Solvay's yield is 80% versus Leblanc's 40%, and the only waste is calcium chloride brines.

nodes.name: Sulfonamide antibiotics: sulfanilamide synthesis
nodes.note: Sulfanilamide (para-aminobenzenesulfonamide) is synthesised by sulfonation of aniline followed by reaction with ammonia. It inhibits bacterial dihydropteroate synthase, blocking folate metabolism. Sulfonamides are the first fully synthetic antibiotics and are miraculous compared to no antibiotics at all, though they have significant toxicity.

nodes.name: Superphosphate: acidulation of rock phosphate
nodes.note: Rock phosphate is insoluble calcium phosphate. Sulfuric acid converts it to a mixture of soluble monocalcium phosphate and gypsum. The product is simply filtered and dried. This produces tens of tonnes of agricultural fertiliser from a tonne of sulfuric acid. The phosphate is now bioavailable to plants. [AUDIT: capability prerequisite(s) cap_heat_1300 were inferred by rome/sim/treetool.py repair, not stated by the author. Treat them as a floor, not a specification.]

nodes.name: TNT: trinitrotoluene synthesis
nodes.note: Toluene is nitrated to mononitrotoluene, then dinitrotoluene, then trinitrotoluene. Each stage requires strong acid and careful temperature control. TNT is relatively stable compared to nitroglycerin and can be melted to pour into shells. Its insensitivity to shock makes it ideal for military use.

nodes.name: Toluene extraction from coal tar
nodes.note: Toluene boils at 111 C, well separated from benzene at 80 C. A fractionating column yields toluene at 99% purity. Toluene is used as a solvent and as a precursor to TNT and saccharin. It is less toxic than benzene but still a CNS depressant at high vapour concentrations.

nodes.name: Chlorination of drinking water for disinfection
nodes.note: Chlorine kills bacteria within seconds at concentrations above 0.2 ppm. Residual chlorine must be maintained to prevent recontamination in pipes. Chlorination remains the standard method for microbiological control of water supplies.

nodes.name: Water treatment by coagulation and settling
nodes.note: Fine clay and organic particles remain suspended in water as colloids. Alum or ferric sulfate ions hydrolyse to form hydroxide gelatine that neutralises colloid charges. Particles flocculate and settle quickly. This is the first step in modern water purification.

nodes.name: Sand filtration and multimedia filter beds
nodes.note: After coagulation, water passes through a filter bed of coarse gravel, sand, and sometimes anthracite coal. The bed removes particles down to 10 microns. The filter must be backwashed periodically when pressure drop becomes excessive.

nodes.name: Weldon process: regeneration of manganese dioxide from manganous chloride
nodes.note: In bleach production, MnO2 is reduced to MnCl2. Weldon's trick: oxidise the manganese back with hypochlorite, then filter and recycle the MnO2. This more than halves manganese consumption. Lime is needed to adjust pH so precipitation is quantitative.

nodes.name: Roman citizenship by grant
nodes.note: Gives provocatio, the right of appeal, which is the difference between a governor executing you and Rome hearing you. Buy it with a public benefaction.

nodes.name: Amphitheatre with tiered seating
nodes.note: Concentric ovals of arched vaults and seating on filled earth. The Colosseum seated 50,000. Ruins of amphitheatres across the empire show that Romans mastered the geometry and structure of large public spaces long before the modern stadium.

nodes.name: Roman aqueduct with inverted siphons
nodes.note: Gravity-fed water under precise gradient over vast distances. At valleys, inverted siphons (pipes under pressure) carried water below ground, then up the other side. Rome's engineering was not obvious; this was clever and stable.

nodes.name: Roman masonry arch
nodes.note: The wedge-shaped stone voussoir locked under compression. Rome perfected this; the arch remains the fundamental load-bearing form through the Middle Ages and beyond. Spans cannot be thrown long without collapse or immense depth, but the principle is unbreakable.

nodes.name: Bending moment and shear diagrams
nodes.note: A beam under load is bent. Shear forces and bending moments vary along its length; calculus (the derivative of shear is load, the derivative of moment is shear) gives the full distribution. Maximum moment indicates the critical section; this is what a designer must check.

nodes.name: Box girder beam
nodes.note: A hollow rectangular tube of steel or concrete. Material is placed far from the neutral axis (the walls), giving maximum rigidity with minimum weight. Bridges and long-span buildings use box girders. Torsional stiffness is also high; useful when spans are asymmetric.

nodes.name: Roman fired brick and tile
nodes.note: Fired clay in standard sizes, facings for concrete, tiles for roofs. Uniform sizing was a Roman innovation; mass production of standard parts. The tiles lock together with ribs and survive centuries of weather.

nodes.name: Cantilever bridge
nodes.note: Pairs of cantilevers extend from towers toward each other, meeting or nearly meeting. Forth Bridge (1890) is a cantilever; it has massive rigidity. Requires deep towers and strong base connections. Spans to 400m. Rivals suspension in elegance.

nodes.name: Cast iron bridge
nodes.note: Cast iron is brittle and strong in compression, weak in tension. Arched cast iron bridges (like the 1779 Ironbridge in Shropshire) mimic the arch form to keep the material in compression. Cast iron does not corrode like wrought iron but is prone to sudden brittle fracture.

nodes.name: Steel arch bridge
nodes.note: An arch of steel riveted or welded. Steel can be made into arched members with joints. Span to 500m. Requires calculation of arch stresses and support reactions. Sydney Harbour Bridge (1932) is a steel arch; it carries road, rail, and pedestrians.

nodes.name: Suspension bridge with wire cables
nodes.note: Cables slung over towers and anchored at the ends, with vertical hangers supporting the deck. The cable takes the shape of a catenary under load (not a parabola). Long spans (1000m+) require understanding catenary geometry and high tensile wire. The first major suspension bridge was Brooklyn (1883).

nodes.name: Timber trussed bridge
nodes.note: Timber trusses on stone piers. Spans to 80 metres were built. Timber is strong in tension and compression but rots; maintenance is perpetual. Covered bridges survive longer (dryness is the enemy of rot).

nodes.name: Wrought iron truss bridge
nodes.note: Wrought iron does not have the span of cast iron arches, but can carry tension. Wrought iron truss bridges (using the method of joints to proportion members) enable spans to 150 metres with light weight. Riveted wrought iron held up until the 1960s.

nodes.name: Building code and regulatory standards
nodes.note: Written rules for minimum structural capacity, fire safety, exits, materials. Enforced by inspection. The first comprehensive code was New York (1901). Codification stops guesswork and protects the public. Elite builders resist rules; lives saved prove the value. [AUDIT: capability prerequisite(s) cap_heat_1300 were inferred by rome/sim/treetool.py repair, not stated by the author. Treat them as a floor, not a specification.]

nodes.name: Caisson and underwater excavation
nodes.note: A large hollow box sunk into water or soft ground, interior pumped dry, filled with concrete. London Bridge (1831) used caissons. Allows foundation work below water. Risk of leaking, and the deeper you go, the harder to keep dry. [AUDIT: capability prerequisite(s) cap_tol_100um were inferred by rome/sim/treetool.py repair, not stated by the author. Treat them as a floor, not a specification.]

nodes.name: Compressed air caisson and decompression
nodes.note: A steam-powered air compressor pressurises the interior, pushing water down. Men work under high pressure digging. Rapid decompression causes the bends (nitrogen bubbles in the blood). Slow decompression prevents it. Brooklyn Bridge (1883) lost 20 workers to decompression sickness; this is physiological, not mechanical.

nodes.name: Canal pound lock for level changes
nodes.note: A chamber with gates at each end. A barge enters the lock, the gates close, water is let in or out (changing the barge's level), then the exit gates open. Brilliant: it allows a canal to climb hills without continuous flow. The canal network (1750-1850) moved goods and coal. [AUDIT: capability prerequisite(s) cap_tol_100um were inferred by rome/sim/treetool.py repair, not stated by the author. Treat them as a floor, not a specification.]

nodes.name: Chorobates: Roman water levelling rod
nodes.note: A long wooden rod with a water-filled groove along its length: the water surface itself is a perfect level. Roman engineers used this to grade aqueducts with millimetre precision over kilometres. Needs no mercury, no instruments.

nodes.name: Cofferdam and underwater concrete
nodes.note: Wooden piling in rings, the interior pumped or bailed dry, filled with pozzolanic concrete that sets underwater. Roman harbour piers used this. The concrete set faster in water than in air; not accident but observed principle.

nodes.name: Treadwheel crane
nodes.note: Large wooden drum turned by men inside a hamster wheel. Could lift tens of tonnes. Documented in Vitruvius; used to build the aqueducts and temples. Survives in medieval and Renaissance construction accounts.

nodes.name: Curtain wall (non-load-bearing facade)
nodes.note: Frames of iron or steel with glass or panels hung from the steel skeleton. The wall does not carry load; the frame does. Allows large glazed areas and flexibility. Every modern tall building uses this principle; it is inseparable from the steel frame.

nodes.name: Arch dam in concrete
nodes.note: A curved dam transfers water pressure sideways to the canyon walls, not to the base. Thinner and lighter than a gravity dam. Requires rock walls on both sides and calculation of the arch stress. The Hoover Dam (1936) is an arch; it can hold a lake with less concrete than gravity. [AUDIT: capability prerequisite(s) cap_heat_1300 were inferred by rome/sim/treetool.py repair, not stated by the author. Treat them as a floor, not a specification.]

nodes.name: Earth fill dam with compacted layers
nodes.note: Layered soil compacted by repeated passes. Far cheaper than masonry. Needs an impermeable core (clay) and stable slopes. Piping (internal erosion along a path of sand) is the enemy. Earth dams can be very large; Aswan High Dam is earth fill.

nodes.name: Gravity dam in masonry or concrete
nodes.note: A thick wall holding back water by its own weight. Water pressure increases with depth (proportional to depth squared). The base must resist both the vertical load and the horizontal thrust. Most dam failures are not structural (cracking) but hydraulic (seepage, overtopping). [AUDIT: capability prerequisite(s) cap_tol_100um were inferred by rome/sim/treetool.py repair, not stated by the author. Treat them as a floor, not a specification.]

nodes.name: Roman concrete dome
nodes.note: The Pantheon dome (126 AD) measures 43.3 metres and is still the largest unreinforced concrete dome ever built. Pozzolanic concrete actually strengthens in seawater. Modern Portland cement does not; Pantheon beats it on durability.

nodes.name: Dredging for channel maintenance
nodes.note: Sediment fills harbours and channels; dredges scoop it up. Early dredges were buckets on a chain driven by water power. Suction dredges (pump-driven) are later but far more powerful. Maintenance dredging is expensive and continuous. The removed material can be sold or used for land reclamation.

nodes.name: Theory of elasticity
nodes.note: Stress-strain relationship for materials. Young's modulus relates stress to strain; Poisson's ratio the transverse to axial strain. Allows prediction of deformation, not just failure. Requires testing to find material constants; without it, design is guesswork.

nodes.name: Elevator with safety brake (Otis)
nodes.note: A steam-powered cab on a rope. If the rope breaks, mechanical wedges jam against the guide rails and lock the cab. Otis (1853) demonstrated this at a fair by cutting the rope; the cab held. Without the brake, nobody will ride it. The brake is the actual invention; vertical transport scales only after people trust their lives.

nodes.name: Euler buckling of slender columns
nodes.note: A slender column under axial load will suddenly buckle sideways at a critical load, not from material failure but from geometric instability. Euler's formula shows the critical load depends on length squared and moment of inertia; long thin columns buckle easily. Calculation replaces guessing.

nodes.name: Factor of safety concept
nodes.note: Design load times a safety factor (typically 2 to 5) must not exceed the material strength. A codification of caution. Different factors for different risks; this is risk management, not ignorance. Without it, every overload is a surprise failure.

nodes.name: Fireproofing and fire-resistant structure
nodes.note: Steel loses strength at high temperature (500 C is critical). Concrete or ceramic encasement keeps the steel cool. Compartmentation (fire walls, fire doors) stops spread. The triangle: materials (incombustible), structure (load paths survive local fire), and exits (life safety). All three matter.

nodes.name: Foundation piles and pile driving
nodes.note: Drive long timber posts into soft ground to reach firm strata. The pile takes vertical load and transfers it down. Rome used piles under the Theatre of Pompey; medieval builders drove thousands for cathedrals. Bearing capacity is guessed; soil testing came much later.

nodes.name: Spread footing on compacted soil
nodes.note: A wide stone or brick base distributes the wall load over a larger footprint. Soft clay will compress under load; settlement cracks the building. Soil testing (boring and observation) tells you what depth to go. Without it, you guess and hope.

nodes.name: Sluice gate for water control
nodes.note: A wooden or iron gate that slides vertically in a groove, controlling the flow of water. Water pressure increases with depth (the force is immense at the base). The gate must be strong; friction resistance must be manageable. Used for mills, docks, and irrigation.

nodes.name: Plate glass for windows and storefronts
nodes.note: Large flat panes of clear glass. Cast plate glass (poured onto a flat table, then ground and polished) allows sizes to 3-4 metres. Transforms storefronts and windows. Sheet glass (drawn from a bath) is cheaper but smaller. Large panes are fragile but stunning. [AUDIT: State interest and suspicion were unset and have been defaulted from the category.]

nodes.name: Glass panes for windows
nodes.note: By 100 AD Roman glassblowers produced clear soda-lime panes, often small. A luxury in Rome, it was still cheaper than oiled linen or mica. Roman houses with glass windows survive; the material itself is durable.

nodes.name: Harbour and dock with breakwaters
nodes.note: A protected basin with stone or wooden walls. Breakwaters outside reduce waves. Quays allow cargo loading and unloading. Docks with gates can maintain constant water level despite tides. Venice was the model; modern container ports are different in scale only. [AUDIT: capability prerequisite(s) cap_tol_100um were inferred by rome/sim/treetool.py repair, not stated by the author. Treat them as a floor, not a specification.]

nodes.name: Insula: Roman apartment block
nodes.note: Multi-storey blocks of small rented rooms around a courtyard, using brick and timber joists. Rome housed its poor in dense urban clusters; the form remains standard. Fire risk was immense (hence frequent collapse in literature).

nodes.name: Wrought iron working and riveting
nodes.note: Wrought iron from bloomery furnace is ductile, tough, and resistant to corrosion. Smith heating and hand-forging creates toughness. Rivets are driven hot; the cooled rivet locks parts together. Roman and medieval smiths knew this; it is not high art, but skilled work. [AUDIT: capability prerequisite(s) cap_heat_0700 were inferred by rome/sim/treetool.py repair, not stated by the author. Treat them as a floor, not a specification.]

nodes.name: Lightning conductor and grounding
nodes.note: A copper or iron rod running from the roof to ground rod(s) in moist earth. Captures lightning and shunts it safely into the ground. Franklin (1752) invented this; it saved many buildings. Reduces fire and injury. Requires good earth contact; a dry ground rod does nothing. [AUDIT: capability prerequisite(s) cap_tol_100um were inferred by rome/sim/treetool.py repair, not stated by the author. Treat them as a floor, not a specification.]

nodes.name: Marble veneer and ashlar facing
nodes.note: Thin slabs of marble or stone cut to dimension and affixed to concrete, creating facade and surface. Aesthetic, durable, and separates structure (concrete) from facing, a principle unchanged to this day.

nodes.name: Materials testing and calibration
nodes.note: Pull samples to failure and measure the load. Cast a batch and test it; the material constants you need (tensile strength, Young's modulus, elongation to failure) come from experiment. No two batches are identical; testing catches the weakest.

nodes.name: Method of joints for truss analysis
