nodes.note: At each joint of a truss, forces are in equilibrium. By solving joint by joint (starting from known loads), the tension or compression in each member can be calculated. This displaced rule-of-thumb proportioning; calculation is faster and correct.

nodes.name: Neutral axis in bending
nodes.note: When a beam bends, the top fibres go into compression, the bottom into tension, and there is a neutral surface in the middle with no stress. The stress magnitude increases linearly with distance from the neutral axis. This is why deep beams (I-beams) are efficient: material far from the axis is stronger.

nodes.name: Precise levelling and level network
nodes.note: A telescope on a spirit level, with a graduated rod. From one point, sights the rod at a distant point and reads the height difference. Chain many such sightings and you have a network of height reference points. Modern mapping uses electronic total stations; the principle is 200 years old.

nodes.name: Prestressed concrete
nodes.note: Steel cables under high tension are embedded in concrete, then the tension is released. The concrete is compressed throughout. This pre-compression means the concrete can resist higher loads before cracking. Beams can span further. Freyssinet (1928) pioneered this.

nodes.name: Pumping station and mechanical lift
nodes.note: A water-powered pump (or steam-powered later) lifts water uphill against gravity. The Archimedean screw predates Rome; centrifugal pumps came later. Lifting water to a tower gives pressure for distribution. Without lift, you must be lower than the source.

nodes.name: Reinforced concrete construction
nodes.note: Steel bars embedded in concrete take tension; concrete takes compression. Their thermal expansion coefficients happen to match (both expand at roughly 10-12 ppm/K). Steel does not rust in the alkaline environment of concrete. This works; Coignet patented it (1891). Allows thin slabs and long spans.

nodes.name: Roman paved road with surveying
nodes.note: Multilayered stone and gravel bed, crowned for drainage, aligned by groma (X-staff with plumb bobs). Roman roads lasted centuries. The technique is durable and maintainable; paving without surveying is wasteful.

nodes.name: King post roof truss
nodes.note: Two sloped rafters meeting at a peak, with a vertical king post from peak to tie-beam, and a horizontal tie keeping the rafters from thrusting outward. The tie is in tension, the post in compression. Simple and elegant; medieval roofs used this.

nodes.name: Queen post roof truss
nodes.note: Two vertical posts between tie and rafters, with a horizontal strut between them. Allows longer spans than king post without intermediate supports. The posts are in compression, the tie in tension, the struts shared the vertical load.

nodes.name: Sewage treatment works and activated sludge
nodes.note: Sewage (biological waste) requires aerobic decomposition. Activated sludge is bacteria and protozoa that eat organic matter when aerated. Germ theory explains why pathogens die in treatment; without it, the mechanism is invisible. Treated effluent is safe to discharge. [AUDIT: capability prerequisite(s) cap_heat_1600 were inferred by rome/sim/treetool.py repair, not stated by the author. Treat them as a floor, not a specification.]

nodes.name: Roman sewer with gravity flow
nodes.note: The Cloaca Maxima in Rome still functions after 2400 years. Gravity-fed, arched, with gradient for scouring. Medieval towns often rebuilt sewers on Roman alignment; the Romans had solved the problem.

nodes.name: Separate foul and storm sewers
nodes.note: Two pipes: foul (sewage) and storm (rain). Storm sewers are large but infrequent flow; foul sewers are constant. Combined sewers overflow during heavy rain, contaminating rivers. Separation is expensive but hygienic; Victorian engineers standardised it. [AUDIT: capability prerequisite(s) cap_tol_100um were inferred by rome/sim/treetool.py repair, not stated by the author. Treat them as a floor, not a specification.]

nodes.name: Soil mechanics and bearing capacity
nodes.note: Terzaghi (1920s) developed the theory of effective stress and bearing capacity formulas. Before this, foundation depth was guess-work. Soil is not a simple material; water content, grain size, cementation all matter. Boring and sampling are the tools.

nodes.name: Spillway and flood management
nodes.note: A controlled overflow weir at a set height. If the dam fills above that level, water goes over the spillway, not over the dam. The spillway must carry high velocity water without erosion. Most dam failures are hydraulic: overtopping erodes the downstream slope.

nodes.name: Statics and equilibrium of forces
nodes.note: Force balance: sum of forces and moments at each point must be zero. Archimedes knew this; the formalism of vectors and moment arms is Renaissance work (Leonardo). Essential to size any structural member without collapse.

nodes.name: Steel frame building
nodes.note: A skeleton of steel beams and columns carries all loads; the exterior walls are non-load-bearing curtain walls. This is the essence of the skyscraper. Bulk steel (converter) and riveted or bolted connections. London's Great Exhibition building (1851) was a proto-steel frame; Chicago's Home Insurance building (1885) was the first true one.

nodes.name: Street lighting with electricity
nodes.note: Gas lamps (post-1800) were bright but hot. Arc lamps (post-1850) were bright and stable. Incandescent bulbs (post-1880) were safer. Electric grid power (post-1900) made street lighting universal. Crime dropped; nightlife boomed. The cost was perpetual maintenance of wiring and poles. [AUDIT: capability prerequisite(s) cap_power_electric were inferred by rome/sim/treetool.py repair, not stated by the author. Treat them as a floor, not a specification.]

nodes.name: Paved street and sidewalk
nodes.note: Concrete or stone surface, crowned for drainage. Sidewalks segregate pedestrians from vehicles. Paving is expensive but lasts decades. Brick or stone is traditional; concrete (post-1900) is cheaper. Proper drainage prevents flooding and freezing damage.

nodes.name: Groma: Roman X-staff surveying tool
nodes.note: Four plumb bobs hanging from the four arms of a cross allow rapid sighting of right angles and straight lines. Crude and ingenious. Used to lay out Roman towns and roads across the empire.

nodes.name: Theodolite for surveying angles
nodes.note: A telescope on a graduated circle; turns to measure angles to two objects. From a point, you can sight two distant landmarks and calculate their angle. Repeated sightings from multiple points give positions by triangulation. Accuracy to seconds of arc changes the scale of surveying from sight to hundreds of kilometres.

nodes.name: Town planning and street layout
nodes.note: Systematic design of streets, squares, and districts rather than organic growth. Rome's colonial towns used a grid (the orthogonal plan). Haussmann (Paris, 1850s) imposed radial avenues and parks. Planning is contentious (disrupts existing patterns), but saves lives (fire lanes, flood avoidance, sanitation) and improves efficiency. [AUDIT: capability prerequisite(s) cap_tol_100um were inferred by rome/sim/treetool.py repair, not stated by the author. Treat them as a floor, not a specification.]

nodes.name: Triangulated truss frame
nodes.note: A truss is fundamentally different from an arch: it carries load by rigid tension and compression in its members, not by geometric compression of wedges. A triangle cannot be deformed without changing member length. This is not intuitive; it requires understanding materials can pull apart.

nodes.name: Rock drilling and tunnelling
nodes.note: Percussion drills (hitting, not rotation) cut rock slowly. Blasting with dynamite (nitroglycerin) broke larger rock faster (1867 onwards). Timbering the walls prevents collapse. Tunnels need gradient and drainage; straight-line surveying through a mountain is hard.

nodes.name: Tunnelling shield and incremental advance
nodes.note: A large cylindrical shield advances meter by meter through soft ground (clay, silt). Men dig at the face inside; segments are assembled behind; the shield is jacked forward. London Underground used this (1863 onwards). Prevents cave-ins but is slow and heavy.

nodes.name: Barrel vault
nodes.note: An arch extruded in the third dimension: a continuous stone tunnel. Massive, permanent, and the ceiling form for the Basilica of Maxentius. Rome pushed vaults to extremes; Renaissance architects still marvelled at them.

nodes.name: Water tower and pressure system
nodes.note: Water stored in an elevated tank. Pressure at the base is proportional to height (0.1 kg/cm2 per metre). Sufficient pressure to feed a city from a single tower. Replaces the Roman need for gentle gradients in aqueducts; now you can serve hilly ground.

nodes.name: Water treatment works and coagulation
nodes.note: Alum added to water causes clay particles to coagulate and settle. Sand filters then remove fine particles and some bacteria. Boiling kills most pathogens. Chlorine (post-1900) kills the rest. Water treatment makes urban life possible; sewage in the water kills you fast.

nodes.name: Drawn wire and wire rope
nodes.note: Fine wire drawn through successive dies, twisted into strands, twisted again into rope. Wire rope has the tensile strength of steel and flexibility of rope. Essential for suspension bridges. High quality drawplates are needed; brittle dies fail.

nodes.name: Pendulum clock and later the balance spring
nodes.note: The Antikythera mechanism proves Roman-era gear-cutting is already good enough; what is missing is the escapement and the pendulum's isochronism. Accurate time gives navigation, longitude, physics, and later electrical measurement. Also a superb luxury product.

nodes.name: Coal, and coking it
nodes.note: Romans burn coal in Britain but never coke it. Raw coal ruins iron through sulfur; coking drives off sulfur and volatiles and leaves a strong porous fuel that will bear the burden in a tall furnace. Breaks the charcoal ceiling permanently.

nodes.name: Licensed collegium of physicians and teachers
nodes.note: Unlicensed associations are illegal; Trajan refuses Pliny even a fire brigade at Nicomedia (Ep. 10.34) for fear of factions. Get the licence or your school is a conspiracy.

nodes.name: Accumulator - arithmetic work register
nodes.note: A register connected to an adder circuit (carries propagate left through carry-look-ahead or similar). A number can be added to the accumulator in one clock cycle. Repeated additions multiply (accumulate a number N times), division by repeated subtraction. The accumulator is the primary work register in early computers, used for nearly all arithmetic. Later CPUs generalize this to multiple general-purpose registers. [AUDIT: State interest and suspicion were unset and have been defaulted from the category.]

nodes.name: Amplitude modulation (AM) - encoding audio on radio
nodes.note: A microphone signal (audio, 0-10 kHz) is added to the RF oscillator output, varying its amplitude. The modulated wave is transmitted; a receiver detects the envelope (the modulation) using a rectifier, recovering audio. The trick: a 1 MHz carrier modulated with 1 kHz audio produces sidebands at 999 kHz and 1001 kHz. Radio stations are spaced 10 kHz apart (AM broadcast). The bandwidth is about 2x the audio frequency. Simple and robust.

nodes.name: Analytical engine - programmable mechanical computer
nodes.note: Babbage's design for a universal mechanical computer: a large mill (arithmetic unit) and store (memory), programmed by punched cards like Jacquard looms. It could perform any sequence of arithmetic operations, conditional on intermediate results. The killer insight: a general-purpose machine can solve many problems if programmed differently. Ada Lovelace sketched an algorithm for it (1843). It was never built (same tolerance problems as the Difference Engine), but it was the conceptual foundation of the stored-program computer.

nodes.name: Antenna and ground system for radio
nodes.note: An antenna is just a wire at a height or length that couples to the air (transmitting) or the air couples to it (receiving). A ground is a connection to earth (literally a copper plate or rod buried 2 metres). Radio waves need an antenna and a return path (ground) to form a closed loop. The antenna length determines efficiency at a given frequency. This was not obvious: early radio pioneers accidentally discovered that tall antennas worked better. Design theory came later. nodes.name: Arithmometer - mass-produced mechanical calculator
nodes.note: The first calculator to reach mass production (thousands made, not just hundreds). Uses standardized parts, precision jigs, and assembly-line methods. Reduced price from 500 denarii to 100 denarii. The Arithmometer (1851 onward) was the accountant's standard tool until electric calculators appeared (1960s). The innovation was not mechanical (same as Pascal's design) but manufacturing: making them cheaply and reliably.

nodes.name: Baudot code - 5-bit telegraph encoding
nodes.note: Each character is encoded as 5 binary digits (bits): mark (current) or space (no current). Letters, numbers, and symbols each have a 5-bit code. A teleprinter has 5 solenoids, one per bit. All 5 are energized simultaneously on reception, positioning the 5 levers correctly, and a mechanical stroke fires the type. This is the first digital telegraph code and the ancestor of modern binary encoding (ASCII, etc.). Standardized by the ITU in 1874.

nodes.name: Binary arithmetic - base-2 number system
nodes.note: Binary: digits 0 and 1 only. Addition, multiplication, and logic are all simpler in binary than decimal. A two-state device (relay on/off, transistor on/off) represents 0 or 1 directly. Decimal requires devices with 10 states (complex and error-prone). All electronic computers use binary for this reason. The conceptual link: binary numbers are data, Boolean logic is control, they use the same substrates (switches). nodes.name: Boolean algebra - logic and switching equivalence
nodes.note: Boolean algebra: true/false, AND, OR, NOT. Claude Shannon's insight (1938): switching circuits are Boolean algebras. A series switch is AND (both must be closed), parallel is OR. This is the single most important conceptual link in computing: abstract logic is isomorphic to physical electronics. nodes.name: Broadcasting as an institution - scheduled transmission and profit model
nodes.note: Not a technical innovation but an economic and political one. Broadcast stations transmit on fixed schedules so listeners know when to tune in. Content (music, news, drama) is produced by local staff. Revenue comes from advertising (selling commercial time). This is a radical model: entertainment and information are free to the listener, paid for by advertisers. By 1930, broadcasting is the dominant communication medium and has shaped politics, culture, and commerce.

nodes.name: Cathode ray tube (CRT) - electron beam display
nodes.note: An evacuated glass tube with a heated cathode that emits electrons, accelerated by 10,000 V towards a phosphor-coated anode. The electron beam is steered by magnetic coils (X and Y deflection). Where the beam hits the screen, the phosphor glows. Varying the beam current modulates the brightness. This is the display technology that made electronic television possible. The key: the beam is fast (MHz), allowing full-screen raster scanning at video rate.

nodes.name: Coherer - primitive radio detector
nodes.note: A tube of glass filled with iron filings between two metal plugs. When RF current (from a radio signal) passes through, the filings cohere (stick together), dropping resistance from 1 megohm to 1000 ohms. A relay responds to this current change, signalling the received dot or dash. After each signal, a tapper mechanically shakes the tube to decohere the filings. Unreliable and slow (tapping delay), but it was the only radio detector before solid-state rectifiers.

nodes.name: Compiler and high-level programming language
nodes.note: A language like FORTRAN or ALGOL (not machine code) that expresses computations in human terms. A compiler translates source code to machine code. The breakthrough: programmers no longer need to think in bits and registers. They write mathematics and logic directly. Compilers handle optimization, memory allocation, and code generation. FORTRAN (1957) became the standard for scientific computing. This raised the abstraction level from machines to problems. [AUDIT: State interest and suspicion were unset and have been defaulted from the category.]

nodes.name: Comptometer - key-driven calculator
nodes.note: Instead of a crank (one operation per second), the Comptometer (1887 onward) uses keys (one per digit). Pressing a key lever multiple times increments that digit, accumulating the sum. Touch typists could use Comptometers almost as fast as they thought of numbers. Faster than Arithmometer. The innovation is that the operator interface is ergonomic and intuitive (press 5 five times to add 5), not just mechanical optimization.

nodes.name: Continuous wave (CW) generation with triode
nodes.note: A triode acts as an amplifier: a small signal on the grid amplifies a large signal in the anode. Fed back to the grid through a tuned circuit, this creates sustained oscillation (feedback), generating continuous RF at the resonant frequency. The generator is stable, efficient, and clean (no spark noise). Morse code is sent by turning the oscillator on/off with a telegraph key. Continuous wave replaced spark transmitters by 1920. [AUDIT: capability prerequisite(s) cap_power_electric were inferred by rome/sim/treetool.py repair, not stated by the author. Treat them as a floor, not a specification.]

nodes.name: Substitution and polyalphabetic ciphers
nodes.note: Caesar cipher (shift alphabet by N) was known to Rome. Vigenere cipher (shift depends on a repeating key) was stronger (1553 onward). Both are vulnerable to frequency analysis (common letters are obvious). The Vigenere cipher remained unbroken until the 19th century (Kasiski examination), making it militarily useful for 300 years. Encryption was the luxury of armies and empires; telegraph traffic required it, making cryptography a core technology. nodes.name: Crystal set receiver - galena rectifier radio
nodes.note: A tuned coil and capacitor select one radio station, a galena rectifier converts the RF signal to audio (crystal detects, headphones reproduce). Crystal sets were toys in 1910, but mass-produced for every youth by 1920. They taught radio to the world, but they are obsolete once vacuum tube amplifiers exist. nodes.name: Difference engine - mechanical polynomial solver
nodes.note: A mechanism that uses the method of differences to evaluate polynomials and tabulate mathematical functions. Babbage built a working prototype in 1832, but the complete engine was never finished. Reason: tolerances. Brass expands and contracts with temperature (5 metres of machinery spans 0.5 mm over 10 degrees Celsius), cams wear, precision degrades. 19th century machine tools could hold 0.1 mm tolerances; the engine needed 0.01 mm consistency. It was engineering overreach, not a bad idea.

nodes.name: Duplex telegraphy - simultaneous two-way transmission
nodes.note: A simple telegraph line is half-duplex: one side transmits while the other listens. Duplex uses a bridge circuit (Wheatstone bridge) to cancel your own transmitted signal at your receiver, so you hear only the far end. The trick: send your signal balanced (symmetrical) through two wires to ground so your receiver sees it as zero, but the asymmetrical current flowing through the line carries the signal. Doubles line capacity.

nodes.name: Error detecting and correcting codes
nodes.note: Parity bit (odd/even) detects single-bit errors. Hamming codes detect and correct single-bit errors. More powerful codes (Reed-Solomon, convolutional) can correct multiple errors. Used in memory (cosmic ray bit flips), transmission (noise corruption), and storage (magnetic media decay). The principle: add redundancy (extra bits) that encodes a checksum. On reception, recompute the checksum; if it mismatches, an error occurred and can be located/corrected. [AUDIT: State interest and suspicion were unset and have been defaulted from the category.]

nodes.name: Flip-flop circuit - one-bit memory
nodes.note: Two relays (or vacuum tube stages) cross-coupled: output of one feeds input of the other. The system has two stable states: relay A on and B off, or vice versa. A pulse on 'Set' line (via a contact closure) fires relay A, which holds itself on. A pulse on 'Reset' line fires relay B, which forces A off. This is a one-bit storage element: it 'remembers' whether it was last set or reset. The flip-flop is the foundation of all memory and state machines. nodes.name: Frequency modulation (FM) - superior radio broadcast
nodes.note: Audio signal varies the frequency of the RF carrier instead of the amplitude. A 100 MHz carrier modulated with 1 kHz audio swings ±75 kHz. FM is immune to amplitude noise (static, ignition noise), so reception is much quieter. Bandwidth is about 10x wider than AM (200 kHz for 15 kHz audio), requiring wider channel spacing. Requires sophisticated receivers (discriminators, limiters). Adopted late (1940s in consumer radio) due to infrastructure cost, but ultimately superior.

nodes.name: Heliograph - sun mirror telegraph
nodes.note: A polished mirror reflects sunlight to encode Morse dots and dashes. Works in daylight at range up to 50 km. Lighter and cheaper than optical towers. Cannot work at night or in cloud. The constraint is weather: an overcast day stops all communication, but the apparatus itself is simpler and more portable. nodes.name: Hollerith tabulation - punched card data processing
nodes.note: Punched cards record data (census: age, occupation, birthplace, etc., each in a column). A machine reads the holes and closes electromagnetic switches, incrementing counters. The 1890 U.S. Census was tallied in months instead of years. This created data processing as an industry: IBM emerged from tabulating machines. The insight: data can be stored and processed mechanically, and this is faster than manual accounting. nodes.name: Information theory - entropy and the bit
nodes.note: Shannon's theory (1948): information is measured in bits (binary digits). Entropy quantifies the average number of bits needed to encode a message. A channel's capacity (bits per second) sets the maximum transmission rate. Compression algorithms reduce redundancy (entropy coding). This theory unified communication, storage, and computation under one mathematical framework. Every modern system (networks, storage, codes) is designed using information theory. nodes.name: Integrated circuit - many transistors on one chip
nodes.note: A single silicon chip (1 cm square) with thousands of transistors and resistors, interconnected by metal lines. The Small Scale Integration (SSI, 1960s) level put 10-100 components on a chip. Later: LSI (1000-10000), VLSI (millions), and beyond. The innovation is not a single transistor but the entire ecosystem: design tools, fabrication processes, testing, and assembly. One chip replaces a circuit board full of discrete components. Cost per transistor drops exponentially.

nodes.name: Jacquard loom - punched card control
nodes.note: A loom with thousands of vertical threads (warp). A deck of punched cards controls which threads are lifted on each pass of the shuttle. Complex patterns (brocade, damask) can be woven automatically. This was the first programmable machine: change the cards and the output changes. The innovation is separating control (the cards) from mechanism (the loom). This idea was revolutionary and inspired Babbage's Analytical Engine. nodes.name: Loading coil - range extension for telegraph lines
nodes.note: A coil of wire inserted periodically into a long telegraph or telephone line. Wire acts as a capacitor that stores charge; the coil inductance smooths it out. This compensates for cable distortion and allows signals to travel further before attenuation kills them. A loading coil every 2 km extends range from 50 km to 500 km on a submarine cable. The physics is: inductance and capacitance in series form a filter that attenuates high frequencies (noise) less than the signal distortion.

nodes.name: Logic gate - elementary switching circuit
nodes.note: A circuit that implements Boolean logic: AND (output high if all inputs high), OR, NOT, NAND, NOR. Diodes and resistors suffice for simple gates. Transistors give active amplification (necessary for cascading gates). By the 1960s, logic gates were the design vocabulary for digital systems. A computer is built by combining gates into larger functions (adder, multiplier, controller). The innovation is recognizing that Boolean algebra and circuits are the same thing. [AUDIT: State interest and suspicion were unset and have been defaulted from the category.]

nodes.name: Magnetic core memory - fast addressable RAM
nodes.note: Toroidal ferrite cores (0.5 mm) arranged in a 2D grid (64x64 cores = 4096 bits). Each core stores 1 bit (magnetized clockwise or counter-clockwise). Access time is 1 microsecond (1000x faster than tape). Each core is addressed by X and Y wires (select row and column), read and write wires complete the circuit. Core memory was the standard for mainframe computers (1960s-1970s) until semiconductor RAM replaced it. Handwiring a core array took weeks.

nodes.name: Magnetic drum storage - early rotating memory
nodes.note: A cylinder coated with iron oxide, rotating at 3600 RPM. Read/write heads are stationary, positioned around the drum. Average access time is half a rotation (8 ms). Faster than tape, but requires synchronization with the rotating medium. Used as main memory in early computers (1950s) and later as auxiliary storage. Eventually replaced by moving-head disk drives (faster, fewer mechanical issues).

nodes.name: Magnetic tape storage - bulk archival memory
nodes.note: Paper or plastic tape coated with iron oxide, wound on reels. Data is stored sequentially (cannot directly access the middle). Cheap storage for large datasets (gigabytes on a compact reel). Speed is slow (minutes to locate a record). Used for daily backups, program storage, and archival data. IBM's System/360 (1965) relied on tape for I/O. Magnetic tape remained standard until optical media and solid-state storage arrived.

nodes.name: Magnetic wire storage - first practical memory
nodes.note: Steel wire wound on a reel, magnetized by a coil (1 bit = magnetized forward or backward). Access time is slow (wait for the right section of wire to pass the read/write head, like tape), but storage is cheap and non-volatile (data survives power loss). Used for audio recording and computer memory (1940s-1950s). Superseded by magnetic tape (cheaper) and later by core memory (faster). The innovation: ferromagnetism stores data, not mechanical position.

nodes.name: Mechanical calculator - Pascal and Leibniz designs
nodes.note: A desktop mechanism with gears and stepped drums that performs addition, subtraction, and multiplication by repeated addition. Operator cranks and manipulates dials. Precision is critical: gears must mesh smoothly, and carries must propagate correctly through multiple decades. Hand-made calculators were expensive (200+ hours labor) and slow (1 operation per minute). But they were used by accountants for payroll and bookkeeping.

nodes.name: Morse code - dot, dash, space encoding
nodes.note: Morse code is not a hardware innovation; it is a language for the telegraph. Dots and dashes match the sounder's 'click' and 'hold', encoded by hand at the key. The genius is that it is rhythmic and acoustic: a skilled operator hears the message, not reading visual symbols. Fast hands can send 30 words per minute.

nodes.name: Morse register - recording apparatus
nodes.note: An electromagnetic solenoid pulls a stylus down onto a paper tape moving past it. When current flows, the dot or dash is recorded as a mark. The register was the original telegraph receiver: it married mechanical motion to electrical signal. A human operator then reads the tape and transcribes the message. The key limitation: without a sounder (sound output), it was slow to read and error-prone.

nodes.name: Morse sounder - audio telegraph receiver
nodes.note: A solenoid pulls an armature down onto a metal block (click), springs push it back (click). Morse is designed to be heard: a short current = dot sound, long current = dash sound. This was the killer innovation: skilled operators hear the message directly instead of squinting at paper tape. It increased speed tenfold. The sounder, not the relay, is the human interface to telegraphy.

nodes.name: Multiplexing - combining multiple signals on one line
nodes.note: Time-division multiplexing: 4 calls take turns using the same trunk line, each getting 1/4 of the time (switching at 1000 Hz, fast enough that voice sounds continuous). Frequency-division: use different frequency bands on the same line. Both require precision filters and were impractical until vacuum tube amplifiers. The principle: more calls per cable = more revenue per infrastructure dollar. [AUDIT: capability prerequisite(s) cap_vac_1torr were inferred by rome/sim/treetool.py repair, not stated by the author. nodes.name: Napier's bones - calculating rods
nodes.note: Rods with multiplication tables engraved in rows (one rod for each digit 0-9). To multiply 45*67, lay out the 4 and 5 rods, read the rows for 6 and 7, add diagonally. Reduces multiplication to table-lookup and addition. Slow compared to memorized multiplication, but eliminates error. Used by merchants and accountants. Fell out of use by 1700 as slide rules became popular, but conceptually important (separation of the multiplication table into components that can be recombined). [AUDIT: capability prerequisite(s) cap_tol_100um were inferred by rome/sim/treetool.py repair, not stated by the author. Treat them as a floor, not a specification.]

nodes.name: One-time pad - information-theoretically secure cipher
nodes.note: A random key, used once, added to plaintext bit-by-bit (XOR). No amount of codebreaking can recover the plaintext without the key (Shannon's proof, 1945). The catch: you must generate, securely transmit, and store a key as long as the message. For millions of messages, this is impractical (key logistics). Used for highest-security traffic (Red Phone, diplomatic cables). The OTP is the gold standard, but its key distribution is a nightmare.

nodes.name: Codebook for optical signal tower
nodes.note: Not the tower itself, but the agreed language it speaks. Without a standardised codebook (a government document), each tower operator invents his own alphabet. The innovation is making it systematic: three-position arms encode 8 letters per second in groups (like Morse). Requires coordination across the empire.

nodes.name: Optical semaphore tower
nodes.note: Tall wooden or brick tower with rotating wooden arms on three axes (shutter positions: open, half, closed). Operator turns cranks to set position, next tower sees it through telescope, relays instantly. No power needed. Can send 20 words per minute across 100 km chain. The killer innovation: a message travels the length of France in hours instead of weeks. nodes.name: Photolithography - precision pattern transfer
nodes.note: UV light exposes a photoresist layer (thin polymer) through a mask. Exposed regions polymerize, unexposed regions dissolve. The pattern is then etched into the silicon with acid, creating trenches and ridges. This process repeats dozens of times (layers of metal, oxide, silicon). Feature size starts at 10 micrometers (1970), shrinks to 1 micrometer (1980), 0.1 micrometer (1995), and continues. Photolithography is the core of all semiconductor manufacturing.

nodes.name: Public-key cryptography - RSA and successors
nodes.note: A key pair: public key (known to all) encrypts, private key (secret) decrypts. Asymmetric encryption (different keys for encode/decode) solves key distribution: no need to send a shared secret. RSA (1977) bases security on integer factorization (hard for large numbers). Each party publishes their public key; anyone can encrypt for them, only they can decrypt. This invented secure communication without pre-shared keys: revolutionary for email, web, and digital signatures.

nodes.name: Quadruplex telegraphy - four signals on one wire
nodes.note: Quadruplex uses two independent duplex channels on the same wire: one at high current (positive), one at low current (negative). Requires precise impedance matching and filtering. The circuit is fragile (crosstalk is constant enemy), but it quadruples capacity. Thomas Edison's major telegraphy innovation. Marginal returns made it uneconomical by the 1900s, but it did prove the principle: multiplex the line, not the wire.

nodes.name: Magnetron - compact high-power microwave generator
nodes.note: A thermionic tube with a hot cathode that emits electrons, a strong axial magnetic field that curves them into a circular path, and resonant cavities around the periphery. Electrons oscillate between cavities, exchanging energy with the RF field. The result: very high power (kilowatts) at very high frequency (microwave, 9 GHz). Compact because the wavelength is tiny. Invented in 1939, it was classified as a weapon; it made radar practical for aircraft detection. nodes.name: Spark transmitter - radio broadcast generator
nodes.note: A high-voltage battery (5000 V) charged a capacitor that discharged across an air gap, creating a spark. The spark radiates radio waves across a broad spectrum. A telegraph key interrupts the spark stream, encoding Morse code. Inefficient (most energy is heat and light), unreliable (spark gap is erratic), and creates tons of radio interference across all frequencies. But it works and requires no vacuum tubes. Replaced by continuous wave (CW) generation after 1915. [AUDIT: capability prerequisite(s) cap_power_electric were inferred by rome/sim/treetool.py repair, not stated by the author. nodes.name: Register - multi-bit storage and transfer
nodes.note: Multiple flip-flops (one per bit) cascaded: an 8-bit register holds 8 bits. A control pulse transfers data into the register (latch), or shifts the data left/right (shift register). Registers are the basic building blocks of CPU architecture: accumulator (for arithmetic), memory buffer (for I/O), instruction register (for control). Every arithmetic operation reads from registers and writes back to them. [AUDIT: State interest and suspicion were unset and have been defaulted from the category.]

nodes.name: Relay - current amplification for long lines
nodes.note: A weak current (from the distant telegraph key) flows through a solenoid, pulling a switch that closes a local circuit with a strong battery. This solves the fundamental problem: telegraph wire has resistance; after 100 km, the signal is too weak to operate the sounder. A relay at each station regenerates the signal at full strength. Without relays, the telegraph network stops at about 50 km. With relays, it can span continents.

nodes.name: Relay computer - automated logic and arithmetic
nodes.note: A computer built entirely from relays (Zuse Z1-Z3, 1930s-1940s). Thousands of relays form registers, accumulators, and adders. A paper tape feeds instructions, step by step. The computer executes addition and subtraction in one second per operation. Multiply takes 20 seconds. The machine works, but it is slow, loud, and unreliable (relays stick, wear out). Replaced by vacuum tube computers (1000x faster) by 1950. The relay computer proved the principle: automation of calculation is feasible.

nodes.name: Ring counter - timing and sequencing circuit
nodes.note: A shift register with the output of the last stage fed back to the input. A single 1-bit propagates around the ring. On each clock pulse, the 1 moves to the next position. This generates a sequence of pulses on N different output lines, one line active at a time. Used for timing and sequencing in computers: generating control signals for memory access, ALU operations, etc. Simple and reliable, particularly in relay computers. [AUDIT: State interest and suspicion were unset and have been defaulted from the category.]

nodes.name: Rotor cipher machine - Enigma and successors
nodes.note: A rotor (circular disk) with internal wiring that implements a substitution. As you type, each rotor rotates one position (like an odometer), changing the substitution. Three to five rotors in sequence give enormous key space (26^N combinations). The Enigma machine (1923 onward) was adopted by German military and was believed unbreakable until codebreakers (Turing, Rejewski) found flaws. The rotor machine was the standard for military encryption until electronics arrived.

nodes.name: Semiconductor diode - p-n junction rectifier
nodes.note: A junction between p-type (hole-doped) and n-type (electron-doped) semiconductor. Forward bias allows current flow (low resistance), reverse bias blocks it (high resistance). Used as rectifier (AC to DC), detector, and digital switch. Silicon and germanium diodes were reliable by 1952. In logic, diodes replace vacuum tubes: smaller, cooler, longer-lived. The key is that the diode's threshold voltage sets the logic swing (0-5V typical). [AUDIT: State interest and suspicion were unset and have been defaulted from the category.]

nodes.name: Signal flags for maritime communication
nodes.note: Flags of different colours and patterns, read at distance. First step beyond simple smoke: it is quick, daylight-reliable, and needs no line-of-sight relay network. A ship can read flags from another ship miles away. Codebook is implicit in sailor tradition.

nodes.name: Slide rule - mechanical multiplier
nodes.note: Two wooden rules with logarithmic scales, aligned by hand and compared visually. To multiply 5*7, you find 5 on one scale and 7 on the other, align them, and read 35 off the fixed scale. Uses the log identity: log(a*b)=log(a)+log(b). Accuracy is 3 digits, good enough for engineering work. Ubiquitous by 1900, slide rules were the dominant calculation tool until electronic calculators (1970s). Simple, cheap, and fast enough for design iteration. nodes.name: Stepped drum - mechanical counter and incrementor
nodes.note: A drum with 10 pins at different radial distances (0 to 9 steps). A rotating arm engages the appropriate pin and lifts a counter register once per turn. Used in Pascal's and Leibniz's calculators to perform addition and carry-over (successive addition is multiplication). The stepped drum was a brilliant mechanical innovation, but hand-cranked operation was tedious. Every mechanical calculator from 1600 onward used this principle or something similar. nodes.name: Stock ticker - financial telegraph terminal
nodes.note: A telegraph receiver modified to print stock prices and ticker symbols on a paper tape instead of requiring manual transcription. A ticker in each brokerage receives the same broadcast telegraph signal from the exchange, all printing simultaneously. The innovation is not technical but economic: it creates a new product (real-time pricing data) and a new business model (subscription service). The telegraph system becomes a data distribution network.

nodes.name: Stored program computer - code as data in memory
nodes.note: The conceptual breakthrough: a program is data. Instead of hand-rewiring circuits (ENIAC, 1945), the program sits in memory as numbers. The computer fetches each instruction, decodes it, and executes it. Changing the program is trivial (rewrite memory). This is Babbage's Analytical Engine concept finally realized in electronics. Every computer since has this architecture (von Neumann). This distinction (code vs. data, processor vs. memory) is fundamental. [AUDIT: State interest and suspicion were unset and have been defaulted from the category.]

nodes.name: Strowger automatic exchange - mechanical switching
nodes.note: A caller dials pulses on the handset (1=one pulse, 2=two pulses, etc). These pulses drive a stepper motor which rotates a wiper across a grid of contacts, selecting the called party's line. No human operator needed. The 1890 Strowger exchange was a mechanical marvel: 100 stepper units could handle 10,000 lines. Reliability was marginal (mechanical wear, misalignment), but no wage bill. Replaced manual exchanges over 30 years. The real innovation is replacing human labor with electromechanics.

nodes.name: Submarine telegraph cable
nodes.note: A copper core (signal), wrapped in gutta percha (insulator), wrapped in steel armour, laid on the ocean floor. PROBLEM: Gutta percha is unobtainable (tropical tree). SUBSTITUTE: Use rubber-impregnated cloth (expensive) or pitch-soaked jute, accepting higher leakage. The cable capacitance is enormous; signals attenuate and blur over 3000 km. Needs a relay every 500 km, but submersion makes access impossible. Solution: repeater amplifiers at each end only.

nodes.name: Superheterodyne receiver - fixed intermediate frequency design
nodes.note: Instead of amplifying the RF signal directly (hard at high frequencies), a mixer combines the received signal with a local oscillator, producing a difference frequency (intermediate frequency, typically 455 kHz or 10.7 MHz). Tuning changes only the local oscillator; the intermediate frequency is fixed and easy to amplify. This is the most important radio innovation after AM: it made high-gain, selective receivers practical. Nearly all radio since 1920 is superheterodyne.

nodes.name: Telegraph power supply - voltaic cells in series
nodes.note: Telegraph stations need reliable, large current (amps, not milliamps). A Daniell cell or Grove cell in series provides 1-2 volts. A telegraph key and relay need about 1 amp at 10-100 volts. The maintenance burden is high: cells need refilling, electrodes corrode, acid must be managed safely. This cost and complexity drives later adoption of central powerhouses.

nodes.name: Carbon microphone - pressure-to-resistance transducer
nodes.note: Sound waves move a diaphragm that presses down on loose carbon granules. Pressure changes resistance. A steady current through the carbon, modulated by this resistance change, creates a modulated signal that can be sent down a telegraph wire. The key: carbon is cheap, robust, and changes resistance reliably from 100 to 1000 ohms with pressure. Early telephone transmitters were simple and effective.

nodes.name: Diaphragm receiver - electromagnet hearing aid
nodes.note: A thin iron diaphragm is magnetized by an electromagnet. Modulated current in the coil varies the magnetic field, moving the diaphragm in and out, creating sound waves. No power source needed at the receiver (signal current from the microphone drives it). Early telephone receivers were just magnets and thin iron discs, very similar to telegraph sounders. The diaphragm must be flat enough and thin enough to vibrate freely at audio frequencies.

nodes.name: Manual switchboard exchange
nodes.note: A grid of copper jacks (one per subscriber line), with plug cords and a central battery supplying current to all lines. An operator plugs a caller's line into the called party's line, completing a circuit. The breakthrough: no longer does each person need a separate wire to every other person. A central office with 100 operator positions can switch 10,000 customers with 100 lines. Manual exchanges require hundreds of staff and are limited by operator speed (one plug per second).

nodes.name: Teleprinter - automated telegraph typing
nodes.note: Operator types on a keyboard (like a typewriter). Solenoids pull levers that position type wheels for each character, a hammer fires on command, the character prints on paper, and the whole sequence is transmitted as electrical pulses down the telegraph line. The receiving teleprinter receives the same pulses and reproduces each character. No skilled Morse operator needed; anyone who can type can use a teleprinter. Slower than Morse (40 words/minute vs. 100+), but usable by clerical staff.

nodes.name: Triode oscillator - audio and RF frequency synthesis
nodes.note: A triode with feedback can generate any frequency from audio (10 Hz) to microwave (1000 MHz), tuned by the LC circuit. The oscillation amplitude is limited by the triode's power supply and efficiency. Used in radio transmitters, local oscillators for superheterodyne receivers, and audio oscillators for music synthesis. The triode is THE electronic oscillator until solid-state transistors arrive.

nodes.name: Trunk lines - long-distance telephone routes
nodes.note: Heavy-gauge copper wire strung on poles between cities, with loading coils every 2 km. A trunk line connects two exchanges, not individual subscribers. Calls are routed: local exchange A -> trunk to distant exchange B -> local delivery. The killer problem: telephone signals attenuate badly over distance. A 50 km trunk line needs repeater amplifiers every 15 km, which requires vacuum tubes (not available until 1915). Before that, trunk lines were limited to 50-100 km range. [AUDIT: capability prerequisite(s) cap_vac_1torr were inferred by rome/sim/treetool.py repair, not stated by the author. Treat them as a floor, not a specification.]

nodes.name: Tuned LC circuit and resonance
nodes.note: An inductor (coil) and capacitor in series, tuned so that capacitive and inductive reactances cancel at a chosen frequency. At resonance, the impedance is minimum (current maximum), and the circuit selects only that frequency, rejecting others. This is THE solution to radio crowding: without tuning, all radio stations interfere. With tuning, each receiver selects one station and rejects the rest. Frequency = 1/(2*pi*sqrt(L*C)). A variable capacitor lets listeners tune across the band.

nodes.name: Electronic camera tube (iconoscope) - real-time image capture
nodes.note: A vacuum tube where an electron beam scans a photosensitive mosaic (thousands of tiny silver-mica capacitors). Light on each capacitor charges it; the beam discharges each spot sequentially, producing a current proportional to light. This is a camera: it converts an optical image to an electrical signal suitable for transmission. The iconoscope was unreliable (mosaic damage, burn-in), but it launched electronic television and was the standard for decades.

nodes.name: Mechanical television scanning - early image transmission
nodes.note: A spinning disc with holes arranged in a spiral (Nipkow disc) scans an image line by line. Light from the scene passes through a hole onto a selenium photocell, which modulates current proportional to brightness. This signal is transmitted by radio; a receiver feeds it to a similar spinning disc, with light shining behind it, reconstructing the image on a screen. The whole system is mechanical, unreliable, and limited to about 30 lines of resolution. Electronic television replaced it by 1935.

nodes.name: Raster scan and synchronisation
nodes.note: The beam scans left-to-right (fast sweep), then retraces to the left (blanking), then drops one line down (slow sweep). It repeats 60 times per second (60 Hz frame rate), scanning 525 lines (NTSC) or 625 lines (PAL). At the receiver, an oscilloscope (CRT) must scan in exact synchronism. A sync pulse in the transmitted signal tells the receiver when each line begins and when each frame begins. Without tight synchronisation, the image tears and jitters. This is engineering at the microsecond level.

nodes.name: Vacuum tube computer - high-speed electronic switching
nodes.note: ENIAC (1945): 18,000 vacuum tubes, 150 kilowatts, does 5,000 additions per second (instead of 1 per second with relays). The tube acts as an electronic switch: no moving parts, microsecond speed. The killer limitation: reliability. Tubes fail constantly (one failure every 30 minutes). Maintenance requires replacing tubes and debugging. This drove the search for a smaller, more reliable switch: the transistor.

nodes.name: Pentode vacuum tube - suppressor grid output stage
nodes.note: A tetrode with a fifth electrode (suppressor grid, at cathode potential) that prevents secondary electrons from the anode reaching the screen. This was a problem in tetrodes (screen current wasted power). A pentode has higher efficiency and better linearity. It became the standard audio output tube and RF power tube from 1930 onward. Five or more grids became common in specialized tubes (hexode, heptode) for mixing and frequency conversion. [AUDIT: State interest and suspicion were unset and have been defaulted from the category.]

nodes.name: Tetrode vacuum tube - screen grid amplifier
nodes.note: A triode with an added fourth electrode (screen grid), held at a positive but lower voltage than the anode. The screen shields the anode from the control grid, preventing feedback and allowing higher gain without oscillation. A tetrode is more stable and more powerful than a triode, better for RF amplifiers. The voltage between screen and cathode must be regulated, adding circuit complexity. By the 1930s, tetrodes replaced triodes in most high-power applications. [AUDIT: State interest and suspicion were unset and have been defaulted from the category.]

nodes.name: Waveguide - pipe for microwaves
nodes.note: At microwave frequencies (GHz), conventional wires radiate their signal into space (useless). A rectangular copper tube confines the microwave to propagate only in the TM01 mode (specific to the tube dimensions). Loss is low, and the signal is contained. Waveguide is like a plumbing system for microwaves: you assemble it with flanges and bolts, couple to a magnetron at one end and an antenna at the other. This solved the long-standing problem of transmitting high-frequency signals over distance.

nodes.name: Fire-refined copper stock
nodes.note: Poling and fire refining to get copper clean enough to draw into long fine wire without breaking. A separate node from electro-refining because you need it before you have any electricity.

nodes.name: High-purity copper and insulated wire
nodes.note: You have no rubber and no gutta percha and will not have either. Silk wrapping, oiled linen, shellac varnish from the Indian trade, and bitumen for cables. Impurities in copper cost you conductivity badly, so fire-refine now and electro-refine as soon as you have current to spare.

nodes.name: Print and disperse hundreds of copies across three continents
nodes.note: THE highest expected-value node in the tree, and it is cheap. The lesson of Alexandria is not that books burn, it is that single copies burn. Push copies into every library, temple archive and private collection from Britain to India. This is what carries the programme through 235-284 AD. CALENDAR FLOOR is set by diffusion, not by construction: the economy needs roughly a generation to train the trades, form the capital and build the suppliers. Money cannot buy this down. Same objection as the press, multiplied. Hundreds of copies of a technical corpus in private hands is exactly what an anxious regime dislikes. Present it as a gift to the libraries of the Empire and give the first copies to the emperor's own foundations.

nodes.name: Write the corpus: everything you know, in plain quantitative Greek and Latin
nodes.note: The largest single call on your personal hours in the entire game, and the one you must not cut. Write plainly and with numbers. The alchemists' habit of deliberate obscurity destroyed centuries of work. Assume every reader is competent and knows nothing.

nodes.name: Crank, connecting rod, flywheel, cam and trip hammer
nodes.note: Not attested in the Roman world until the Hierapolis sawmill relief, c. 3rd century. One afternoon for a good carpenter. Unlocks sawmills, ore stamps, forge hammers, pumps and eventually every engine. [AUDIT: capability prerequisite(s) cap_heat_1100 were inferred by rome/sim/treetool.py repair, not stated by the author. Treat them as a floor, not a specification.]

nodes.name: Legume rotation, heavy plough, marling, selective breeding
nodes.note: Columella already recommends legumes; the systematic three-field rotation and controlled comparison are yours. Slow because you cannot rush a growing season, which is why the yrs floor is 6. Feeds the surplus population that a technical civilisation requires and buys you enormous goodwill.

nodes.name: Crucible steel
nodes.note: Melt blister steel in a closed crucible so the composition homogenises and the slag separates. The crucible surviving 1600 C is the hard part and is why this waits on good refractories. Gate on every cutting tool, every lead screw, and therefore on all precision. CALENDAR FLOOR is set by diffusion, not by construction: the economy needs roughly a generation to train the trades, form the capital and build the suppliers. Money cannot buy this down.

nodes.name: Copper-iron brine cell
nodes.note: A poor cell, and you can have it on arrival. Copper and iron in brine give roughly 0.4 to 0.7 volts with high internal resistance, and it polarises within minutes. It will not electroplate and it will not electrolyse water usefully. It WILL deflect a compass needle and it will bias a galena crystal, which means the crystal rectifier and the first electrical measurements do not have to wait thirty years for zinc metal. Use it as the teaching instrument and the proof of concept, then replace it the day the pile exists.

nodes.name: Daniell cell and reliable current sources
nodes.note: The two-solution design stops polarisation, so the cell holds its voltage for hours instead of minutes. Around 1.1 volts and dependable, which is what makes telegraphy and electroplating practical rather than theatrical. [AUDIT: capability prerequisite(s) cap_power_water were inferred by rome/sim/treetool.py repair, not stated by the author. Treat them as a floor, not a specification.]

nodes.name: Destructive distillation of wood and coal
nodes.note: Wood gives methanol, acetic acid, tar and charcoal. Coal gives coke, coal gas, coal tar and ammonia liquor. Coal tar is the gateway to phenol, benzene, aniline dyes and eventually plastics; coal gas gives you street lighting, which is a spectacular and profitable public benefaction.

nodes.name: Rotary and mercury diffusion pumps
nodes.note: Gets you from roughly 1e-4 to 1e-6 torr and below, which is what vacuum tubes and later semiconductor processing require. Needs a motor for the backing pump, so it waits on the electrical programme.

nodes.name: Discharge tubes, cathode rays, X-rays, the electron
nodes.note: You already know the answers, so this is instrument building rather than discovery and it compresses enormously. Medical radiography will make you famous and, if you are careless, will kill your operators. Publish the dose warnings before the first demonstration; the early history of X-rays is a catalogue of amputations.

nodes.name: Worm condenser, distilled spirits, essential oils
nodes.note: Alexandrian alchemists already have alembics; the worm condenser is the missing part. Rose attar and other essential oils carry the margin. Also gives you your first laboratory solvent and your first antiseptic. Do not tell anyone it burns until you have a patron.

nodes.name: The drawplate and drawn wire
nodes.note: Rome makes wire by cutting strip and swaging it. A hardened plate with graded tapered holes, tallow lubricant and annealing between passes gives long round wire cheaply. You will need tens of kilometres for a single dynamo, so build it now and forget about it.

nodes.name: Dynamo with self-excitation
nodes.note: The chicken-and-egg looks fatal: you need a field to make current and an electromagnet needs current. Residual magnetism in the iron core is enough to start it and the output builds itself up. Nobody guesses this and everybody wastes years on permanent magnets. Put it on the millpond shaft you already built. CALENDAR FLOOR is set by diffusion, not by construction: the economy needs roughly a generation to train the trades, form the capital and build the suppliers. Money cannot buy this down.

nodes.name: Chlor-alkali, aluminium and industrial electrochemistry
nodes.note: Aluminium needs cryolite (Greenland) or a synthetic fluoride bath from your own hydrofluoric acid, which is the realistic route for you. Chlorine gives bleach and disinfectant, which loops back into public health. CALENDAR FLOOR is set by diffusion, not by construction: the economy needs roughly a generation to train the trades, form the capital and build the suppliers. Money cannot buy this down.

nodes.name: Electromagnet, relay, and the Wheatstone bridge
nodes.note: Iron amplifying a current's magnetism is the effect on which motors, generators, telegraphs and relays all rest. It is also the most alarming demonstration you will give: heavy iron moving at a distance with no visible cause.

nodes.name: Electroplating and electro-refining
nodes.note: Immediately and enormously profitable: silvered and gilded ware for the rich. It also gives you electrolytically pure copper, which you need for conductors, and it teaches your staff quantitative electrochemistry as a side effect.

nodes.name: Friction machine, Leyden jar, electroscope
nodes.note: Spectacular, cheap, and it produces exactly the kind of effect that gets a man tried for magic. Do it in daylight, in front of a magistrate, and explain it as a property of amber long known to the Greeks, which is even true (elektron is Greek for amber). High voltage, negligible current: useless for chemistry, excellent for persuasion. CORRECTION to an earlier version of this tree: this no longer requires electromagnetic theory. Franklin and Volta had none. Making the theory a prerequisite for the experiment put the whole of calculus on the electrical critical path, which is backwards. The State neither wants this nor forbids it. It simply looks like sorcery, which is a different and worse problem. [AUDIT: capability prerequisite(s) cap_tol_100um were inferred by rome/sim/treetool.py repair, not stated by the author. Treat them as a floor, not a specification.]

nodes.name: Electromagnetic theory
nodes.note: Write it down before you can demonstrate any of it. Faraday's and Maxwell's conclusions handed to a school that can already do calculus collapses a century into a decade.

nodes.name: Endow the institute in land, not coin
nodes.note: Roman testamentary law and the fundatio (Pliny's alimenta, Trajan's own) are durable vehicles. Coin will be debased to nothing by 270 AD. Land will not. This is how the programme outlives you.

nodes.name: Finery forge and the puddling furnace
nodes.note: Cast iron is brittle and useless for anything that must bend. Decarburise it back to wrought iron in a finery, then in a reverberatory puddling furnace where the fuel never touches the metal. Now you have cheap bar iron in quantity, which is the input to everything mechanical.

nodes.name: Buy, train and manumit a technical staff
nodes.note: Buy skilled slaves, teach them, free them, pay them, keep them. Freedmen retain obligation to their patron, can hold property, and ran much of Roman commerce. A paid literate freedman transmits knowledge; a coerced labourer does not. This is both the ethical and the efficient answer. Grants +8 artisans.

nodes.name: Written agricultural treatises and knowledge codification
nodes.note: Codify agricultural knowledge in written treatises: crop rotation schedules, soil types, fertilizer rates, machinery designs, preservation methods. Spreads best practices beyond oral tradition. Requires literacy and sustained scholarship.

nodes.name: Alfalfa (lucerne) cultivation
nodes.note: Perennial legume for permanent meadows; fixes nitrogen, produces 4-6 cuts per season for fodder. Survives winter in warmer regions. Imported from Central Asia; needs good drainage and lime on acid soils. Transforms winter feeding.

nodes.name: Sugar beet cultivation and crystallization
nodes.note: Grow sugar beets in cool northern climates where cane fails. Extract juice, treat with lime and acid to remove impurities (sulfur dioxide helps), evaporate under vacuum, and crystallize. Refinery is capital-intensive. Enables sugar production independent of tropical trade. [AUDIT: capability prerequisite(s) cap_vac_1torr were inferred by rome/sim/treetool.py repair, not stated by the author. Treat them as a floor, not a specification.]

nodes.name: Bone meal as phosphate fertilizer
nodes.note: Collect bones from butchers and boil with manure to break them down and create a phosphate-rich mulch. Slower than guano but reliably produced locally. Improves root development and seed formation.

nodes.name: Bottling with cork closure and sealed glass
nodes.note: Store liquids in strong glass bottles, insert cork and secure with wire or cage. Anaerobic storage preserves wine, beer, vinegar. Glass is Roman technology; cork sealing enables long-term aging and transport. Enables wine trade and aging in cellars.

nodes.name: Brewing with hops for flavor and preservation
nodes.note: Add dried hop flowers to boiling wort; the alpha acids bitter and preserve the beer, preventing spoilage. Replaces gruit (herb mixtures). Grew in southern Germany in the 9th century; spread north over centuries. Enables longer storage and transport of beer.

nodes.name: Can opener device for tin cans
nodes.note: Cutting tool with rotating wheel or wedge to pierce and cut can edge, or butterfly handle lever that turns a cutting wheel around the rim. Arrives decades after cans become common. Without it, consumers use knives and hammers.

nodes.name: Canning by Appert's method (heating in sealed glass)
nodes.note: Pack food in strong glass jar, seal with cork and wire, heat in water bath to 95-100 C for 30-60 minutes depending on acid content. Low-acid foods (meats, vegetables) are risky without understanding of clostridium botulinum and its toxin. Works for high-acid foods (pickles, jams) without germ theory. Revolutionary for food security if done carefully.

nodes.name: Chocolate from cacao (New World, unobtainable)
nodes.note: Chocolate is made from cacao, a New World crop, unobtainable. Ground, fermented cacao nibs mixed with sugar and spices produce luxurious chocolate. Cannot be pursued in this scenario.

nodes.name: Clover as winter grazing and fodder
nodes.note: Nitrogen-fixing legume sown in fallows or as early spring feed; survives winter in milder regions, providing grazing and supplementary hay. Combines nitrogen restoration with animal fodder. Seed production is key constraint.

nodes.name: Coffee import from Near East and Ethiopia
nodes.note: Import coffee beans from Arabian and Ethiopian merchants. Roast, grind, and brew with hot water. Later becomes urban necessity in coffeehouses. Currently rare and expensive in the Mediterranean. [AUDIT: capability prerequisite(s) cap_heat_1100 were inferred by rome/sim/treetool.py repair, not stated by the author. Treat them as a floor, not a specification.]

nodes.name: Cold chain and refrigerated railway shipping
nodes.note: Insulated railway cars with mechanical refrigeration carry fresh meat, dairy, and vegetables hundreds of miles to distant markets. Requires coordination with meatpacking plants, railways, and distribution. Breaks ancient food supply constraints; enables urban growth and meat consumption.

nodes.name: Combine harvester (reaper, thresher, winnower integrated)
nodes.note: Reaper feeds cut grain into threshing drum and winnowing mechanism; discharges bagged grain and straw bales. Steam- or petrol-powered. Requires flat or gentle ground, good visibility, and skilled operators. 20-30 acres per day vs 1 acre hand harvest.

nodes.name: Controlled pollination of crop plants
nodes.note: Hand-pollinate selected plants using brushes to cross desired traits: large seeds with disease resistance, for instance. Works on grains and legumes. Requires understanding flower anatomy and patience; gains compound with pedigree records.

nodes.name: Butter production at scale from dairy cattle
nodes.note: Churn milk in barrel or wooden churn to separate butterfat from buttermilk. Butter stores for months salted in wooden vessels. Higher value than milk for trade. Requires cool cellar and daily production.

nodes.name: Controlled cheese aging and storage
nodes.note: Store cheese wheels in cool caves or cellars; maintain humidity and temperature for months or years. Aged hard cheeses develop flavor and keep indefinitely. Requires careful cave management to prevent mold and rot.

nodes.name: Distillation of spirits and liqueurs
nodes.note: Heat fermented beer or wine in copper alembic with condenser; collect vapors as high-proof spirit. Required copper work and heat control. Spirits store longer than wine and command high prices. Banned in some jurisdictions as luxury and fire hazard.

nodes.name: Drying and concentration of evaporated milk
nodes.note: Heat milk gently in copper pan under partial vacuum (reduces boiling point) or in open pan to evaporate water until thick. Can milk solids are concentrated 2-3 fold. Stores several months in sealed tin. Reconstitutes with water or used directly in cooking. [AUDIT: capability prerequisite(s) cap_vac_1torr were inferred by rome/sim/treetool.py repair, not stated by the author. Treat them as a floor, not a specification.]

nodes.name: Enclosure of common land and private farming
nodes.note: Fence and claim private ownership of formerly communal pasture and fields. Allows strategic crop rotation without community approval. Displaces peasants and common folk; generates social resistance. Enables capital-intensive farming but concentrates wealth and land ownership.

nodes.name: Farm as capital enterprise with investment and profit
nodes.note: Treat farming as a business venture: invest capital in land, buildings, machinery, and labor; track costs and revenue; aim for profit rather than subsistence. Requires accounting, written records, and credit access. Transforms peasant farming into an industrial enterprise.

nodes.name: Large-scale fish curing and smoking
nodes.note: Salt-dry fish over winter, then hang and smoke over oak or beech. Produces shelf-stable protein that survives transport. Atlantic cod and herring can be processed at scale by coastal villages. Cheap protein for armies and urban poor.

nodes.name: Freezing food with mechanical refrigeration
nodes.note: Use mechanical refrigeration to freeze meat, fish, and vegetables at -18 C. Frozen foods preserve for months. Thaw and cook before use. Requires reliable electricity or steam power and insulated freezer chambers.

nodes.name: Cylindrical silos for bulk grain storage
nodes.note: Build tall cylindrical brick or wooden towers for grain storage. Pressure from grain weight above excludes insects and rodents. Chutes at bottom for withdrawal. More efficient than rectangular granaries. Enables large centralized storage for grain dole. [AUDIT: capability prerequisite(s) cap_tol_100um were inferred by rome/sim/treetool.py repair, not stated by the author. Treat them as a floor, not a specification.]

nodes.name: Guano import and application as fertilizer
nodes.note: Import bird guano from coastal cliffs or islands (Peru, North Africa) via merchants. Rich in nitrogen and phosphorus; application can double grain yields locally. Expensive, but supply is predictable. Builds dependency on trade and distant supply chains.

nodes.name: Haber process for synthetic ammonia and nitrate
nodes.note: Compress hydrogen and nitrogen at 200 atmospheres over iron catalyst at 400-500 C to synthesize ammonia; oxidize ammonia to nitric acid. Requires high-pressure steel vessels, control systems, and electric power. Enables synthetic fertilizer production at scale but only late in the tree.

nodes.name: Hay making and dry storage
nodes.note: Cut grass at peak nutrition, dry thoroughly in sun and wind, store in dry barn or haybarn. Timing and weather are critical - rain-soaked hay rots or molts. Enables winter feeding of draft animals when pasture is gone.

nodes.name: Heavy mouldboard plough with coulter (regional)
nodes.note: Heavy plough with iron coulter, share, and mould board on two wheels, drawn by team of oxen. Turns thick clay sods on cold northern soils where the Mediterranean ard is useless. Expensive and slow but enables fertile northern lands. Do not use on light Mediterranean soils. [AUDIT: State interest and suspicion were unset and have been defaulted from the category.]

nodes.name: Horse-drawn hoe for weeding between rows
nodes.note: Simple cultivator or hoe frame pulled by horse along seed drill rows to cut weeds between plants. Requires plants spaced precisely by the drill. Eliminates hand-hoeing drudgery and allows larger plantings.

nodes.name: Ice harvesting from frozen lakes and rivers
nodes.note: Cut blocks of ice from frozen water with saw and chisel during winter thaw, transport quickly to ice house, layer with sawdust or hay. Most ice melts in transport and storage, requiring multiple harvests per winter. Requires cold climate and labor.

nodes.name: Ice house construction and storage
nodes.note: Build underground or half-underground stone or brick chamber with thick insulation (sawdust, straw, or hay). Roof with thatch and timber. Store blocks of winter ice with straw layers. Temperature stays below freezing even in summer if well-insulated. Enables ice cream and chilled foods.

nodes.name: Trade and logistics of ice transport
nodes.note: Transport harvested ice via wagon or ship to towns 50-100 miles away, insulated with sawdust and straw. Arrive with 30-50% loss. Sells to affluent households and restaurants for drinks and food preservation. High loss but profitable if demand is strong. [AUDIT: capability prerequisite(s) cap_tol_100um were inferred by rome/sim/treetool.py repair, not stated by the author. Treat them as a floor, not a specification.]

nodes.name: Liming of acidic soils
nodes.note: Spread quicklime or slaked lime on clay and peat soils to neutralize acidity and improve drainage. Enables cultivation of marginal northern lands. Effects last 5-10 years; must be repeated. Transform intractable soil into productive land.

nodes.name: Selective breeding of draft and dairy cattle
nodes.note: Breed cattle for strength (draft animals) or milk production (dairy cattle) over many generations. Selective breeding can double milk yield or hauling power. Requires pedigree tracking and patience; gains compound over 5-10 years.

nodes.name: Selective breeding of sheep for wool and meat
nodes.note: Breed sheep for fine fleece and lean meat. Selective breeding improves wool fineness and meat quality over generations. Wool becomes higher value product. Requires pedigree tracking.

nodes.name: Maize cultivation (New World, unobtainable)
nodes.note: Maize is a New World crop, unobtainable. Incomparably high yield per hectare and stores well, transforming food security. Cannot be pursued in this scenario.

nodes.name: Malt production from barley and other grains
nodes.note: Soak barley, allow it to germinate, then dry in kiln to stop germination. Malting converts starches to fermentable sugars. Malt stores for months and is essential for brewing consistent beer. Requires cool storage to prevent mold. [AUDIT: capability prerequisite(s) cap_heat_1100 were inferred by rome/sim/treetool.py repair, not stated by the author. Treat them as a floor, not a specification.]

nodes.name: Margarine from refined and hardened vegetable oils
nodes.note: Bubble hydrogen through liquid vegetable oil over nickel catalyst to saturate double bonds and raise melting point. Result resembles butter in texture. Cheaper than dairy butter. Requires understanding of hydrogenation chemistry and high-purity hydrogen.

nodes.name: Mechanical grain reaper
nodes.note: Horse-drawn frame with reciprocating knife blade and conveyor tray delivers cut grain to platform or wagon. Reaps four to six acres per day versus one acre for hand scythe. Requires training and maintenance. Leaves stubble taller than scythe.

nodes.name: Mechanical refrigeration using compression and evaporation
nodes.note: Compress ether or ammonia vapor, cool it with water, then expand through throttle valve to evaporate. Evaporation absorbs heat from a chamber, cooling it to 5-10 C. Requires high-precision pump, copper tubing, and steam power. Toxic if ammonia leaks.

nodes.name: Recognition of nitrogen-fixing legume crops
nodes.note: Understand that legumes (peas, beans, clover, alfalfa) restore soil fertility where grain depletes it; systemize the rotation. Not chemistry, but empirical observation that legume-rich fields grow better grain. Foundation for three-field rotation success.

nodes.name: Pasteurisation of milk and beverages
nodes.note: Heat milk to 63-65 C for 30 minutes or 72 C for 15 seconds, then cool rapidly. Kills spoilage bacteria and pathogens without destroying nutritional value or flavor of fresh milk. Works without germ theory; empirically known to prevent souring and spoilage.

nodes.name: Potato cultivation (New World, unobtainable)
nodes.note: Potato is a New World crop, unobtainable. Note: if somehow acquired (which cannot happen), it has extraordinary yield and stores for months, making it transformative for population growth and army feeding. Cannot be pursued in this scenario.

nodes.name: Rice cultivation in paddies
nodes.note: Cultivate rice in water-filled paddies in warm regions with reliable summer irrigation. Requires leveled fields, water control, and careful timing. High yield per acre but demands labor-intensive transplanting. Imported seed and knowledge from Asia.

nodes.name: Roller mill for grain (replacing millstone)
nodes.note: Pairs of hardened steel rollers crush grain more uniformly than stones. Multiple roller pairs reduce grain progressively, producing finer flour with less grit. Can produce white flour by separating bran. Requires precision machining and hardened steel.

nodes.name: White flour from roller milling and bran separation
nodes.note: Run milled flour through bolters (cylindrical silk screens) to separate white endosperm from brown bran. Produces elegant white bread prized in cities. Bran removal discards B vitamins and niacin; prolonged white-flour diet causes pellagra and beriberi. Major population health risk.

nodes.name: Root cellar and cool storage construction
nodes.note: Dig cool underground chamber below frost line with air vents; temperature stays 4-10 C year-round. Stores turnips, apples, onions, potatoes for months. Requires only soil, timber, and patience; enables winter feeding and food security.

nodes.name: Mechanical seed drill
nodes.note: Hopper with rotating cams or gears deposits seed at regular intervals in furrow. Spacing is controllable. Saves 40-60% of broadcast seed waste and improves germination by consistent burial depth. Requires precision woodwork.

nodes.name: Selective breeding with written pedigrees
nodes.note: Record traits of seed plants and breeding animals over generations; select for yield, disease resistance, or size. Pedigree tracking allows avoiding inbreeding and accumulating improvements. Requires literacy and 5-7 year commitment before visible yield gains.

nodes.name: Silage production and fermented fodder storage
nodes.note: Pack fresh grass tightly in pits or wooden silos with salt, exclude air, and let anaerobic bacteria ferment it. Preserves nutrition without sun-drying and works in wet climates. Requires understanding of fermentation and airtight storage design. [AUDIT: capability prerequisite(s) cap_tol_100um were inferred by rome/sim/treetool.py repair, not stated by the author. Treat them as a floor, not a specification.]

nodes.name: Understanding and testing soil composition
nodes.note: Test soil pH, organic matter, and nutrient content via chemical analysis or simple tests. Informs liming, fertilizer, and crop choices. Precision farming based on data rather than guess.

nodes.name: Sourdough starter culture maintenance
nodes.note: Maintain a living culture of wild yeast and lactic acid bacteria in flour and water. Feed it regularly and use it to leaven bread. Improves flavor and digestibility compared to unleavened bread. Requires discipline but produces superior bread.

nodes.name: Sugar cane cultivation and juice extraction
nodes.note: Grow sugar cane in warm coastal regions, crush stalks with ox-powered mill to extract juice. Simmer juice to crystallize sugar. Imported from Mediterranean and later from tropical colonies. Labor-intensive but high value product.

nodes.name: Superphosphate from bones and sulfuric acid
nodes.note: React bone meal with sulfuric acid to convert insoluble phosphates into soluble form. More effective than guano but requires acid production and handling. Arrives in late agricultural revolution when industrialized.

nodes.name: Tea import and trade channels
nodes.note: Establish merchant contacts for tea via trade routes (by late Roman era via Parthia from China). Expensive, luxury item, consumed hot. Requires trade infrastructure and wealth. Demand creates mercantile networks.

nodes.name: Three-field crop rotation with fallowing
nodes.note: Grain, legume, fallow rotation sustains soil nitrogen and allows continuous cultivation on two-thirds of land; fallow fields provide grazing for animals, multiplying manure. Requires written record-keeping and community coordination.

nodes.name: Mechanical threshing machine
nodes.note: Flailed drum rotating against fixed comb beats grain from heads mechanically, replacing hand flailing. Powered by horses treading or pulled by oxen. Three to five fold increase in threshing speed. Multiplies bottleneck from threshing to grinding.

nodes.name: Tin plate cans for food preservation
nodes.note: Roll thin iron sheet and coat with tin to prevent rust and corrosion from acidic food. Seal with solder or lead. Can be sealed hot for sterilization without glass fragility. Requires rolling mill, tin coating process, and soldering skill. Cans are reusable if handled carefully.

nodes.name: Turnips as storable winter animal feed
nodes.note: High-yield root crop stores in cool cellars through winter, feeding oxen and sheep when pasture dies. Single biggest gain in animal husbandry: overwintered animals produce manure year-round and retain strength for spring ploughing and hauling. Revolutionary.

nodes.name: Oil extraction from seeds and olives
nodes.note: Press rapeseed, walnut, or sesame with mechanical screw press to extract oil for cooking and lamps. Olive oil already exists (tier 0). New seed crops provide additional supply. Oil keeps several months in sealed vessels.

nodes.name: Vinegar production via acetification
nodes.note: Pass fermented wine or weak ale through wood shavings and let acetic bacteria oxidize alcohol to acetic acid. Slower than heating but requires no energy. Preserves excess wine as vinegar for cooking and cleaning. Used medicinally as well.

nodes.name: Organized whaling industry for oil and meat
nodes.note: Organize fleets of whaleboats and processing ships to hunt large whales. Render whale blubber into oil for lamps (the best non-animal oil light). Whale meat is tough but provides protein. Dangerous work; whales fight back. Requires capital and international coordination. [AUDIT: capability prerequisite(s) cap_tol_100um were inferred by rome/sim/treetool.py repair, not stated by the author. Treat them as a floor, not a specification.]

nodes.name: Mechanical winnowing fan
