nodes.note: Rotating fan or hand-cranked blower separates grain from chaff with controlled airstream. Manual winnowing baskets remain for small quantities, but the machine handles output from mechanical threshing. Driven by hand crank or powered by oxen.

nodes.name: Pure yeast culture isolation and maintenance
nodes.note: Isolate yeast strain from wild fermentation by serial dilution and propagation in sterile medium. Maintain culture in sealed glass vials. Enables reproducible beer and bread fermentation without wild cultures. Looks like alchemy; requires careful technique and documentation. [AUDIT: capability prerequisite(s) cap_tol_100um were inferred by rome/sim/treetool.py repair, not stated by the author. Treat them as a floor, not a specification.]

nodes.name: Fused silica working
nodes.note: Needs an oxy-hydrogen flame at roughly 1700-2000 C. Indispensable for the semiconductor endgame: you cannot zone-refine germanium in anything that contaminates it, and quartz is the only affordable material that does not.

nodes.name: Galena cat's whisker point-contact rectifier
nodes.note: A working semiconductor device in Rome, using mineral lead sulfide straight out of the mine and a springy wire. No purification, no doping, no vacuum, no theory. It is nearly free, it is a genuine rectifier, and it is the proof-of-concept that justifies a two-century programme to a sceptical patron. Build it the moment you have a cell and fine wire. It depends on the crude brine cell, not on the voltaic pile, which is what makes the year-three claim in 00_NONOBVIOUS_TRICKS actually true. [AUDIT: capability prerequisite(s) cap_vac_1torr were inferred by rome/sim/treetool.py repair, not stated by the author. Treat them as a floor, not a specification.]

nodes.name: Tangent galvanometer and electrical metrology
nodes.note: A coil of known radius and turn count, a compass needle, and the Earth's field give absolute current from pure geometry, with no calibrated instrument to start from. This solves the electrical metrology bootstrap that otherwise looks circular.

nodes.name: Reduction of germanium dioxide to metal under hydrogen
nodes.note: Hydrogen at roughly 650 C reduces the dioxide to grey powder; melt it into an ingot in a high purity graphite boat under hydrogen. Everything that touches the metal from here on contaminates it, so the boat, the tube and the gas must all be purer than the product. [AUDIT: capability prerequisite(s) cap_pure_6N were inferred by rome/sim/treetool.py repair, not stated by the author. Treat them as a floor, not a specification.]

nodes.name: Germanium tetrachloride fractional distillation
nodes.note: The door. Germanium is a nightmare to purify as metal or oxide and easy as a volatile chloride boiling at about 86 C, which you can fractionate like brandy. Distil repeatedly in a tall packed column, hydrolyse back to the dioxide with ultrapure water, and you are already at parts per million before you have done anything clever. [AUDIT: capability prerequisite(s) cap_pure_6N were inferred by rome/sim/treetool.py repair, not stated by the author. Treat them as a floor, not a specification.]

nodes.name: Coordinate geometry and trigonometric tables
nodes.note: Hipparchus and Ptolemy already have chord tables, so this lands on prepared ground.

nodes.name: Germ theory of disease
nodes.note: The bead microscope makes this demonstrable rather than assertable, which is the whole difference. Galen's humoral theory is the obstacle and it is defended by the entire medical profession.

nodes.name: Germanium concentrate from flue dust and coal ash
nodes.note: Germanium is 1.6 ppm in the crust and essentially never occurs as its own workable ore in reach. Zinc flue dust and certain coal ashes are the realistic sources. The spectroscope is how you find it at all: without emission spectroscopy you would be searching blind for an element nobody has ever seen.

nodes.name: Single-bead microscope
nodes.note: Cost is trivial and the payoff is germ theory, cell biology and a demonstration nobody can dismiss. Build this in your first year. Van Leeuwenhoek out-resolved compound microscopes with it for fifty years.

nodes.name: Borosilicate glass
nodes.note: Needs boron. The Larderello fumaroles in Tuscany emit boric acid and are inside the Empire, which is a genuinely lucky break if it holds; verify on arrival before planning around it. Low thermal expansion is the difference between a laboratory and a pile of broken retorts. [AUDIT: capability prerequisite(s) cap_heat_1300 were inferred by rome/sim/treetool.py repair, not stated by the author. Treat them as a floor, not a specification.]

nodes.name: Deliberately water-clear soda-lime glass to specification
nodes.note: Rome already makes near-colourless glass and already knows pyrolusite is glassmaker's soap. What it does not have is control: iron-free sand chosen deliberately, a weighed manganese dose, and a proper annealing lehr. Cheapest high-value upgrade to a live industry in the Empire. [AUDIT: capability prerequisite(s) cap_heat_1100 were inferred by rome/sim/treetool.py repair, not stated by the author. Treat them as a floor, not a specification.]

nodes.name: Retorts, flasks, condensers, tubing, graduated vessels
nodes.note: The single item that most limits early chemistry. You will break a great deal of it. Until borosilicate, thermal shock is your main enemy: heat on a sand bath, never on a flame.

nodes.name: Corned gunpowder
nodes.note: 75/15/10 by mass, and the ratio is worthless without corning: wet the mix, press the cake, break it into grains, sieve. OPTIONAL AND DANGEROUS. It buys imperial favour instantly and it makes every future usurper more dangerous, including during the Third Century Crisis when you most need the Empire to hold. Recommended: develop the chemistry, withhold the corning, and keep it as a survival card.

nodes.name: Regenerative and forced-draught furnaces to 1600 C+
nodes.note: Siemens regenerative preheat recycles flue heat into the incoming air and is the cheapest route past what charcoal and a bellows can do. Gate on fused quartz, on high-grade steel, and on most of Module 50. CALENDAR FLOOR is set by diffusion, not by construction: the economy needs roughly a generation to train the trades, form the capital and build the suppliers. Money cannot buy this down.

nodes.name: Attar of roses
nodes.note: Distilled rose oil (4 kg of petals for 1 g of oil). Extremely expensive and high-margin. Attar is one of the best early revenue products: small weight, non-perishable, high demand from the wealthy. Bulgarian and Persian atar dominate the market.

nodes.name: Bath with piped hot water
nodes.note: A boiler (steam-driven or later electric) supplies hot water on demand. Luxurious; middle-class homes gain hot water later than wealthy houses. Requires pressurised pipes and heating infrastructure. Modern thermostatic mixing valves prevent scalding.

nodes.name: Board games, dice games, and pieces
nodes.note: Latrunculi (small stones on a board), duodecim scripta (twelve marks, ancestor of backgammon), and knucklebones for gaming. Dice are carved bone or stone.

nodes.name: Button with eyelet
nodes.note: Buttons exist in Rome but are rare and made of stone or bone. The eyelet (sewn loop) adds cost. Horn buttons become viable later with better tools. Buttons displace expensive brooches, freeing wealth.

nodes.name: Beeswax candle
nodes.note: Expensive, clean-burning, fragrant. Beeswax is a byproduct of honey extraction and remains expensive through the early modern period.

nodes.name: Tallow candle
nodes.note: Cheap animal-fat candles; smoky and foul-smelling but accessible to the poor. Tallow is rendered from beef and mutton fat.

nodes.name: Carpet sweeper
nodes.note: Wheeled frame with rotating brush underneath. Push it across carpet to collect dust and lint. No electricity needed. Precedes vacuum cleaners; faster than hand-brushing. Carpet sweepers are labour-replacing and displace sweeping servants. [AUDIT: capability prerequisite(s) cap_vac_1torr were inferred by rome/sim/treetool.py repair, not stated by the author. Treat them as a floor, not a specification.]

nodes.name: Cosmetics with safety warnings
nodes.note: Once germ theory and toxicology establish that white lead causes chronic poisoning, cosmetics reformulate. Lead face paint is phased out; zinc oxide and iron oxides replace it. Labels warn of hazards. Modern cosmetics prioritise safety and truthful marketing. [AUDIT: capability prerequisite(s) cap_heat_1600 were inferred by rome/sim/treetool.py repair, not stated by the author. Treat them as a floor, not a specification.]

nodes.name: Roman cosmetics
nodes.note: Powders, kohl eyeliner, rouge, and white lead face paint (cerussa). The white lead is cosmetically effective but chronically poisoning users. No warning label exists.

nodes.name: Deodorant
nodes.note: Alum or zinc oxide in a fat or powder base. Alum acts as an astringent, reducing sweat and odour. Roman use of alum for textiles; applied to skin for personal use. Modern antiperspirants require aluminium chloride (20th century).

nodes.name: Dishwasher, mechanical and electric
nodes.note: Cochran's 1886 machine uses pressurised water spray, hot water, and soap. Requires a pressurised water supply (pump), a heat source (steam or electric), and a motor. Hot water and soap do most of the work; the machine's innovation is automation and pressure. Kitchen staff is displaced.

nodes.name: Fashion doll with clothing sets
nodes.note: Articulated wooden or bisque doll with interchangeable clothing. Allows girls to dress dolls in fashionable gowns. Drives textile consumption and toy industry growth. Later porcelain and plastic dolls command higher prices; bisque allows fine detail.

nodes.name: Double glazing (two panes)
nodes.note: Two panes of glass with an air gap reduces heat loss by half. Expensive to produce and install; assembly requires careful spacing and lead frame. Widespread only in the 18th-19th centuries as glass prices fall.

nodes.name: Electric fan for air circulation
nodes.note: Small electric motor drives a blade assembly. Expensive initially; prices fall with mass production. Rome would value this enormously in a Mediterranean summer; ceiling punkah fans pulled by servants are the low-tech precursor.

nodes.name: Electric lighting in home
nodes.note: Incandescent bulbs (Edison carbon, then tungsten filament) or arc lamps. Grid electricity required. Replaces gas lamps and kerosene. Cost per lumen falls; brightness increases. Urban electrification spreads from 1880s onward.

nodes.name: Eraser, breadcrumb substitute
nodes.note: Breadcrumbs (white bread preferred) erase pencil marks by mechanical abrasion. Later rubber erasers require natural rubber, which is UNOBTAINABLE. Breadcrumb remains the substitute through the 19th century in resource-limited settings.

nodes.name: Fireplace and chimney
nodes.note: Rome never develops the chimney. The innovation is the flue and draft that draws smoke out of a room while allowing air intake from below. Transforms cold-weather living. Early chimneys are smoky and dangerous; the design improves over centuries.

nodes.name: Flush latrine with running water
nodes.note: Rome has flush latrines connected to running water and sewers, but lacks the water trap. Sewer gas backs up into the house at night when flow stops. This is the fatal gap.

nodes.name: Flush toilet with S-bend water trap
nodes.note: The water trap is the non-obvious critical innovation: standing water in an S-bend or U-bend below the bowl blocks sewer gas from backing into the house. Crapper patents an improved design in 1884. Modern plumbing code mandates traps.

nodes.name: Fountain pen
nodes.note: Ink reservoir under the nib, with capillary feed. Early designs leak; improved feeds (Waterman, Parker) in the 1880s fix this. Replaces dip pens and quills. Refillable or cartridge designs follow; mass production drives prices down.

nodes.name: Wooden furniture
nodes.note: Chairs, tables, beds, and chests. Quality varies from crude to fine (imported citrus wood). Beds are typically frames with rope supports, no springs.

nodes.name: Gas lamp and gasolier
nodes.note: Coal-gas (coke-oven gas) piped to rooms. Brighter than oil lamps but smoky and dangerous (carbon monoxide, explosions). Gas lighting spreads in cities; rural areas remain oil-lit for decades. Gasolier chandeliers replace candles in urban mansions.

nodes.name: Glass windows, wealthy houses
nodes.note: Rare and expensive. Glassblowing technology exists, but glass remains thick, poorly transparent, and valuable. Most windows are oil-paper or shutters.

nodes.name: Central heating by hot water radiator
nodes.note: Boiler in basement or furnace room heats water, which circulates through cast-iron radiators in all rooms. Replaces fireplaces and central stove heating. Enables uniform comfort; transforms house design. Requires piping, a circulating pump, and constant fuel supply.

nodes.name: Hypocaust underfloor heating
nodes.note: Hot air from a furnace flows through hollow spaces beneath the floor. Expensive; only wealthy houses and public baths use it. Rome never develops the chimney, so room heating otherwise requires a brazier and open flame. [AUDIT: capability prerequisite(s) cap_heat_0700 were inferred by rome/sim/treetool.py repair, not stated by the author. Treat them as a floor, not a specification.]

nodes.name: Jigsaw puzzle
nodes.note: Hand-cut wooden jigsaw (using a saw, hence the name). Early puzzles are mounted hand-coloured prints glued to wood, then sawn into interlocking pieces. Expensive and educational for wealthy families.

nodes.name: Kitchen range (cast iron)
nodes.note: A fireplace-integrated cooking structure with a hot surface (cooking plate) and an oven. Cast iron conducts heat evenly. Requires blast furnace for casting; transforms cooking from dangling pots over flames. Labour-displacing for kitchen servants (negative gov).

nodes.name: Argand oil lamp
nodes.note: The flat circular wick and glass chimney allow air circulation from both sides of the flame, increasing brightness 3x over simple lamps. The chimney creates draft, keeping the flame in the hot zone. Oil consumption stays the same; light output soars.

nodes.name: Kerosene lamp
nodes.note: Kerosene (paraffin) burns hotter and cleaner than whale oil or plant oil. Brighter than Argand lamps with less smoke. Requires refined petroleum; supply depends on oil fields and distillation capacity.

nodes.name: Latrine water trap (S-bend)
nodes.note: The water trap is the critical innovation: standing water in an S-bend or U-bend below the toilet bowl blocks sewer gas from backing into the house. Non-obvious but essential for sanitary plumbing. Rome discovers this late or not at all in the West.

nodes.name: Lead and ceramic plumbing
nodes.note: Rome masters lead pipe-making and ceramic drainage. The lead slowly poisons users; Rome's elite show signs of lead poisoning but attribute it to other causes.

nodes.name: Locks and keys
nodes.note: Pin-tumbler locks exist in Egypt; Rome develops excellent examples in bronze and iron. Locks are expensive and a sign of wealth (or slavery).

nodes.name: Mangle and wringer
nodes.note: Paired hard rollers (wood or stone) squeeze water from cloth under pressure. Early mangling flattens linen; later wringer versions extract water faster. Eliminates the wringing-by-hand step; hand-wringer maids face unemployment.

nodes.name: Friction matches
nodes.note: White phosphorus matches ignite easily but cause phosphorus necrosis (rotting jawbone) in workers from chronic exposure. Safety matches use red phosphorus instead, less toxic. Early matches are dangerous to makers and users alike.

nodes.name: Mechanical clock for home
nodes.note: Escapement mechanism converts continuous power (falling weight or spring) into regulated ticks. Medieval clocks are weight-driven with iron verge escapement; later designs use springs. Accuracy improves from hours to minutes as escapements advance.

nodes.name: Metronome
nodes.note: Pendulum-driven clock ticking at adjustable rates for musical practice. Inverted design pivots the weight on a rod. Musicians find it essential; composers use metronome markings to standardise tempo. Early metronomes are wooden; later all-metal designs are more durable.

nodes.name: Mirror, polished bronze
nodes.note: Polished bronze reflects poorly (70-80% at best) and tarnishes. Small, expensive, and slowly replaced by silvered glass mirrors.

nodes.name: Mirror, silvered glass
nodes.note: Mercury and tin amalgam fused to glass back creates a reflective layer (90%+ vs 70% for bronze). Expensive and technically demanding; production moves to Venice in the 13th century. Frames are precious metal or fine wood.

nodes.name: Musical instruments
nodes.note: Lyres, kitharas, flutes, Pan pipes, and percussion. All handmade; quality varies by maker. String instruments require catgut or sinew from animals.

nodes.name: Oil lamp, simple
nodes.note: Rome has simple clay and bronze oil lamps, burning olive oil or animal fat. The innovation ahead is the flat wick and glass chimney, which doubles brightness.

nodes.name: Pencil, graphite in wood
nodes.note: Graphite pencils arrive in the 16th century after graphite discovery in Cumberland. Early designs slot graphite into wood holders; later hexagonal wood casing is carved around it. Graphite is cheap once located; supply is the constraint.

nodes.name: Perfume, distilled alcohol base
nodes.note: Alcohol dissolves and carries fragrance far better than fat alone. Volatile alcohols evaporate, leaving scent on skin and clothes. Concentrated distilled perfumes (attar) command high prices and excellent margins. The innovation is distillation, not enfleurage.

nodes.name: Perfume by enfleurage
nodes.note: Flower petals are laid on cold fat, which absorbs fragrance. Repeated; expensive and used by the wealthy. Yields poor revenue; the innovation is distillation for concentrates.

nodes.name: Piano with hammer action
nodes.note: Struck strings with escapement mechanism allowing rapid re-strike. Cristofori invents the hammer action around 1700, replacing plucked harpsichords. Touche and dynamic range enable entirely new music. Expensive; requires years of training to play well.

nodes.name: Playing cards, printed
nodes.note: Woodcut or engraved cards printed in volume. Early printed decks (15th century) are hand-coloured. Standardised designs (Italian, Spanish, French suits) emerge later. Cards were originally hand-painted and very expensive.

nodes.name: Pocket watch
nodes.note: Miniaturized spring-driven mechanism with balance wheel (spiral spring regulating oscillation). Requires high precision machining and jeweled pivots to reduce friction. Early watches lose 5-10 minutes per day; later escapements improve accuracy.

nodes.name: Pressure cooker (Papin's digester)
nodes.note: A sealed vessel where steam pressure raises water boiling point, accelerating cooking 3x. Papin invents the digester in 1679 to demonstrate steam power; it becomes both a cooking device AND the conceptual ancestor of the steam engine. Requires safety valve.

nodes.name: Printed books for home
nodes.note: Printed volumes replace hand-copied manuscripts. Early books are expensive; gradually price falls as standardisation and competition reduce costs. Literacy spreads; libraries become personal, not institutional.

nodes.name: Public bath (thermae)
nodes.note: The thermae are social centers with heated water pools, caldarium and frigidarium. Rome's public hygiene infrastructure is remarkable for its era; yet most private homes lack hot water.

nodes.name: Ceiling punkah, servant-pulled
nodes.note: A large cloth fan suspended from the ceiling, pulled by a cord to and fro by a servant. Provides air circulation and cooling in hot climates. Entirely mechanical and labour-intensive; electric fans are the obvious 19th-century replacement.

nodes.name: Refrigeration, mechanical ice machine
nodes.note: Ammonia or ether evaporation in a compressor cools an ice chamber. Requires a steam engine to drive the compressor. Early mechanical ice-makers (Carve, 1850s) free wealthy households from dependence on natural ice harvesting and storage.

nodes.name: Home refrigerator, electric
nodes.note: Domestic refrigerator with electric compressor. Freon (CFC) replaces ammonia for safety (1930s). Standard feature in wealthy homes by 1950s; middle-class penetration spreads with electrification and price falls. Transforms food preservation and cooking.

nodes.name: Safety pin
nodes.note: Bent iron wire with a catch. Simpler than brooches and more secure for fastening cloth or diapers. Mass production requires drawn wire and stamping, both later innovations.

nodes.name: Safety razor
nodes.note: Replaceable blade held at a fixed angle in a handle guard, preventing deep cuts. Earlier straight razors require stropping and honing; safety razors are simpler for users. Gillette disposable blades (early 1900s) create a consumable product with huge margins.

nodes.name: Sewer separated from stormwater drain
nodes.note: Sewage and rain runoff follow separate pipes to prevent sewage backup during storms. Public health innovation; requires city-scale investment. Many 19th-century cities combine sewers (causing problems); separation is a later upgrade. [AUDIT: capability prerequisite(s) cap_heat_1300 were inferred by rome/sim/treetool.py repair, not stated by the author. Treat them as a floor, not a specification.]

nodes.name: Sewing machine, hand-crank
nodes.note: Reciprocating needle driven by crank mechanism. Howe and Singer commercialize sewing machines in the 1850s; hand-crank models precede treadle and electric drives. Stitches much faster than hand-sewing; domestic servants' value plummets.

nodes.name: Shampoo, soap-based
nodes.note: Soap solution with perfume. Romans wash hair with lye (harsh) or oil. Soap-based shampoo is gentle and effective. Liquid and powdered forms compete; bars arrive later. Fragrance matters for premium products.

nodes.name: Hard soap, sapo
nodes.note: Hot saponification of animal fat and plant oil with caustic lye, producing hard soap. Rome lacks this; soap is invented in the Eastern Mediterranean around 6th century. Labour-intensive but small-scale.

nodes.name: Spectacles, corrective lenses
nodes.note: Convex lenses for presbyopia (age-related farsightedness) arrive around 1300. Concave lenses for myopia come later. The hinge and bridge are crafted from brass. Spectacles are luxury goods until mass production.

nodes.name: Sprung mattress
nodes.note: Coiled iron springs in a wood frame topped with ticking and stuffing (wool, horsehair, or coconut fiber). Dramatically more comfortable than rope-frame beds. Requires drawn wire and coil-forming tools. Mass production follows industrial tooling.

nodes.name: Enclosed stove
nodes.note: A metal or ceramic box with fire inside, heating room air by radiation and conduction. More efficient than open fireplace because less heat escapes up the chimney. Requires cast iron or tile manufacture.

nodes.name: Toothbrush
nodes.note: Bone or wood handle with bristles of horsehair or bamboo fiber. Romans use twigs and charcoal powder for dental cleaning. The toothbrush format is luxury; mass adoption requires cheap bristles and handles.

nodes.name: Toothpaste, commercial formulation
nodes.note: Soap base with abrasive chalk or pumice powder, flavoured. Early toothpastes are gritty; fluoride is added in the 1950s. Toothbrushes + paste replace charcoal and salt rubbing. Marketing drives adoption; modern formulations include whiteners and stain removers.

nodes.name: Toys and dolls
nodes.note: Carved wooden dolls with jointed limbs or cloth bodies. Lead and tin soldiers for boys; fashion dolls for girls. Decoration and articulation increase cost. Toys become a significant retail category in the 18th and 19th centuries.

nodes.name: Umbrella
nodes.note: Wood frame with linen canopy. Rome and later cultures have parasols (sun protection); rain umbrellas arrive in northern Europe around 1500s. Widespread adoption requires industrial metal frames and waterproof cotton textiles.

nodes.name: Vacuum cleaner
nodes.note: Electric motor drives a suction fan that pulls dirt through a cloth bag filter. Replaces carpet sweepers and hand-brushing entirely. Servants become redundant. Cord length and motor noise are early limitations; wireless and quiet models come later. [AUDIT: capability prerequisite(s) cap_vac_1e3 were inferred by rome/sim/treetool.py repair, not stated by the author. Treat them as a floor, not a specification.]

nodes.name: Vacuum flask, thermos
nodes.note: Double-walled glass with vacuum between walls and silvered inner surface. Dewar invents it in 1892 for laboratory use; commercial thermos bottles follow. Keeps hot drinks hot for hours; cold drinks cold. Expensive; mass production eventually lowers cost.

nodes.name: Washing machine, electric-powered
nodes.note: Motor-driven drum or agitator. No cranking required. Faster cycles, cooler operation, less wear on fabric. Laundry becomes a household task rather than a full-time servant job. Early motors are noisy and prone to breakage; reliability improves.

nodes.name: Washing machine, hand-powered
nodes.note: A wooden or metal tub with paddles or rollers rotated by crank. Hot soapy water and mechanical action replace hours of hand-scrubbing. Laundry maids become surplus; wealthy households buy machines rather than slaves.

nodes.name: Zip fastener
nodes.note: Interlocking teeth or loops fastened by sliding slider. Whitcomb L. Judson invents the 'clasp locker' in 1891; Gideon Sundback perfects the modern zip in 1913. Requires precision stamping and assembly. Replaces buttons for boots and jackets.

nodes.name: Rigid padded horse collar, whippletree, nailed horseshoe
nodes.note: Roman throat-and-girth harness chokes a horse under heavy draught. The size of the improvement is disputed in modern scholarship, so claim a real but modest gain, not the old textbook figure of four times. Politically the safest technology in this document: it feeds people and moves army supplies and threatens nobody.

nodes.name: Hot air balloon for observation
nodes.note: Low technology, moderate cost, high spectacle, and the State wants it for siege observation and signalling. Also one of the fastest ways to be accused of sorcery, so fly it first for the army with the governor watching, never privately at night. Linen sized with oil is the envelope; Rome has excellent sailcloth.

nodes.name: Hydrochloric acid and aqua regia
nodes.note: Salt plus oil of vitriol. The salt-cake residue is the feedstock for the Leblanc soda process, so nothing is wasted. Aqua regia dissolves gold, which is a demonstration that will terrify the mint and delight your patron; use it carefully.

nodes.name: Hydrofluoric acid
nodes.note: Lead or wax vessels only; it eats glass, which is also what makes it useful. Extreme and insidious toxicity: it penetrates skin painlessly, seeks calcium in bone, and kills hours later. You have no calcium gluconate. Treat it as the most dangerous substance in your laboratory.

nodes.name: Establish the Alexandrian physician-philosopher persona
nodes.note: Buy books, a house, clothes, a Greek freedman secretary, and a reputation for piety. Reduces all future suspicion.

nodes.name: Oxygen and hydrogen in quantity
nodes.note: Zinc or iron with acid gives hydrogen; heating manganese dioxide or a chlorate gives oxygen. Needed for the oxy-hydrogen torch, for fused quartz, for balloons, and later for reducing germanium oxide to metal. Hydrogen and air is an explosive mixture over a very wide range; be disciplined.

nodes.name: Tolerances, jigs, fixtures and interchangeable manufacture
nodes.note: A management and measurement innovation more than a mechanical one, and it is what turns a workshop into an industry. The army will want it for weapons before anyone else does, which is your funding argument. CALENDAR FLOOR is set by diffusion, not by construction: the economy needs roughly a generation to train the trades, form the capital and build the suppliers. Money cannot buy this down. THE STATE WILL RESIST THIS. Interchangeable manufacture visibly replaces free urban artisans with unskilled hands and gauges. Suetonius, Vespasian 18: an engineer offers a cheap machine for hauling columns to the Capitol, and Vespasian rewards him but declines to use it, saying he must be allowed to feed his poor commons. Site it in the provinces, staff it conspicuously with freedmen, and frame it as arming the legions rather than as saving wages.

nodes.name: Grown and alloy junction transistors
nodes.note: The point-contact device is a laboratory curiosity. The junction transistor is manufacturable, rugged and reproducible, and it is what actually replaces the vacuum tube. If you only get one generation past the goal, get this one.

nodes.name: A working laboratory: retorts, baths, lutes, crucibles, fume management
nodes.note: Alexandrian alchemy already looks like this, so it is culturally normal, which is your cover. Fume management is not optional; the classic way a bootstrapper dies is chlorine or nitrogen dioxide in a closed room.

nodes.name: Lead chamber sulfuric acid at industrial scale
nodes.note: Burn sulfur with saltpetre in a lead-lined chamber; the nitrogen oxides shuttle oxygen catalytically. Lead is the only Roman-available material that survives the conditions, and Rome has a great deal of cheap lead. This is the node that turns chemistry from a laboratory curiosity into an industry. CALENDAR FLOOR is set by diffusion, not by construction: the economy needs roughly a generation to train the trades, form the capital and build the suppliers. Money cannot buy this down.

nodes.name: Lead sheet, pipe, litharge and cupellation control
nodes.note: Rome does this already and does it well. You need lead in bulk for the lead chamber process, for cable sheathing, for accumulators, and for acid plumbing. Also secures your galena supply for the crystal detector.

nodes.name: Ground and polished spherical lenses
nodes.note: Reading spectacles for a literate elite that goes presbyopic at forty and has no remedy. Enormous margin, obvious utility, zero threat. This is your best year-one revenue product and it also buys you your first patron.

nodes.name: Air brake (locomotive and train)
nodes.note: Compressed air from the engine applies brake pressure to all wheels simultaneously through pipes. Without it, trains over ten cars cannot stop reliably. This is the prerequisite for modern freight.

nodes.name: Assembly line and mass production
nodes.note: Workers do one task repeatedly as car moves on conveyor. Each worker becomes highly skilled at one assembly step. Huge overhead but makes cars affordable for ordinary people.

nodes.name: Automobile (self-propelled carriage)
nodes.note: Engine drives wheels through gearbox. Steering wheel controls front wheels. Four-wheel suspension. Replaces horse-drawn carriages. Major social disruption from independence and speed.

nodes.name: Pivoting front axle
nodes.note: ROME POSSIBLY HAS THIS but is disputed. Turning is impossible without it; evidence in Roman relief carvings is ambiguous. Assume present but mark confidence low.

nodes.name: Ball bearing
nodes.note: Steel balls in a cage roll between races. Reduces friction in wheel hubs and pedal cranks by 90 percent. Makes the bicycle practical and comfortable for long rides. [AUDIT: State interest and suspicion were unset and have been defaulted from the category.]

nodes.name: Block system (railway safety)
nodes.note: Divide the line into blocks with signals; only one train per block. This is not a mechanical invention; it is an information system. Railway safety is fundamentally a communication problem.

nodes.name: Boneshaker (pedal bicycle)
nodes.note: Pedals drive the front wheel directly via crank. Frame and wheels are wood and cast iron, hence the name. Rider feels every rock; suspension comes later. Speed gain over walking is 2x. [AUDIT: State interest and suspicion were unset and have been defaulted from the category.]

nodes.name: Bridge
nodes.note: ROME ALREADY HAS THIS. Stone arch bridges, magnificent examples, part of road network. This is why Roman roads are faster than mountain paths.

nodes.name: Carburettor
nodes.note: Fuel nozzle sprays petrol into an air stream at variable rates. Mixture must be tuned to engine speed. Precise ratio is critical; too rich or too lean and the engine stalls. [AUDIT: State interest and suspicion were unset and have been defaulted from the category.]

nodes.name: Caterpillar track (crawler)
nodes.note: Steel shoes on chains loop around drive sprockets. Distributes weight over ground to reduce sinking in mud. Allows cross-country movement on otherwise impassable terrain.

nodes.name: Chain drive (for bicycle)
nodes.note: Roller chain connecting pedal sprocket to rear wheel. Allows gearing: the rear wheel turns multiple times per pedal stroke. Reduces effort and enables comfortable cruising speed. [AUDIT: State interest and suspicion were unset and have been defaulted from the category.]

nodes.name: Coach
nodes.note: Enclosed four-wheel carriage with seating inside, drawn by horses. No suspension yet, so routes must be smooth roads. This is personal transport for the wealthy.

nodes.name: Coal tar gas (coal gas)
nodes.note: Coke and steam passed through hot coal produces combustible gas. Used for lighting and early engines. Supply is local and pipeline-dependent; replaced by petrol in vehicles.

nodes.name: Cursus publicus courier service
nodes.note: ROME ALREADY HAS THIS. Imperial dispatch relay using stations and fresh horses. Shows that Rome recognizes speed of information matters; this logic applies to freight.

nodes.name: Diesel cycle (compression ignition)
nodes.note: Compress air to 500 psi, inject fuel which ignites by heat alone. No spark plugs needed. More efficient than Otto cycle but requires massive precision in boring. Heavier and more expensive.

nodes.name: Diesel supply chain
nodes.note: Heavy-oil fraction from crude, more energy-dense than petrol, flows at cold temperatures. Essential for trucks and industry. Distribution network similar to petrol but slightly different specifications.

nodes.name: Differential (rear axle)
nodes.note: Bevel gear system that allows both rear wheels to turn at different speeds during cornering. Without it, inside wheel scrapes and car is hard to steer. [AUDIT: State interest and suspicion were unset and have been defaulted from the category.]

nodes.name: Fishplate rail jointer
nodes.note: Iron plates bolted across a rail joint prevent gaps and shearing. Eliminates the bump and clatter of wheels crossing joints. Maintenance of alignment becomes predictable. [AUDIT: State interest and suspicion were unset and have been defaulted from the category.]

nodes.name: Flanged wheel
nodes.note: The flange is on the WHEEL, not the rail. Inward-facing rim keeps the wheel on track. This is the counterintuitive choice that makes all railway systems work. [AUDIT: State interest and suspicion were unset and have been defaulted from the category.]

nodes.name: Four-wheeled cart
nodes.note: ROME ALREADY HAS THIS. Four-wheel design allows steering the front axle independently, a fundamental shift from two-wheel carts. Capacity and maneuverability.

nodes.name: Atmospheric gas engine (Lenoir)
nodes.note: Mix illuminating gas with air, ignite, expansion drives piston, atmospheric pressure returns it. Inefficient but quieter than steam. Industrial benchmark before petrol engines.

nodes.name: Gearbox and clutch
nodes.note: Friction clutch allows engine to spin freely when disengaged. Gear trains multiply torque at low speed and allow high speed at high RPM. Without gearing, a small engine cannot move a heavy car. [AUDIT: State interest and suspicion were unset and have been defaulted from the category.]

nodes.name: Harness of throat and girth type
nodes.note: ROME ALREADY HAS THIS. Rope and leather harness distributes pull across the shoulders and chest. Impedes breathing but enables pulling; the rigid collar is later and better.

nodes.name: Hobby horse (pedal-less bicycle)
nodes.note: Rider straddles a frame with two wheels and propels by pushing feet on the ground. Faster than walking, no pedals. Proof of concept for the bicycle, then abandoned as impractical.

nodes.name: Horse saddle (basic)
nodes.note: ROME ALREADY HAS THIS. Basic saddle with cloth and leather distributes rider weight. Allows long-distance mounted travel. Stirrups come later.

nodes.name: Nailed horseshoe
nodes.note: Iron shoes nailed to hoof allow horses to work on stone roads for weeks without going lame. This is not efficiency; this is making the horse usable on paved ground instead of destroying it.

nodes.name: Iron edge rail
nodes.note: Cast iron rails with one edge raised to guide flanged wheels. First used in mines. The innovation is the raised edge, not the metal; it prevents derailment and reduces friction.

nodes.name: Litter
nodes.note: ROME ALREADY HAS THIS. Pole-carried passenger carriage used by the wealthy. Humans as motive power but avoids the discomfort of horseback for dignitaries.

nodes.name: Macadam road surface
nodes.note: Broken stone, graded by size, compacted without binding agent. Much cheaper to build and maintain than Roman dressed-stone roads but degrades faster in wet. An economic trade-off, not an improvement.

nodes.name: Magneto (ignition system)
nodes.note: Rotating magnet in coil generates high-voltage spark without needing a battery. Works on any engine speed. This simple approach powered all early cars. [AUDIT: State interest and suspicion were unset and have been defaulted from the category.]

nodes.name: Milestone
nodes.note: ROME ALREADY HAS THIS. Stone pillars marking distance along roads. Enables speed prediction, time scheduling, loss prediction. Information infrastructure.

nodes.name: Road network for motor vehicles
nodes.note: Smooth, level roads with safety markings, regular maintenance, and drainage. Cars need better surface than macadam; tarmac wears out faster under car weight but is faster to repair.

nodes.name: Mule transport
nodes.note: ROME ALREADY HAS THIS. Mules are preferred for mountain work because they are surefooted and eat less than horses. The pack mule is the backbone of supply in rough terrain.

nodes.name: Omnibus (motor bus)
nodes.note: Large motor carriage for 20-50 passengers. Replaces horse-drawn omnibus. Speed, capacity, and lack of animal waste transform urban public transport.

nodes.name: Otto cycle four-stroke engine
nodes.note: Intake, compression, power, exhaust in four strokes per cycle. More efficient than atmospheric engines. Forms the foundation of all automotive engines.

nodes.name: Ox transport
nodes.note: ROME ALREADY HAS THIS. Oxen pull heavier loads than horses at slower speed and cost less to feed. Used for slow supply and field work; horses for speed.

nodes.name: Paved trunk road network
nodes.note: ROME ALREADY HAS THIS. The via system of stone-laid trunk roads is the network substrate for everything below. Permits high-speed carriage travel and reliable supply movement.

nodes.name: Penny farthing (high-wheel bicycle)
nodes.note: Huge front wheel, tiny back wheel. Higher wheel passes obstacles; one turn of the crank moves you further. Unstable and dangerous but fast. Rider height makes it impractical for most. [AUDIT: State interest and suspicion were unset and have been defaulted from the category.]

nodes.name: Pneumatic tyre (rubber tyre)
nodes.note: REQUIRES NATURAL RUBBER (tier 9 unobtainable in Rome). Air-filled tube and tyre absorb shocks perfectly. Solid rubber or leather tyre is a poor substitute: rides are harsh and efficiency is lost. This is an honest limitation. [AUDIT: State interest and suspicion were unset and have been defaulted from the category.]

nodes.name: Point and switch
nodes.note: Movable rails allow a train to switch between two tracks. The mechanism must be sturdy enough to guide a moving train cleanly. Enables sidings and branch lines.

nodes.name: Safety bicycle (chain drive)
nodes.note: Equal-size wheels with chain drive; seat low and central. The chain and the differential-free rear drive are the inventions. Safe, stable, and fast. Modern bicycle geometry. [AUDIT: State interest and suspicion were unset and have been defaulted from the category.]

nodes.name: Railway signal
nodes.note: Semaphore arms and flag signals allow operators to communicate over distance. Necessary before trains run on tight schedules; without them, collisions are inevitable.

nodes.name: Spark plug (spark ignition)
nodes.note: Electric spark across a gap ignites fuel mix at the exact moment of compression. Timing is everything; even small errors cause misfires and loss of power. [AUDIT: State interest and suspicion were unset and have been defaulted from the category.]

nodes.name: Leaf spring
nodes.note: Flexing steel leaf under a carriage absorbs shocks and bumps. This single innovation makes long-distance travel on rough roads bearable. Suspension is what makes the journey tolerable, not the speed.

nodes.name: Stagecoach
nodes.note: Coach with leaf-spring suspension and scheduled stops; a business model for passenger transport. The springs change everything: bumpy roads become tolerable for long hours.

nodes.name: Standard gauge (railway)
nodes.note: All railways must use the same track spacing for freight transfer between lines. Without standardisation, each line is an island. The cost of standardisation is high; the cost of not doing so is higher.

nodes.name: Steam locomotive
nodes.note: Steam engine mounted on rails propels itself and train. Requires constant water and fuel stops. The locomotive does not pull faster than horses until distances exceed 30 miles; then volume and fuel logistics matter.

nodes.name: Steering geometry (Ackermann)
nodes.note: Front wheels must turn at different angles during a turn so both follow the same curved path. This geometry is counterintuitive but essential for stable handling. [AUDIT: capability prerequisite(s) cap_heat_1300 were inferred by rome/sim/treetool.py repair, not stated by the author. Treat them as a floor, not a specification.] [AUDIT: State interest and suspicion were unset and have been defaulted from the category.]

nodes.name: Stirrup
nodes.note: Metal foot-loops hanging from saddle revolutionise horseback riding. Rider can brace legs, rise from seat, and deliver force in combat or work. This is as much a military technology as a transport one.

nodes.name: Superheater (steam locomotive)
nodes.note: Heat the steam further after leaving the boiler to expand it more in the cylinder, improving efficiency 20 percent. Complexity and maintenance cost are high; only justified on long-distance engines. [AUDIT: State interest and suspicion were unset and have been defaulted from the category.]

nodes.name: Tarmacadam road surface
nodes.note: Macadam with tar binding is cheaper to build than Roman stone but still degrades. The advantage is speed of repair, not quality. Honest assessment: it is an economic choice for volume, not engineering superiority.

nodes.name: Tender (coal and water car)
nodes.note: Water and coal are consumed continuously; a dedicated car attached to the engine carries supplies. Without the tender, the engine range is measured in tens of miles. [AUDIT: State interest and suspicion were unset and have been defaulted from the category.]

nodes.name: Tractor (motor field vehicle)
nodes.note: Powerful engine mounted on crawler tracks for traction in mud. Can pull multiple ploughs or work in woods. Changes farmwork from oxen to machines; entire labour class displaced.

nodes.name: Truck (motor freight vehicle)
nodes.note: Heavy-duty chassis with open cargo bed. Diesel engine for economy and torque. Replaces the mule and the railway for regional freight. Speed and flexibility change logistics entirely.

nodes.name: Turnpike
nodes.note: Private or chartered toll road maintained by toll gate revenue. Creates incentive to maintain roads better than government roads. Improves speed and reliability. Some hostility from smugglers and bandits.

nodes.name: Two-wheeled cart
nodes.note: ROME ALREADY HAS THIS. Simple two-point suspension, lighter than four-wheel for local work, used everywhere by farmers and traders.

nodes.name: Iron tyre (tire)
nodes.note: ROME ALREADY HAS THIS. Iron band shrunk hot onto the rim protects the wooden wheel and spreads road impact. Vastly extends wheel life over bare wood.

nodes.name: Spoked wheel
nodes.note: ROME ALREADY HAS THIS. Radial spokes in tension carry load far better than solid wood. This invention alone made fast carriages possible.

nodes.name: Wheelbarrow
nodes.note: One-wheel handcart, invented in China, allows manual labour to move bulk goods. Rome does not have this; it is surprisingly absent. An enormous productivity gain once adopted.

nodes.name: Whippletree
nodes.note: The whippletree, or evener, is a pivoting bar that distributes pull evenly between two horses, preventing one from shirking. Without it, tandem teams do not work.

nodes.name: Logarithms and computed tables
nodes.note: The 40,000 scribe-hours are real: Napier spent 20 years and Briggs employed computers. This is a pure money-for-time trade and it is worth it, because every engineer and astronomer after you saves a factor of ten on arithmetic.

nodes.name: The first accurate screw, and thread standards
nodes.note: The bootstrap problem: to cut an accurate screw you need an accurate screw. Escape it by wrapping a strip round a cylinder to generate a first rough helix, then correcting a master by lapping with a long nut, which averages out the errors. Slow, fiddly, and it is the gate on all measurement.

nodes.name: Alum
nodes.note: ROME HAS THIS from Melos. Mordant, styptic, sizing.

nodes.name: Aluminium
nodes.note: Hall-Heroult in a molten fluoride bath. Cryolite is Greenlandic and unobtainable, so you must synthesise the bath from your own hydrofluoric acid. Before electricity aluminium is a precious metal; after it, it is roofing.

nodes.name: Ammonia
nodes.note: Ammonia liquor is a by-product of coking coal, so it is nearly free once you coke. Fertiliser, refrigeration, nitric acid via Ostwald oxidation.

nodes.name: Asbestos
nodes.note: ROME HAS THIS from Cyprus. Pliny describes it. Useful, and it will kill your workers slowly.

nodes.name: Bakelite (phenol formaldehyde)
nodes.note: The first fully synthetic plastic, from coal tar phenol. Electrical insulation, housings, and the thing that makes mass-produced electrical goods possible.

nodes.name: Beeswax
nodes.note: ROME HAS THIS. Lost wax casting, luting, acid-proof coating.

nodes.name: Bitumen and naphtha seeps
nodes.note: ROME HAS THIS from Mesopotamia and the Dead Sea. Cable insulation, waterproofing, and the seed of petroleum chemistry.

nodes.name: Blister steel
nodes.note: Bar iron packed in charcoal at about 1000 C for days. Carbon penetrates on the order of a millimetre a day, so use thin bars.

nodes.name: Brass (by cementation)
nodes.note: ROME HAS THIS, made by heating copper with calamine and charcoal WITHOUT ever seeing zinc metal. See mat_zinc for why.

nodes.name: Bronze
nodes.note: ROME HAS THIS. Casting, bearings, statuary, instruments.

nodes.name: Bulk steel (converter and open hearth)
nodes.note: Thousands of tonnes instead of kilogrammes. NOTE THE PHOSPHORUS PROBLEM: an acid lining cannot remove it and most European ores carry it, so you need a basic dolomite lining (Thomas and Gilchrist). Knowing this in advance saves you the years it cost Bessemer.

nodes.name: Calamine (zinc carbonate/silicate ore)
nodes.note: ROME HAS THIS and already smelts it into brass. [AUDIT: capability prerequisite(s) cap_heat_0700 were inferred by rome/sim/treetool.py repair, not stated by the author. Treat them as a floor, not a specification.]

nodes.name: Camphor (traded)
nodes.note: Reachable via the Indian Ocean and Chinese trade, expensive. Needed for celluloid and for smokeless powder.

nodes.name: Carbon black and lampblack
nodes.note: ROME HAS THIS. Ink pigment, and much later the reinforcing filler that makes rubber into tyres.

nodes.name: Cast iron
nodes.note: Brittle, cheap, castable, 3-4% carbon. Rome has none in the West; Han China has had it for 500 years. Pipes, pots, cannon, machine frames, stoves.

nodes.name: Celluloid (nitrocellulose plastic)
nodes.note: The first thermoplastic. Film base, combs, billiard balls. VIOLENTLY FLAMMABLE and it is what made early cinema so dangerous.

nodes.name: Portland cement
nodes.note: Calcined limestone and clay, ground fine. HONEST NOTE: it is not obviously better than Roman pozzolanic concrete for marine work. Its advantage is consistency and independence from Puteoli.

nodes.name: Charcoal
nodes.note: ROME HAS THIS. The real ceiling on iron output is forest, not ore.

nodes.name: Chile saltpetre
nodes.note: UNOBTAINABLE. Atacama. Your nitrogen comes from nitre beds and, very late, from the electric arc.

nodes.name: Chlorine and bleach
nodes.note: Bleaching powder ends the field-bleaching bottleneck that limited every textile industry, and hypochlorite makes water safe. Also war gas: be careful whom you teach.

nodes.name: Chromium
nodes.note: Aluminothermic or carbon reduction of chromite. Stainless, plating, refractories.

nodes.name: Reinforced concrete
nodes.note: Roman concrete is superb in compression and useless in tension. Steel rod fixes that, and the thermal expansion of steel and concrete happen to match closely enough to work, which is luck rather than design.

nodes.name: Copper (fire refined)
nodes.note: ROME HAS THIS. Not pure enough for good conductors; see cap_pure_4N.

nodes.name: Crucible steel
nodes.note: Homogeneous, slag-free, and the gate on every cutting tool and every lead screw.

nodes.name: Cryolite
nodes.note: EFFECTIVELY UNOBTAINABLE. Greenland. Aluminium smelting must use a synthetic fluoride bath made from your own hydrofluoric acid.

nodes.name: Synthetic dyes (aniline)
nodes.note: Coal tar to benzene to aniline to mauveine and the rest. Historically this single industry funded organic chemistry, created the first industrial research laboratories, and led directly to pharmaceuticals. Enormously profitable and politically harmless.

nodes.name: Emery (Naxos)
nodes.note: ROME HAS THIS. Your abrasive for every ground surface in this document. [AUDIT: capability prerequisite(s) cap_tol_1mm were inferred by rome/sim/treetool.py repair, not stated by the author. Treat them as a floor, not a specification.]

nodes.name: Formaldehyde
nodes.note: Catalytic oxidation of methanol from wood distillation. Resins, and the first practical tissue preservative.

nodes.name: Fused quartz
nodes.note: Pure silica worked at 1700 to 2000 C with an oxy-hydrogen flame. Indispensable later: you cannot zone refine germanium in anything that contaminates it. [AUDIT: capability prerequisite(s) cap_pure_4N were inferred by rome/sim/treetool.py repair, not stated by the author. Treat them as a floor, not a specification.]

nodes.name: Galena (lead sulfide)
nodes.note: ROME HAS THIS everywhere it mines lead. It is also a working semiconductor, which nobody will suspect for 1800 years.

nodes.name: Borosilicate glass
nodes.note: Low thermal expansion. The difference between a laboratory and a pile of broken retorts. Needs boron; the Larderello fumaroles in Tuscany are inside the Empire, which is a genuinely lucky break if it holds.

nodes.name: Lead crystal (flint glass)
nodes.note: High dispersion. Pair it with crown glass and you get the achromatic doublet, which is what makes a compound microscope beat a single bead.

nodes.name: Soda-lime glass
nodes.note: ROME HAS THIS and is genuinely good at it, including deliberately decolourised near-colourless glass.

nodes.name: Glycerol
nodes.note: A by-product of soap making that Rome throws away.

nodes.name: Gold
nodes.note: ROME HAS THIS. Las Medulas, and Dacia from 106 AD.

nodes.name: High purity graphite
nodes.note: Acheson process: heat carbon to about 2500 C. Crucibles and boats that do not contaminate what is melted in them, which is exactly what zone refining needs. [AUDIT: capability prerequisite(s) cap_pure_6N were inferred by rome/sim/treetool.py repair, not stated by the author. Treat them as a floor, not a specification.]

nodes.name: Gutta percha
nodes.note: UNOBTAINABLE in quantity. Malayan Palaquium latex, not traded west until the 19th century. This is the material that made submarine cables possible historically; you will have to solve undersea insulation another way.

nodes.name: Gypsum plaster
nodes.note: ROME HAS THIS.

nodes.name: Artificial ice and mechanical refrigeration
nodes.note: Vapour compression with ammonia. Food preservation, meat shipping, brewing year round, and the seed of gas liquefaction and low temperature physics.

nodes.name: Lead
nodes.note: ROME HAS THIS in enormous quantity from Britannia and Hispania. Cheap. The only common material that survives hot sulfuric acid.

nodes.name: Leather
nodes.note: ROME HAS THIS. Bellows, seals, gaskets, drive belts.

nodes.name: Quicklime and slaked lime
nodes.note: ROME HAS THIS. Mortar, glass flux, causticising, agriculture.

nodes.name: Linen
nodes.note: ROME HAS THIS. Sailcloth, and the feedstock for rag paper.

nodes.name: Magnesium
nodes.note: Electrolysis of fused chloride. Light alloys, flashlight powder, reducing agent.

nodes.name: Manganese and ferromanganese
nodes.note: Deoxidises and desulfurises steel. Rome already mines the ore as a glass decolouriser without knowing it is a metal.

nodes.name: Mercury
nodes.note: ROME HAS THIS from Almaden, an imperial monopoly. Pliny NH 33.118 price-fixes minium at 70 HS per pound.

nodes.name: Natron (sodium carbonate)
nodes.note: ROME HAS THIS from Wadi Natrun. IT IS NOT SALTPETRE. This confusion has wrecked more bootstrap plans than any other single error.

nodes.name: Natural rubber (Hevea)
nodes.note: UNOBTAINABLE. Amazon basin. There is no route to the Americas and there will not be one in your lifetime or your grandchildren's. Every plan that assumes rubber is wrong. Substitutes: gutta percha (also unobtainable), shellac, oiled linen, silk, bitumen, and much later synthetic rubber from coal tar or petroleum, which is a full chemical industry away.

nodes.name: Potato, maize, tomato, cassava, chilli, cocoa, tobacco, vanilla
nodes.note: UNOBTAINABLE. All American. The crops that transformed Old World agriculture are not available to you. Do not plan a population increase around them.

nodes.name: Nickel
nodes.note: Not isolated in antiquity. Coinage, plating, alloy steels, glass-to-metal seals, catalysts.

nodes.name: Nitrocellulose
nodes.note: Guncotton and the base of smokeless powder, celluloid and film. Unstable if badly washed; several early factories destroyed themselves.

nodes.name: Nitroglycerin and dynamite
nodes.note: Absorbed into kieselguhr it becomes handleable. Mining and tunnelling output rises sharply. Also the most likely single thing in this document to kill you and everyone in the building.

nodes.name: Olive oil
nodes.note: ROME HAS THIS in industrial quantity. Soap, lighting, quenching, varnish base. [AUDIT: capability prerequisite(s) cap_heat_0700 were inferred by rome/sim/treetool.py repair, not stated by the author. Treat them as a floor, not a specification.]

nodes.name: Rag paper
nodes.note: Linen rags, retted, limed, beaten by a water-driven stamper, lifted on a wire mould. Cheaper than papyrus, far cheaper than parchment, and the substrate of everything in the information branch.

nodes.name: Papyrus
nodes.note: ROME HAS THIS. An Egyptian near-monopoly, which is a strategic reason to make paper.

nodes.name: Parchment
nodes.note: ROME HAS THIS. Durable and dear.

nodes.name: Refined petroleum fractions
nodes.note: Mesopotamian and Caucasian seeps are workable without drilling. Fractionate into naphtha, kerosene, gas oil, lubricants, wax and residue. Kerosene lighting alone pays for the plant.

nodes.name: Platinum in quantity
nodes.note: EFFECTIVELY UNOBTAINABLE. The workable placers are Colombian and Uralian. Small quantities may reach you; do not design a process around it.

nodes.name: Porcelain and high-fired stoneware
nodes.note: Kaolin plus feldspar at about 1300 C. Chemical ware, electrical insulators, and an extremely profitable luxury export that Europe chased for six centuries.

nodes.name: Pozzolana and hydraulic concrete
nodes.note: ROME HAS THIS and it is better in seawater than Portland cement. Do not try to improve it.

nodes.name: Pyrolusite (manganese dioxide)
nodes.note: ROME HAS THIS and already uses it as glassmaker's soap without knowing why.

nodes.name: Quinine (cinchona)
nodes.note: UNOBTAINABLE. Andean. Malaria is endemic around Rome and you cannot treat it. Drain the marshes instead.

nodes.name: Salt
nodes.note: ROME HAS THIS, taxed and strategically controlled. Feedstock for hydrochloric acid and the whole chlor-alkali branch.

nodes.name: Shellac (traded)
nodes.note: REACHABLE BUT DEAR. Indian Ocean trade via Berenice to Muziris, 1 to 3 year lead time. Your best varnish and the only good coil insulation you will have for a century.

nodes.name: Silk (traded)
nodes.note: REACHABLE BUT RUINOUS. Silk Road via Palmyra. Pliny complains of the bullion drain east. Your best early wire insulation.

nodes.name: Silver
nodes.note: ROME HAS THIS. Cupellation from galena.

nodes.name: Stainless steel
nodes.note: Chromium above about 11% forms a self-healing passive oxide. Chemical plant, cutlery, vacuum systems. [AUDIT: capability prerequisite(s) cap_vac_1e6 were inferred by rome/sim/treetool.py repair, not stated by the author. Treat them as a floor, not a specification.]

nodes.name: Sulfur
nodes.note: ROME HAS THIS from Sicily and the Aeolian islands.

nodes.name: Synthetic rubber
nodes.note: YOUR ONLY ROUTE TO RUBBER. Butadiene from petroleum or from alcohol, polymerised. It sits behind a full petrochemical industry, which is why every plan that casually assumes rubber is wrong by about a century.

nodes.name: Tallow
nodes.note: ROME HAS THIS. Lubricant for wire drawing and machining.

nodes.name: Tin
nodes.note: ROME HAS THIS from Cornwall and Iberia. Expensive, long haul.

nodes.name: High speed and alloy tool steel
nodes.note: Tungsten and chromium carbides that hold an edge red hot. Multiplies every machine tool's output several fold.

nodes.name: Tungsten
nodes.note: Melts at 3422 C, the highest of any metal. Lamp filaments, high speed steel, carbide tooling. Needs the arc furnace or hydrogen reduction of the oxide followed by powder sintering.

nodes.name: Vitriols (iron and copper sulfates)
nodes.note: ROME HAS THIS lying in heaps at pyrite mines as a weathering product, and has no idea what it is for. Feedstock for sulfuric acid.

nodes.name: Wool
nodes.note: ROME HAS THIS.

nodes.name: Wrought iron (bloomery)
nodes.note: ROME HAS THIS at scale. Noricum is famous for it. Soft, tough, weldable, no useful casting.

nodes.name: Zinc metal
nodes.note: CRITICAL PATH AND ALMOST NOBODY SEES IT. Zinc boils at 907 C, below the temperature at which its ore is reduced, so the metal leaves as vapour and reburns at the furnace mouth. That is exactly why Rome makes brass by cementation and has never seen the metal. Seal the retort and condense downward. No zinc, no voltaic pile, no electricity.

nodes.name: Amputation and prosthetics
nodes.note: Rapid limb removal to prevent gangrene. High mortality from shock and infection. Prosthetics of wood and leather follow for dignity and limited function.

nodes.name: Antitoxin and serum therapy
nodes.note: Serum from horses immunized with toxin. Diphtheria antitoxin reduced mortality from 50% to 20%. Anaphylaxis kills 1 in 1000. Passive immunity is temporary.

nodes.name: Aqueducts and public latrines
nodes.note: Rome has abundant clean water and sewage separation. This infrastructure is mature and the foundation for any public health improvement.

nodes.name: Asepsis, antisepsis, and steam sterilization
nodes.note: Asepsis: prevention of contamination. Antisepsis: chemical disinfection. Steam sterilization beats carbolic spray because it kills spores, not just surface germs.

nodes.name: Aspirin (acetylsalicylic acid)
nodes.note: Acetylation of salicylic acid (from willow bark). Safer than salicylate because absorbed slowly. Reduces fever, pain, inflammation. Bayer trademark.

nodes.name: Autoclave for steam sterilization
nodes.note: Sealed vessel with high-pressure steam at 120 C for 15 minutes sterilizes instruments. Requires precision engineering; leaks render it useless.

nodes.name: Blood groups and transfusion
nodes.note: ABO typing discovered 1900. Before this, transfusion killed 1 in 5 from agglutination. Citrate prevents clotting. Saves haemorrhage victims.

nodes.name: Bone setting
nodes.note: Reduction and splinting of fractures. Success depends on immobility for weeks; infection is the main hazard.

nodes.name: Cataract couching
nodes.note: Displacement of opaque lens via a hollow needle, an ancient Roman technique. The rev is patient fees.

nodes.name: Clinical thermometer
nodes.note: Mercury in glass with fixed point at 37 C. Temperature tells severity of infection. Fever is sometimes the body fighting infection.

nodes.name: Case control and randomised controlled trials
nodes.note: Case control: backward look at exposure. Fast and cheap. Randomised controlled trial: random assignment to treatment or placebo, prospective, blind. Eliminates bias but takes years. [AUDIT: capability prerequisite(s) cap_tol_100um were inferred by rome/sim/treetool.py repair, not stated by the author. Treat them as a floor, not a specification.]

nodes.name: Cocaine for local anaesthesia (UNOBTAINABLE)
nodes.note: Cocaine is derived from coca, a New World plant. UNOBTAINABLE before oceanic trade. The substitute is opium solution injected locally, less effective and systemic.

nodes.name: Dentistry and high-speed drill
nodes.note: Electric motor driving high-speed burr removes decay and drills for filling. Eliminates hand-cranked slowness and pain.

nodes.name: Electrocardiogram (ECG)
nodes.note: Electrodes on chest and limbs, galvanometer recording heart's electrical activity. Detects arrhythmias and infarction. Requires stable power and shielded wiring.

nodes.name: Endoscope
nodes.note: Tube with lens at the far end, mirror to reflect light. Inspection of bladder, urethra, rectum. Illumination by candlelight makes diagnosis difficult.

nodes.name: Epidemiology, statistics, and vital registration
nodes.note: John Snow mapped cholera deaths (1854); they clustered around one well. Data beats theory. Vital registration (births, deaths, cause) is the denominator. Null hypothesis testing reveals truth.

nodes.name: Ether, chloroform, and nitrous oxide anaesthesia
nodes.note: Diethyl ether (first 1846) is explosive and irritates airways. Chloroform (1847) is smoother but causes cardiac arrhythmias in 1 per 3000. Nitrous oxide is safest but partial. Pain-free surgery is a miracle.

nodes.name: Forensic medicine and autopsy
nodes.note: Autopsy to establish cause of death. Time of death, toxicology, physical evidence. The state pays well for conviction support.

nodes.name: Bacterial culture and Gram staining
nodes.note: Petri's shallow agar dishes allow colonies to grow. Gram staining distinguishes by cell wall: crystal violet for gram-positive, red for gram-negative. Guides antibiotic choice.

nodes.name: Handwashing protocol (Semmelweis)
nodes.note: Handwashing and instrument cleaning between autopsy and delivery. Maternal mortality dropped from 18% to 1% in Vienna 1847. The physician who discovered this was committed to an asylum.

nodes.name: Herbal pharmacy (Dioscorides Materia medica)
nodes.note: Dioscorides' Materia medica describes 600+ plants. Effective for many uses: willow bark for pain, elderflower for fever. The physician's reference work.

nodes.name: Hospital as an institution with records
nodes.note: Permanent structure with wards, admission records, diagnosis, treatment, outcome. Allows tracking disease patterns and training the next generation.

nodes.name: Hypodermic syringe and hollow needle
nodes.note: Glass or silver barrel with accurately bored needle. Intravenous injection becomes possible. Contamination of the needle kills; strict asepsis required.

nodes.name: Insulin extraction and purification
nodes.note: Extract from porcine pancreas, crystallize, purify. Banting and Best 1921. Before insulin, diabetes is death. Now: life and productivity.

nodes.name: Legal protection for physicians
nodes.note: Imperial edict: physicians who follow established methods are not liable for death. This requires establishing consensus on best practice.

nodes.name: Ligature over cautery for haemostasis
nodes.note: Tying off vessels with linen before cutting. Slower than cautery but less tissue damage and no scar contracture. Requires training to isolate arteries.

nodes.name: Medical education and cadaver dissection
nodes.note: Formal curriculum: dissection of cadavers, demonstration, case study. Rome forbids human dissection; physicians must apprentice illegally or learn abroad.

nodes.name: Microscopy in pathology with histology
nodes.note: Aniline dyes from coal tar make cells visible for the first time. Methylene blue, carmine, safranin stain bacteria and tissue. Identifies cancer, tuberculosis, syphilis. Beautiful dependency on the chemical branch.

nodes.name: Nursing as a trained profession
nodes.note: Formal training programme for nurses. Florence Nightingale proved competent nursing cuts mortality by half. The profession becomes medicine's backbone.

nodes.name: Nutrition, deficiency diseases, and vitamins
nodes.note: Scurvy (vitamin C), rickets (vitamin D), beriberi (thiamine), pellagra (niacin), goitre (iodine). Iodised salt eliminates endemic goitre. Vitamin concept emerges from analytical chemistry.

nodes.name: Antiseptic obstetrics and incubator
nodes.note: Handwashing before delivery, clean gowns, sterile towels. Puerperal fever drops from 25% to 2%. Incubator for prematurity: warm box with temperature control increases survival from 10% to 40%.

nodes.name: Obstetric practice
nodes.note: Manual assistance, podalic version, ergot to hasten delivery. Maternal mortality is 1-2%; assistance often makes it worse.

nodes.name: Ophthalmoscope
nodes.note: Mirror and lens to view the retina. Reveals aneurysms, cotton-wool spots, diabetic changes. Requires skilled assembly.

nodes.name: Opium and mandrake tinctures
nodes.note: Poppy and mandrake extracts in oil, applied topically or given orally. Dosing is unpredictable; overdose causes death or stupor.

nodes.name: Penicillin extraction and purification
nodes.note: Penicillium mold produces beta-lactam antibiotic. Deep-tank fermentation and chromatography extraction are industrial operations. HONEST: this is not bedroom chemistry.

nodes.name: Quarantine, clean water, and sewage
nodes.note: Isolation of sick (quarantine). Filtration removes suspended matter. Alum coagulant precipitates colloids. Chlorination kills pathogens. Sewage separation and S-bend traps prevent backflow.

nodes.name: Saline and fluid resuscitation
nodes.note: Isotonic salt solution administered intravenously. Restores blood volume and prevents shock. Simpler and saves more lives than transfusion.

nodes.name: Spectacles and refraction testing
nodes.note: Ground lenses with trial frame testing. Corrects myopia, hyperopia, astigmatism, presbyopia. One of medicine's easiest wins.

nodes.name: Sphygmomanometer (blood pressure cuff)
nodes.note: Cuff inflated by hand, releasing air while watching mercury and listening to pulse. Requires precision machining and a mercury barometer.

nodes.name: Sterile technique
nodes.note: A complete ritual: sterile drapes, fields, gowns. No cross-contamination. Requires training and discipline. One careless move ruins everything.

nodes.name: Stethoscope and percussion
nodes.note: A rolled tube of paper or wood detects heart and breath sounds. Tapping the chest reveals fluid or consolidation. Simple but requires training to interpret.

nodes.name: Sulfonamides (sulfanilamide)
nodes.note: First broad-spectrum antibiotic 1935, derived from aniline dyes. Inhibits bacterial folate synthesis. Saves millions from streptococcal and gram-negative infections.

nodes.name: Surgical gloves and mask
nodes.note: Linen gloves and mask tied over mouth and nose. Blocks droplets and protects patient. Cloth gloves absorb blood and require frequent changing. Rubber gloves are unobtainable.

nodes.name: Good surgical instrument kit
nodes.note: Rome already has reliable bronze and iron surgical blades, forceps, and spatulas. This is the baseline.

nodes.name: Trepanation
nodes.note: Drilling into the skull to relieve pressure or expel evil spirits. Infection and death are common; Rome will pay for emergency cases.

nodes.name: Vaccination: variolation to attenuated vaccines
nodes.note: Variolation: pus from smallpox pustule (0.5-2% death). Cowpox: Jenner's insight, much safer. Pasteur: heat or chemical attenuation for rabies, anthrax, cholera. Toxoids (diphtheria, tetanus) are safest. [AUDIT: capability prerequisite(s) cap_tol_100um were inferred by rome/sim/treetool.py repair, not stated by the author. Treat them as a floor, not a specification.]

nodes.name: Military field hospital (valetudinaria)
nodes.note: Permanent structure with wards, built adjoining barracks. The state mandates these for legions. Clean water, drainage, and isolation of contagion cut mortality by half.

nodes.name: Vector control and drainage for malaria
nodes.note: Malaria is endemic to Rome's marshes. Quinine is UNOBTAINABLE. Drainage of standing water eliminates mosquito breeding. Laborious but works.

nodes.name: Wound suturing
nodes.note: Linen thread with bronze needle, removing thread after 2-3 weeks. Works well for clean wounds.

nodes.name: X-ray imaging
nodes.note: Cathode ray tube generating X-rays to expose plates. Reveals fractures and foreign bodies. HONEST WARNING: repeated exposure causes burns and cancer. Protection is inadequate.

nodes.name: Secure mercury supply
nodes.note: Almaden is an imperial monopoly, so this is a political node before it is a technical one. Mercury gives you barometers, the Sprengel pump, mirrors and the first hard vacuum humans have ever had. Quantity sized for programme needs, not for trade: 400 kg of cinnabar yields roughly 300 kg of mercury, which is ample for barometers, thermometers, Sprengel pumps and a mirror works. Cinnabar is priced from Pliny NH 33.118. CORRECTION: this no longer requires the imperial mining concession. Cinnabar is traded across the Empire as the pigment minium and you can simply buy it and retort it yourself. The concession buys you BULK mercury cheaply, which matters later for mirrors and pumps, and it is a separate problem from getting your first kilogramme. [AUDIT: capability prerequisite(s) cap_vac_1torr were inferred by rome/sim/treetool.py repair, not stated by the author. Treat them as a floor, not a specification.]

nodes.name: Acetylene from calcium carbide
nodes.note: Heat coke and lime to 2000 C in an electric furnace to make calcium carbide, then mix with water and collect the acetylene gas. The carbide reacts violently with water so the generator must be robust and well-designed or it leaks. Acetylene is unstable and cannot be pressurized above 2 atmospheres without risk of explosion, so it must be dissolved in acetone in a porous mass (a carbide lamp cartridge) for transport. [AUDIT: capability prerequisite(s) cap_power_water were inferred by rome/sim/treetool.py repair, not stated by the author. Treat them as a floor, not a specification.]

nodes.name: Annealing and recrystallization
nodes.note: Heat work-hardened metal to a dull red and cool slowly. Atoms rearrange into stress-free grains and the metal becomes soft and ductile again. Must not overheat or grains grow coarse and the metal becomes brittle. The window is narrow—a difference of 50 degrees C makes the difference between a good anneal and scrap. Requires experience to recognize the right color.

nodes.name: Arc welding with electrode
nodes.note: Strike an arc between a consumable electrode and the work. The arc melts both the electrode and the parent metal; electrode metal and flux coat the weld pool. Much faster than oxy-acetylene and less sensitive to wind. Requires a DC power supply and reliable electrical grid. The flux coating prevents oxidation and lowers the melting point of the surface oxide, so the weld pools together instead of balling up.

nodes.name: Basic lining and the phosphorus problem
nodes.note: Bessemer's acid lining cannot remove phosphorus because both are acidic. Most European ores carry phosphorus which makes the steel cold-short (brittle when cold). Thomas and Gilchrist discovered that a basic (limestone) lining does remove phosphorus as slag, but it eats lining fast and requires obsessive maintenance. This one fact cost Bessemer years and made British iron obsolete until solved.

nodes.name: Blasting with black powder and dynamite
nodes.note: Drill a hole, tamp black powder down with sand, light a fuse. The explosion fractures the rock around it. Later, dynamite (nitroglycerin absorbed in kieselguhr) replaced powder: more powerful, more stable, but far more hazardous. The critical skill is calculating the powder quantity and hole depth to maximize fragmentation without wasting powder or causing a flyrock accident. [AUDIT: State interest and suspicion were unset and have been defaulted from the category.]

nodes.name: Chill casting and directional solidification
nodes.note: Insert copper or iron plates (chills) into the mold where you want fast cooling. Fast cooling refines grain and suppresses segregation. Works only if you understand that large grains are weak and fine grains are strong. The chill must be positioned precisely or it creates stress concentrations.

nodes.name: Continuous casting and ingot casting
nodes.note: Pour molten steel into an iron mold and let it cool into an ingot, then break the mold away. Continuous casting pulls the ingot from the mold as it sets, which reduces segregation and avoids the pipe (voiding) that ruins large ingots. The trick is copper-alloy molds that resist sticking and heat cycling.

nodes.name: Converter furnace for steel
nodes.note: Blast compressed air through molten iron-carbon; exothermic oxidation of silicon and carbon raises temperature while generating heat. Brittle and rapid—if the converter tips or the air supply fails during a heat, you have a disaster of molten metal on the floor. Speed and low labour cost per ton is the payoff.

nodes.name: Cupola furnace for iron casting
nodes.note: A small tall furnace that melts scrap and pig iron for casting into sand moulds. Much hotter than an open hearth because the stack draft is strong. The problem is contamination from coke ash unless you use charcoal and then your fuel bill is punishing. Solves small-batch casting need cheaply.

nodes.name: Deep drawing and pressing dies
nodes.note: Press a flat metal sheet with a die into a deep cup shape in a single stroke. The metal must be annealed and soaped to prevent sticking and tearing. Multiple draws with annealing between are needed for very deep cups. The challenge is uniform thickness—the metal flows unevenly and thin spots tear or wrinkle. Needs precision dies and pressure control.

nodes.name: Deep shaft sinking techniques
nodes.note: Going deeper than 200 meters requires support sets (timber or steel frames), continuous pumping of inflow water, adequate ventilation at depth, and precise control of powder charges to avoid enlarding the hole. The pressure of overlying rock increases shear stress on timbering. Major collapses are common. The time to sink a shaft grows non-linearly with depth—doubling depth more than quadruples time.

nodes.name: Die casting and hot chamber casting
nodes.note: Inject molten zinc or aluminum into a hardened steel die at high speed under high pressure. Cool rapidly and eject. Produces dimensionally consistent parts at high volume. The die cost is enormous and only amortizes over thousands of parts. Porosity from trapped gas is the chronic defect—degassing the metal before injection is essential.

nodes.name: Drawn tube production
nodes.note: Anneal a tube, coat with soap as lubricant, draw it through a die on a water-powered wire draw to reduce diameter and thicken walls uniformly. Much slower than rolling but gives excellent surface finish and precise dimensions. The soaped tube must be perfectly round or it jams in the die.

nodes.name: Drop hammer for heavy forging
nodes.note: Raise a heavy hammer by water power to a fixed height and drop it. The impact force is proportional to the weight and drop height. Allows forging of massive pieces that hand hammering cannot touch. The anvil must be buried deep in earth to absorb the recoil or the whole forge building shakes apart.

nodes.name: Dry sand molding for fine castings
nodes.note: Allow the mold to dry completely and fire it in a kiln to vitrify the clay bond. Produces precise smooth castings with clean surfaces. Much slower than green sand, the kiln step adds time and fuel cost. Used for fine machine parts, gears, and weapons where surface finish matters. Defects like scabs are less common than in green sand.

nodes.name: Dynamite and modern explosives
nodes.note: Three times more powerful than black powder per unit mass and much more reliable. Nitroglycerin is unstable and prone to detonation from shock, so it is absorbed in diatomite to stabilize it. Dynamite revolutionized mining and tunneling but also killed thousands during its development. A single accident in handling or storage is catastrophic. Must be stored separately from fuses and primers. [AUDIT: State interest and suspicion were unset and have been defaulted from the category.]

nodes.name: Electro-refining for high-purity copper
nodes.note: Impure copper as the anode, pure copper cathode, in a sulfuric acid bath. Current causes impure copper to dissolve; pure copper plates out on the cathode; impurities settle as anode slime. Removes gold and silver efficiently, which is both a blessing (refining) and a problem (recovering those valuable metals from the slime takes more work). Produces 99.99 percent pure copper.

nodes.name: Electroplating and coating
nodes.note: Pass current through a solution of metal salt with the object as the cathode and a pure metal anode. Metal ions migrate to the cathode and deposit as a coating. Works only with a pure metal anode that dissolves at the same rate as plating proceeds. The deposit quality depends on current density and bath chemistry—too fast and it is rough and porous, too slow and it is slow and expensive.

nodes.name: Extrusion and the extrusion press
nodes.note: Push hot metal through a shaped die with a hydraulic press. The die mouth narrows, so the pressure rises enormously and plastic flow follows the die shape. Makes complex hollow sections impossible to roll or draw. Temperature is critical: too cold and the metal cracks, too hot and the die erodes. Each shape needs its own die, so tooling cost is high.

nodes.name: Fatigue testing and fracture mechanics
nodes.note: Cyclic loading of a specimen kills machines that passed static tests. A defect that lies dormant under steady load will grow under cyclic stress until the component fails suddenly.
